Although the clauses regarding Peshwa Baji Rao II accepting a permanent British subsidiary force of 6,000 troops, ceding territories worth 26 lakh rupees, and surrendering claims over Surat are accurate, the Treaty of Bassein (December 1802) was concluded by Lord Wellesley, not Lord Cornwallis.

Row 4 is correctly matched. Concluded under Governor-General Lord Amherst in February 1826 at the end of the First Anglo-Burmese War, the Treaty of Yandabo obligated the Burmese Court at Ava to pay a war indemnity of one crore rupees, cede Arakan and Tenasserim, renounce claims over Assam, and receive a British Resident at Ava.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 4; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 5

stem: Consider the following events related to the expansion of the Subsidiary Alliance system under Lord Wellesley:
items: 1. Conclusion of the Subsidiary Alliance with the Peshwa at Bassein
2. Acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance by the Maratha ruler of Tanjore
3. Acceptance of the Subsidiary Alliance by the Bhonsle Raja of Berar under the Treaty of Deogaon
4. Signing of the Subsidiary Treaty by the Nawab of Awadh
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above events, starting from the earliest?
core: Lord Wellesley methodically encircled the Maratha Confederacy by first bringing Hyderabad (1798), Mysore (1799), Tanjore (October 1799), and Awadh (November 1801) under the Subsidiary Alliance before exploiting internal Maratha civil strife to sign the Treaty of Bassein with the Peshwa (December 1802) and defeat Bhonsle and Scindia (December 1803).

exp.why: After being defeated by Jaswant Rao Holkar at the Battle of Hadapsar (Poona) in October 1802, Peshwa Baji Rao II fled to British protection and signed the Treaty of Bassein on 31 December 1802, entering the Subsidiary Alliance third in this sequence.

Following the fall of Mysore in mid-1799, Lord Wellesley intervened in a succession dispute in the Maratha principality of Tanjore. Raja Serfoji II signed a treaty accepting the Subsidiary Alliance and transferring the administration of Tanjore to the Company in October 1799, making it the earliest among the listed events.

During the Second Anglo-Maratha War triggered by the Treaty of Bassein, Arthur Wellesley defeated the forces of Raghuji Bhonsle II at Argaon, compelling the Bhonsle Raja of Berar to sign the Subsidiary Treaty of Deogaon on 17 December 1803, making it the last in this sequence.

Invoking the alleged threat of an Afghan invasion by Zaman Shah and the inefficiency of the Nawab's troops, Lord Wellesley coerced Nawab Saadat Ali Khan II of Awadh into signing a Subsidiary Treaty in November 1801, under which Awadh ceded Rohilkhand and the Lower Doab (nearly half its territory) to fund the expanded subsidiary force. Thus, the chronological order is 2 (Oct 1799) -> 4 (Nov 1801) -> 1 (Dec 1802) -> 3 (Dec 1803).

ref: Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 5; Grover & Mehta, A New Look at Modern Indian History, Ch. 11

stem: With reference to the economic and commercial imperatives underlying British territorial annexations in India during the first half of the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Lord Dalhousie emphasized the commercial importance of annexing Nagpur (1854) and acquiring the Assigned Districts of Berar (1853) to secure prime cotton-producing tracts for British textile mills and link the Bombay and Calcutta presidencies.

2. Beyond geopolitical rivalry on the north-western frontier, the British conquest of Sindh (1843) enabled the East India Company to plug the untaxed smuggling of Malwa opium through Karachi to Portuguese Daman and enforce its Bombay transit pass monopoly.

3. The primary commercial driver behind Charles Napier's annexation of Sindh was the immediate acquisition of indigenous wild tea-growing uplands along the lower Indus delta to break China's global tea monopoly.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Mid-nineteenth-century British annexations were heavily driven by metropolitan industrial and fiscal needs: securing central Indian raw cotton in Berar and Nagpur for Lancashire mills, and sealing the Indus-Karachi smuggling corridor in Sindh to protect the Company's lucrative Malwa opium revenue.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In his official minutes justifying the annexation of Nagpur under the Doctrine of Lapse (1854) and the Treaty of 1853 taking over the Cotton Assigned Districts of Berar from the Nizam of Hyderabad against military arrears, Lord Dalhousie explicitly stressed that these territories comprised the finest raw cotton tracts in India—essential to reduce Manchester's reliance on American slave-grown cotton—while geographically linking Bombay and Calcutta for trunk railway and telegraph lines.

Statement 2 is correct. While geopolitical panic following the First Anglo-Afghan War provided the strategic pretext for invading Sindh in 1843, economic historians note a crucial fiscal driver: indigenous merchants in Malwa were bypassing British territory by transporting Malwa opium via Pali and Hyderabad (Sindh) to the port of Karachi and onward to Portuguese Daman, evading the Company's Bombay opium monopoly. Annexing Sindh closed the Karachi route and forced all Malwa opium through Bombay under heavy British transit pass duties.

Statement 3 is incorrect. The arid alluvial plain of the lower Indus delta in Sindh had no wild tea uplands. Indigenous wild tea plants (Camellia sinensis var. assamica) were discovered by Robert Bruce in the Brahmaputra valley of Upper Assam, and the commercial rush to establish tea plantations to break China's monopoly drove the annexation of Purandar Singh's territory in Upper Assam (1838), not the conquest of Sindh.

ref: Shekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; Claude Markovits, The Global World of Indian Merchants

stem: With reference to the institutional mechanics and contemporary critiques of the Subsidiary Alliance system, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Senior Company administrators like Thomas Munro observed that the Subsidiary Alliance structurally fostered misgovernance because guaranteeing the Indian ruler against internal rebellion removed the natural political check against fiscal oppression.

2. In its fourth and final developmental stage under Lord Wellesley, the Subsidiary Alliance demanded a fixed annual cash tribute from the ally while explicitly barring the permanent cession of sovereign territory in the event of payment arrears.
3. To prevent financial maladministration, the East India Company strictly prohibited private European agency houses from lending money to Indian rulers to meet their military subsidy obligations.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Subsidiary Alliance operated as a self-reinforcing fiscal trap: insulating rulers from internal revolt eroded administrative accountability, while inflated military subsidies plunged states into usurious debt with British agency houses, ultimately supplying the pretext for territorial cessions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. In his famous 1817 minute to Governor-General Lord Hastings, Sir Thomas Munro (as well as Arthur Wellesley earlier) critiqued the Subsidiary Alliance for destroying the internal vitality of Indian states. By using British troops to protect the prince unconditionally against domestic insurrection, the system removed the fear of popular overthrow that traditionally restrained rulers from extreme fiscal extortion and misrule.

Statement 2 is incorrect. As classified by Alfred Lyall, the fourth and final stage of the Subsidiary Alliance inaugurated by Lord Wellesley (1799–1801) specifically replaced precarious annual cash subsidies—which chronically fell into arrears—with the permanent cession of sovereign territory yielding equivalent revenue in perpetuity, as implemented in the Ceded Districts of Hyderabad (1800) and the Rohilkhand-Doab districts of Awadh (1801).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Rather than strictly preventing such loans, the Company often abetted them. Most notoriously, Governor-General Lord Hastings granted a special exemption from the 1797 anti-usury statute to the British agency house William Palmer & Co. in Hyderabad, enabling them to lend vast sums to the Nizam's government at exorbitant interest rates (up to 24–25%) to pay for the British-officered Hyderabad Contingent, pushing the state into deep fiscal bankruptcy until Resident Charles Metcalfe exposed the scandal.

ref: Shekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; Michael Fisher, Indirect Rule in India

stem: With reference to the shift in British imperial policy toward the Indian Princely States following the Revolt of 1857 and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858, which one of the following statements best describes the new political framework of 'Subordinate Union'?

opts.A: The British Crown restored the pre-Wellesley diplomatic status of sovereign equality to the Princely States and relinquished the right to station British Residents in their capitals.
opts.B: While the Doctrine of Lapse was formally abandoned, the Adoption Sanads issued by Lord Canning recognized the right of adoption only for Hindu rulers and continued the policy of annexing states in cases of disputed succession.
opts.C: Territorial annexation was abandoned and the right of princely rulers to adopt heirs was guaranteed through Adoption Sanads, yet the states were completely subordinated to the British Crown's paramountcy, which retained the power to recognize successions and depose rulers for misgovernance without annexing the state.
opts.D: The Princely States were exempted from British intervention in their internal administration and succession disputes in exchange for transferring the direct collection of their land revenue to the Viceroy's Executive Council.

core: After 1857, British policy shifted from the 'Subordinate Isolation' and rapid annexations of Dalhousie to 'Subordinate Union': preserving princely rulers as conservative 'breakwaters in the storm' by abandoning annexation via Adoption Sanads, while simultaneously asserting unlimited Crown Paramountcy over successions and internal administration.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct. Recognizing that loyal Indian princes (such as Scindia, Holkar, the Nizam, and the Phulkian states) had acted as 'breakwaters in the storm' during the Revolt of 1857, Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 renounced further territorial extension. Viceroy Lord Canning issued over 140 'Adoption Sanads' (1860) to both Hindu and Muslim rulers guaranteeing their right to adopt heirs according to their respective religious laws. However, this abandonment of annexation came with a tighter assertion of Crown Paramountcy ('Subordinate Union'): Indian rulers held their thrones not as sovereign equals, but as feudatories whose succession required formal recognition by the Paramount Power, which now punished misrule by deposing the individual ruler (as in Baroda in 1875) and installing another family member rather than annexing the state. Option (A) is incorrect because sovereign equality was permanently extinguished and Residents gained even greater intrusive authority. Option (B) is incorrect because Adoption Sanads were granted to both Hindu and Muslim princes and annexation for disputed succession ceased. Option (D) is incorrect because the British interfered heavily in internal administration while leaving local land revenue collection to the princely durbars.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 3; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 27

stem: Consider the following institutional milestones in the evolution of early colonial land revenue administration in Bengal:
items: 1. Appointment of the Amini Commission by Warren Hastings to investigate land revenue resources and Zamindari accounts
2. Introduction of the Quinquennial (Five-Yearly Izaredari) Settlement by the Committee of Circuit
3. Promulgation of the Decennial Settlement across Bengal and Bihar under Lord Cornwallis
4. Statutory directive under Pitt's India Act instructing the Company to frame permanent rules for land revenue collection from Rajas and Zamindars
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the above events from the earliest to the latest?
core: Between the abolition of the Dual System in 1772 and the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the East India Company moved from speculative revenue farming to statutory fixation of Zamindari tenures. The Committee of Circuit's Quinquennial Settlement (1772–1777) was followed by the Amini Commission inquiry (appointed 1776, report 1778) and Annual Settlements (1777–1789), while Pitt's India Act (1784) mandated permanent rules that culminated in Cornwallis's Decennial Settlement (1789–1790).

exp.why: In November 1776, ahead of the expiry of the five-year farming leases in 1777, Warren Hastings appointed the Amini Commission (which submitted its report in March 1778)—the first technical revenue commission in British India—to compile empirical data on land tenures and Zamindari accounts as the Company reverted to Annual Settlements.

In 1772, Warren Hastings ended the Dual System, assumed direct Diwani administration, and through the Committee of Circuit introduced the Quinquennial (Five-Yearly) Izaredari Settlement (1772–1777), auctioning revenue collection rights to the highest bidders.

Acting on the instructions of the Court of Directors following Pitt's India Act, Lord Cornwallis promulgated the Decennial (Ten-Yearly) Settlement with the Zamindars of Bengal and Bihar in 1789–1790, which was subsequently declared permanent in March 1793.

Chronological Anchor (1784): Section 39 of Pitt's India Act of 1784 directed the East India Company to inquire into the grievances of displaced landholders and establish permanent rules for the collection of tribute, rents, and services from Rajas, Zamindars, and Talukdars—laying the statutory foundation for Cornwallis's reforms.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; B.R. Grover, Land Rights and Revenue Administration in British India

stem: With reference to the ideological and policy debates among East India Company officials preceding the enactment of the Permanent Settlement of 1793, consider the following statements:
items: 1. James Grant contended that the Zamindars were the hereditary proprietors of the soil, whereas John Shore maintained that the State was the sole owner of all land and Zamindars were merely removable tax-collecting officials.

2. While agreeing that revenue settlements should be concluded with the Zamindars as proprietors, John Shore opposed declaring the revenue assessment permanent immediately and advocated an initial ten-year trial period.

3. Lord Cornwallis overruled the plea for a provisional assessment on the conviction that only an irrevocable, permanently fixed revenue demand would incentivize Zamindars to invest capital in agricultural improvement.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Permanent Settlement emerged from a protracted tripartite debate (1786–1790) among James Grant, Sir John Shore, and Lord Cornwallis over the nature of pre-colonial property rights and fiscal expediency. While Grant viewed the sovereign state as the sole landowner and Zamindars as mere tax officials, both Shore and Cornwallis recognized Zamindari proprietorship, diverging only on whether the assessment should be fixed in perpetuity immediately or after a ten-year empirical trial.

exp.why: The ideological positions of James Grant and John Shore are swapped. In his 'Historical and Comparative Analysis of the Finances of Bengal' (1786), James Grant (Chief Sheristadar) argued that under Mughal law the State was the sole proprietor of the soil and Zamindars were merely removable state officials (sanad-holders) collecting revenue. Conversely, Sir John Shore in his Minute of June 1789 argued that Zamindars possessed hereditary proprietary rights over the land.

Although John Shore strongly defended the proprietary claim of the Zamindars, he argued that the Company lacked accurate survey data on estate boundaries, wasteland extent, and actual rent rolls. He therefore advocated a provisional Decennial (10-year) Settlement so the administration could assess true agrarian capacity before freezing the demand.

Influenced by Whig notions of landed property and Physiocratic doctrine, Lord Cornwallis argued in his Minutes of September 1789 and February 1790 that a temporary ten-year lease would deter capital investment and encourage concealed cultivation. Backed by Prime Minister William Pitt and Henry Dundas, he declared the Decennial Settlement permanent via Regulation I of 1793.

ref: Ranajit Guha, A Rule of Property for Bengal; Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 5

stem: With reference to the structural provisions of the Permanent Settlement of 1793 in Bengal and Bihar, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The land revenue demand of the State was fixed in perpetuity at ten-elevenths of the rental assessed on the estate at that time, leaving one-eleventh as the Zamindar's share.
2. The settlement was implemented without conducting a detailed cadastral survey of field boundaries, village holdings, or soil fertility.

3. Uncultivated wastelands and pastures located within the boundaries of a Zamindari estate were retained by the Company as Crown property, to be assessed for additional revenue whenever reclaimed for cultivation.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Regulation I of 1793, the East India Company sacrificed all future fiscal claims to expanding agrarian output in exchange for an assured, punctually paid lump-sum revenue (10/11ths of the 1790 assessed rental). Crucially, because estates were settled in lump sum without a cadastral survey, all uncultivated wasteland within Zamindari boundaries passed rent-free to the Zamindars, enabling them to appropriate 100% of future reclamation rents.

exp.why: Under the Permanent Settlement, the Company fixed the state demand at 10/11ths (approx. 89–90%) of the gross rental calculated on the basis of past collections, leaving 1/11th (approx. 10–11%) to the Zamindar for his trouble and responsibility, along with the right to retain any future increase in rental income.

Unlike the later Ryotwari and revised Mahalwari settlements, the Permanent Settlement of 1793 was enacted without any field-to-field cadastral survey, measurement of cultivated area, or classification of soil fertility; assessments were based on rough historical accounts and past collections.

Uncultivated wastelands, forests, and pastures situated within the limits of a Zamindari estate were NOT retained as Crown property for separate future taxation. Instead, they were handed over to the Zamindars as part of their proprietary estate completely free of additional revenue assessment, directly fueling massive rent expansion for Zamindars as demographic growth brought wasteland under the plough in the 19th century.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Colonialism and the Countryside); Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the working of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal:
items: Statement-I: Within the first two decades of the introduction of the Permanent Settlement in 1793, nearly half of the Zamindari estates in Bengal were put up for public auction under the Sunset Law.
Statement-II: The vast majority of these auctioned estates were purchased by British plantation companies and newly emerging urban industrial capitalists who displaced the indigenous rural gentry.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While the rigid Sunset Law (Regulation XIV of 1793) and a high initial pitch of assessment triggered massive auction sales of great Zamindaris like Rajshahi, Nadia, and Dinajpur between 1794 and 1815, this did not signify a takeover by British plantation companies or industrial capitalists. Instead, agrarian historians have demonstrated that the vast majority of sales involved fictitious (benami) purchases by the defaulting Zamindars' own relatives and agents, or transfers among existing Zamindari families and their former revenue officials (amlahs).

exp.why: Under the Sunset Law, if the fixed revenue installment was not paid by sunset of the stipulated date, the Zamindari (or a portion of it) was mandatorily attached and auctioned. Because the initial assessment of 1793 was pitched very high amidst depressed agricultural prices in the 1790s, and because Regulation VII of 1799 (Haftam) had not yet armed Zamindars with summary coercive powers over ryots, between one-third and one-half of Bengal's landed estates changed hands at auction within two decades.

The buyers at these revenue auctions were NOT British plantation companies (Europeans were in fact restricted from holding vast interior lands prior to the Charter Act of 1833) or urban industrial capitalists. As research by Sirajul Islam and Ratnalekha Ray shows, over 75% of the auctioned estates were bought either through fictitious (benami) bids arranged by the defaulting Zamindars themselves using their servants, relatives, and officials (amlahs) to evade revenue arrears, or by neighboring Zamindars and rural courtiers.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10; Ratnalekha Ray, Change in Bengal Agrarian Society

stem: In the context of the agrarian structure of nineteenth-century Bengal, what was the primary institutional significance of the 'Patni Taluk Regulation' (Regulation VIII of 1819)?

opts.A: It conferred heritable occupancy rights directly upon the actual tillers of the soil, shielding them from arbitrary eviction and rent enhancement by the Zamindars.
opts.B: It legalized a hierarchy of perpetual, heritable, and transferable intermediary tenures with fixed rents beneath the Zamindar, replicating the mechanism of the Sunset Law for summary auction of defaulting tenures.
opts.C: It abolished the intermediary rent-collecting rights of traditional Talukdars and brought village communities under direct periodic revenue assessment by District Collectors.
opts.D: It empowered the East India Company to resume and assess rent-free religious and charitable land grants (Lakhiraj lands) held by indigenous magnates.

core: Pioneered by the Maharaja of Burdwan to insulate his vast estate from the Sunset Law and formally legalized by Regulation VIII of 1819, the Patni system institutionalized multi-tiered sub-infeudation in Bengal. It enabled a Zamindar to carve his estate into perpetual, heritable, and transferable leaseholds (Patni tenures) at a permanently fixed rent, which Patnidars further sub-leased to Dar-patnidars and Se-patnidars, while granting the Zamindar the right to hold semi-annual summary auctions of defaulting Patni tenures.

exp.why: Option B is correct: Faced with the rigors of the Sunset Law, Tejchand, the Raja of Burdwan, devised the Patni tenure—essentially a miniature Permanent Settlement within the Zamindari. Regulation VIII of 1819 (the Patni Taluk Regulation) gave statutory recognition to these perpetual, heritable, and transferable intermediary tenures, explicitly legalizing further sub-infeudation (Dar-patni, Se-patni) and empowering the superior Zamindar to petition the Collector twice a year for summary public auction of a Patni tenure if the Patnidar defaulted on rent. Option A is incorrect because occupancy rights for ryots were first defined forty years later under the Bengal Rent Act (Act X of 1859) and the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885. Option C describes the anti-taluqdari Mahalwari policy in the North-Western Provinces. Option D refers to the Resumption Regulation (Regulation II of 1819) concerning Lakhiraj (rent-free) lands.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10

stem: With reference to the rise and socio-economic position of the 'Jotedars' in North Bengal during the early nineteenth century (as documented in Francis Buchanan-Hamilton's survey of Dinajpur), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the Zamindars who resided in rural villages, the Jotedars were predominantly urban-based salaried officials appointed by the East India Company to audit estate collections.

2. A substantial portion of the extensive lands acquired by the Jotedars was cultivated through sharecroppers (Adhiyars or Bargadars), who brought their own ploughs and handed over half the produce after the harvest.

3. Because they simultaneously controlled local village trade and moneylending, the Jotedars exercised more direct authority over the village peasantry than absentee Zamindars and frequently mobilized ryots to delay rent payments.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: As highlighted by Francis Buchanan-Hamilton's survey of Dinajpur and analyzed by Ratnalekha Ray, the Jotedars (also known as Haoladars, Gantidars, or Mandals) were a powerful stratum of resident rich peasants in North Bengal. While many great Zamindars were urban-based absentees living in Calcutta, the Jotedars lived directly in the villages, controlled local grain trade, rural credit, and sharecroppers (Adhiyars/Bargadars), and frequently obstructed the Zamindars' officials (amlahs) to purchase auctioned estates themselves.

exp.why: Statement 1 inverts the residence pattern and conflates Jotedars with Company officials or Zamindari amlahs. In reality, many big Zamindars were urban-based absentees residing in Calcutta or district towns, whereas the Jotedars were rich peasants who lived directly within the villages. They were independent tenure-holders/landholders, not salaried Company officials.

By the early nineteenth century, Jotedars in North Bengal had acquired vast tracts of land—sometimes running into several thousand acres. Rather than cultivating all of it with hired wage labor, they had a large portion cultivated by sharecroppers known as Adhiyars or Bargadars, who supplied their own ploughs and bullocks, labored in the fields, and surrendered half (adh) of the harvested crop to the Jotedar.

Located within the village and combining landholding with moneylending (advancing grain and cash loans to poor cultivators) and local commerce, Jotedars wielded immense direct power over poor villagers. They fiercely resisted attempts by Zamindars to enhance the jama (rent roll) of the village, prevented Zamindari amlahs from executing attachments, incited dependent ryots to delay revenue payments, and often bought up the Zamindar's estate when it was auctioned under the Sunset Law.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Section 1.4: The Rise of the Jotedars)

stem: With reference to the agrarian regulations enacted by the East India Company in the Bengal Presidency following the Permanent Settlement of 1793, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Regulation VII of 1799 (Qanun-i-Haftam) was enacted in response to widespread Zamindari defaults under the Sunset Law, aiming to secure the punctual inflow of Company revenue during Lord Wellesley's administration.

2. Under Regulation VII of 1799, a Zamindar was legally required to obtain a prior summary decree from the District Diwani Adalat before distraining a defaulting ryot's standing crops or personal property.

3. Regulation V of 1812 (Qanun-i-Panjam) modified the 1799 framework by requiring Zamindars to serve a written demand on the tenant prior to distraint and exempting plough cattle and agricultural implements from attachment.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Permanent Settlement of 1793 initially subjected Zamindars to the rigid Sunset Law without corresponding coercive powers over tenants, Regulation VII of 1799 (Haftam) armed Zamindars with sweeping extrajudicial powers of distraint and arrest to safeguard the Company's wartime revenue needs. Regulation V of 1812 (Panjam) later softened the procedural excesses of Haftam without dismantling the landlord's core power of extrajudicial distraint.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Between 1793 and 1798, numerous large Zamindaris in Bengal faced auction under the Sunset Law. Zamindars complained that while the state demanded punctual payment from them, the cumbersome judicial procedures under the 1793 Cornwallis Code prevented them from recovering rent swiftly from recalcitrant ryots and intermediate tenure-holders. Facing urgent fiscal pressures during the Mysore wars, Lord Wellesley's government enacted Regulation VII of 1799 (popularly called Qanun-i-Haftam) to tilt the legal balance decisively in favour of the Zamindars.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The defining feature of Regulation VII of 1799 (Haftam) was that it empowered Zamindars to distrain (seize and sell) a defaulting ryot's standing crops, cattle, and personal property directly and even compel the ryot's personal attendance without any prior reference to or decree from the District Diwani Adalat or police authorities. Instead, the aggrieved peasant bore the nearly impossible burden of approaching the civil court afterward to challenge an wrongful distraint.

Statement 3 is correct. Recognising that the unchecked coercive powers of Haftam were causing severe rural oppression, the colonial administration enacted Regulation V of 1812 (Qanun-i-Panjam). It withdrew the Zamindar's power to arrest or compel the personal attendance of ryots, mandated the service of a written notice of demand prior to attachment, and exempted plough cattle and agricultural implements from seizure, although extrajudicial distraint of crops remained intact until the Bengal Rent Act X of 1859.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 5

stem: In the context of the administrative and economic history of British India, which of the following best describes the historical significance of the 'Fifth Report' of 1813?

opts.A: It was drafted by Lord Cornwallis's Governor-General-in-Council to persuade the British Parliament to extend the Bengal Permanent Settlement uniformly across the Madras and Bombay Presidencies.
opts.B: It was the foundational report of the First Law Commission that recommended replacing the Sunset Law with statutory occupancy rights for Bengal ryots.
opts.C: It was a royal commission inquiry appointed after the Santhal Rebellion to demarcate the Damin-i-Koh and prohibit Zamindari moneylending in tribal tracts.
opts.D: Submitted by a Select Committee of the British Parliament during debates over the renewal of the East India Company's Charter, it documented the breakdown of traditional Zamindar estates in Bengal and reinforced official opposition to extending the Permanent Settlement to newly conquered territories.

core: The Fifth Report (1813), authored primarily by Samuel Davis and C. Grant for a Select Committee of the British House of Commons, provided an exhaustive parliamentary indictment of the administrative and revenue workings of the East India Company in Bengal and Madras. By exposing the mass auctioning of traditional Zamindaris, widespread sub-infeudation, and the loss of state revenue elasticity in Bengal, it decisively shifted British policy toward the Ryotwari model in Madras.

exp.why: Option D is correct. The Fifth Report was submitted to the British Parliament in 1813 by the Select Committee appointed to inquire into the affairs of the East India Company on the eve of the Charter Act of 1813. Spanning over a thousand pages of petitions, collector reports, and statistical appendices, it highlighted how the Permanent Settlement had triggered the ruin and auction of established Zamindari houses in Bengal while depriving the colonial state of any share in rising agricultural revenues. Far from advocating the extension of the Bengal system (making Option A a causal reversal), the Fifth Report bolstered the arguments of Thomas Munro and the Court of Directors in favour of implementing the Ryotwari settlement in the Madras Presidency. Option B is incorrect because the First Law Commission was established much later under the Charter Act of 1833 (and occupancy rights came via the Rent Act of 1859). Option C is incorrect because the Santhal Rebellion occurred in 1855-56.

ref: NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III, Theme 10 (Colonialism and the Countryside); Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the geographical reach and administrative implementation of the Permanent Settlement in British India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Outside the administrative provinces of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, the Permanent Settlement was not implemented in any territory of the Madras Presidency or the North-Western Provinces.
2. The extension of the Permanent Settlement to the Banaras division in 1795 was carried out by Robert Merttins Bird as an early component of the Mahalwari regulations.

3. In the Northern Sarkars of the Madras Presidency, the colonial administration bypassed the indigenous chieftains and rajas altogether to settle the permanent revenue demand directly with village communities.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although primarily associated with Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa (1793), the Permanent Settlement covered roughly 19% of British India because it was also extended to the Banaras division (1795), the Northern Sarkars, parts of Karnatak/Chingleput in the Madras Presidency (1802-1805), and parts of North-Western Assam (Goalpara/Sylhet). In Northern Madras, ancient Zamindars, poligars, and newly auctioned mootahdars were vested with landlord rights modeled on Bengal.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. While Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa formed the core of the Permanent Settlement enacted in 1793, the system was legally extended to several other regions: the Banaras division (later part of the North-Western Provinces/United Provinces) in 1795, and the Northern Sarkars as well as parts of Karnatak and the Jagir (Chingleput) district in the Madras Presidency under the Madras Permanent Settlement Regulation XXV of 1802.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The Permanent Settlement in the Banaras division in 1795 was introduced by Jonathan Duncan (the British Resident at Banaras) under the direction of Lord Cornwallis and Sir John Shore. Robert Merttins Bird was associated with the Mahalwari settlement in the North-Western Provinces nearly four decades later under Regulation IX of 1833.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under Lord Wellesley's directives between 1802 and 1805, the Madras administration applied the Permanent Settlement to the Northern Sarkars specifically because that region possessed a well-entrenched class of indigenous hereditary chieftains, rajas, and ancient Zamindars. Far from bypassing them to settle with village communities, the Company recognized these ancient Zamindars—alongside purchasers of newly parcelled estates called mootahs—as proprietary landlords on the Bengal model.

ref: B.R. Grover & Grover, A New Look at Modern Indian History; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideological foundations of British land revenue policy in the early nineteenth century:
items: Statement-I: From the late 1810s onwards, British revenue policymakers at East India House increasingly rejected the extension of the Bengal-style Permanent Settlement and favoured direct Ryotwari settlements with periodic revenue revisions.

Statement-II: Influenced by David Ricardo's Law of Rent and Utilitarian political economy, theorists like James Mill argued that agricultural rent constituted an unearned surplus which the colonial state should capture directly as the supreme landlord rather than surrendering it permanently to parasitic intermediaries.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While early advocates of the Ryotwari system like Thomas Munro drew upon Scottish Enlightenment paternalism to preserve indigenous peasant society, its decisive triumph in London after 1818 was driven by Utilitarian doctrine and David Ricardo's Law of Rent (1817). Examiner of India Correspondence James Mill used Ricardian rent theory to argue that fixing revenue permanently with Zamindars forfeited the state's rightful claim to the 'net produce' or unearned increment of the soil.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. By the late 1810s, both the Court of Directors and the Board of Control in London had turned firmly against extending Cornwallis's 1793 Permanent Settlement to newly conquered territories in Madras, Bombay, and the Ceded and Conquered Provinces. Instead, they mandated direct settlements with cultivators (Ryotwari) or village bodies (Mahalwari) coupled with temporary, periodically revisable assessments so the colonial state could capture rising land values.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. David Ricardo formulated his Law of Rent in 1817 (long after Cornwallis's 1793 settlement), defining rent as the differential surplus left after deducting the cost of cultivation and normal wages/profits on marginal land. Because this surplus rose purely due to population growth and cultivation of inferior soils without any productive effort by landlords, Utilitarians like James Mill (appointed to East India House in 1819) contended that taxing the entire economic rent directly from the cultivator was the sole scientifically sound revenue policy,as it maximized state revenue without distorting production incentives.

ref: Eric Stokes, The English Utilitarians and India; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3

stem: With reference to the evolution of the Ryotwari system in the Madras Presidency, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Following the Treaty of Seringapatam (1792), Captain Alexander Read and Thomas Munro conducted the earliest institutional experiment with the Ryotwari settlement in the Baramahal district.

2. Once introduced in Baramahal in 1792, the Ryotwari arrangement was continuously and uninterruptedly applied across all districts of the Madras Presidency without any interim experiments with Zamindari or village-lease settlements.
3. Thomas Munro advocated the Ryotwari model on the ground that South India historically lacked a large class of hereditary landed aristocrats comparable to the big Zamindars of Bengal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Ryotwari system did not enjoy a linear, uninterrupted rise in Madras after the 1792 Baramahal experiment. Between 1801 and 1818, the Madras Board of Revenue experimented first with Mootahdari (Zamindari) settlements and subsequently with triennial and decennial village leases (Mirasi/Mouzewar) before Thomas Munro returned as Governor of Madras in 1820 to establish Ryotwari as the general settlement of the Presidency.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. After Tipu Sultan ceded the Baramahal (Salem) tract to the British under the Treaty of Seringapatam in 1792, Lord Cornwallis entrusted its administration to Captain Alexander Read and his assistants, notably Thomas Munro. Between 1792 and 1799, they surveyed the fields and settled revenue directly with individual cultivators, laying the operational blueprint for the Ryotwari system.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The expansion of Ryotwari in Madras was neither continuous nor uninterrupted. Under pressure from Lord Wellesley in 1799-1802, the Madras government initially introduced a Permanent Zamindari (Mootahdari) settlement in the Northern Sarkars, Jagir, and even parts of Baramahal. Later, after Munro departed for Britain in 1807, the Madras Board of Revenue (led by Hodgson) abandoned Ryotwari in most districts in favour of triennial and decennial village leases (1808-1818) settled with village headmen or mirasidars. Only after the Court of Directors intervened and appointed Munro as Governor of Madras in 1820 was Ryotwari instituted as the general system across the non-permanently settled districts of the Presidency.

Statement 3 is correct. Munro and Read argued that outside the hill tracts and Northern Sarkars, the agrarian structure of southern India had historically involved direct revenue collection by indigenous rulers from peasant cultivators through village officials, with no counterpart to the vast territorial Zamindars of Bengal. Creating artificial landlords via auctioned mootahs, Munro argued, violated indigenous custom and alienated the peasantry.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India, Ch. 2

stem: With reference to the legal and operational features of the Ryotwari settlement during British rule in India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Because the settlement was made directly with the individual cultivator (ryot), the colonial state relinquished its claim to the ownership of uncultivated wasteland and classified the levy strictly as an income tax rather than rent.
2. Each registered ryot was issued a patta recognizing his heritable and transferable right of occupancy, subject to the punctual payment of the assessed revenue.

3. Unlike the permanently fixed demand of the 1793 Bengal settlement, the revenue assessment under the Ryotwari system was temporary and subject to periodic revision, generally every twenty to thirty years.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Ryotwari system, the colonial state positioned itself as the supreme landlord (sole proprietor of the soil), retaining exclusive ownership over uncultivated wastelands and treating the cultivator's payment as economic rent rather than a tax. While the ryot received a heritable and transferable occupancy title via a patta, the state replaced many smaller landlords with one giant sovereign landlord whose demand was periodically revised upward.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Under the Ryotwari system, the colonial state explicitly asserted that the sovereign was the supreme landlord and ultimate proprietor of the soil. Consequently, the state retained full proprietary ownership over all uncultivated wastelands, grazing commons, and forests (releasing wasteland only when a cultivator agreed to pay assessment on it), and British revenue theorists explicitly classified the Ryotwari demand as land rent paid to the state-landlord rather than an agricultural income tax.

Statement 2 is correct. Under the Ryotwari mechanism, the state entered into an annual engagement with each registered cultivator (pattadar), issuing a patta (title deed) in exchange for a muchalka (agreement to pay). So long as the ryot paid the assessed land revenue on time, he could not be evicted and enjoyed the right to sell, mortgage, lease, or bequeath his holding, alongside the theoretical right to relinquish plots he no longer wished to cultivate.

Statement 3 is correct. A foundational distinction between the Permanent Settlement and the Ryotwari system was that the Ryotwari assessment was temporary. Following the Wingate-Goldsmid survey in Bombay (1835-36) and the Madras revenue survey reforms of the 1850s, revenue rates were systematically revised at intervals of 20 to 30 years to absorb increases in agricultural prices and land values.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 5; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part III

stem: With reference to the evolution of the Ryotwari settlement in the Bombay Deccan during the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Influenced by Utilitarian and Ricardian rent theories, early colonial revenue planners in Bombay sought to capture the unearned 'economic rent' directly from the cultivator rather than sharing it with hereditary Deshmukhs and Deshpandes.

2. While R.K. Pringle's early Indapur survey (1824–28) relied on pragmatic soil classification and historical rent-paying capacity, the subsequent Goldsmid–Wingate Revised Survey System (1835–36) replaced it with a rigid theoretical calculation of 'net produce' per acre.

3. Under the Bombay Survey System codified by the Joint Report of 1847, revenue rates were fixed in perpetuity for each demarcated field so long as the registered occupant did not alienate the land to a non-agriculturist.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: In the Bombay Deccan, R.K. Pringle's failed 1824–28 survey attempted a rigid Ricardian calculation of 'net produce' per acre (fixing demand at 55% of net produce), whereas the Goldsmid–Wingate Revised Survey System (1835–36) abandoned theoretical net-produce calculations in favour of pragmatic soil classification and 30-year periodic settlements.

exp.why: Following the conquest of the Peshwa's territories in 1818, Bombay administrators led by disciples of James Mill and David Ricardo argued that the state was the supreme landlord entitled to absorb the 'economic rent' (unearned surplus) directly from the ryots, bypassing hereditary district officers like Deshmukhs and Deshpandes.

This statement swaps the two systems. It was R.K. Pringle (1824–28) who attempted an abstract Ricardian calculation of gross and 'net produce' for every field, resulting in severe over-assessment and agrarian desertion. Conversely, H.E. Goldsmid and Lieutenant George Wingate (1835–36) abandoned theoretical net-produce calculations and introduced a pragmatic geological soil classification combined with moderated aggregate district demands based on past fiscal history.

Under the Joint Report of 1847 (framed by Goldsmid, Wingate, and Davidson), assessments under the Bombay Survey System were not fixed in perpetuity; they were periodic settlements revised every 30 years. Furthermore, the ryot's occupancy right was made freely heritable and transferable (including to moneylenders) subject only to the continued payment of the state's revenue assessment.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Eric Stokes, The English Utilitarians and India

stem: With reference to the persistence of privileged land tenures within the Ryotwari presidencies of colonial India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the wet-land river valleys of the Madras Presidency, hereditary Mirasidars retained control over large landholdings by securing Ryotwari pattas and getting the fields cultivated by untouchable bonded labourers (Pannaiyals) and sharecroppers.

2. In the Konkan region of the Bombay Presidency, the colonial state accommodated the Khoti tenure, under which hereditary Khots functioned as village-level revenue collectors and landlords over subordinate tenants.

3. Far from converting all actual tillers into direct proprietors, the conferral of Ryotwari pattas frequently reinforced pre-existing caste hierarchies by denying land titles to depressed-caste agricultural labourers.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the Ryotwari system theoretically eliminated intermediaries between the state and the cultivator, in practice it accommodated powerful pre-colonial village elites—such as Mirasidars in Madras and Khots in the Bombay Konkan—who became registered pattadars or revenue farmers over landless untouchable labourers and sub-tenants.

exp.why: In fertile irrigated districts of Madras like Tanjore and Chingleput, pre-colonial Mirasidars (predominantly upper-caste Brahmins and Vellalas) held hereditary coparcenary shares in village lands. Under Ryotwari, they were recognised as the registered pattadars, while the actual physical cultivation continued to be performed by untouchable farm-servants (Pannaiyals/Padiyals) and tenants (Payakaris/Ulkudis).

In the Ratnagiri and Konkan districts of the Bombay Presidency, the British preserved the indigenous Khoti system (later regulated under the Khoti Settlement Act of 1880), where hereditary Khots collected revenue from privileged occupants (Dharekaris) and extracted high produce rents and unpaid labour (veth) from tenants-at-will (Ardhelis).

Because colonial revenue officials equated the 'ryot' with the traditional tax-paying village elite rather than the physical tiller of the soil, traditional ritual and customary bans preventing Dalit/Pariah agricultural labourers from owning land remained intact for much of the nineteenth century.

ref: Dharma Kumar, Land and Caste in South India; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the colonial revenue administration in South India:
items: Statement-I: The Madras Torture Commission (1855) documented the systemic use of physical coercion and corporal torture by native revenue officials across the Madras Presidency to realise state land revenue demands.

Statement-II: Prior to the administrative reforms of the late 1850s, the Ryotwari system in Madras combined excessively high, unsurveyed revenue assessments with the concentration of police, magisterial, and revenue-collecting powers in the same executive officials.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Madras Torture Commission Report (1855) exposed that state revenue collection under the Madras Ryotwari system relied heavily on physical torture because exorbitant, unscientific revenue demands were enforced by Tahsildars and Amildars who simultaneously wielded both revenue and police/magisterial powers.

exp.why: Appointed in 1854 (submitting its report in 1855), the three-member Madras Torture Commission confirmed that physical coercion—such as using the kittee (hand-press) and anundal (tying a ryot in a bent posture under the sun)—was routinely practised by state revenue subordinates to extract land tax arrears from Ryotwari peasants, not merely by autonomous Zamindars.

Statement-II directly explains why such coercion was pervasive: under Thomas Munro's 1816 regulations, native revenue officers (Tahsildars) had been vested with police and magisterial functions alongside revenue collection. Faced with oppressive, unsurveyed revenue targets and no independent police check, officials resorted to illegal physical compulsion, prompting the Commission to recommend separating police from revenue functions and launching a scientific survey in 1855–1864.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Report of the Commissioners for the Investigation of Alleged Cases of Torture in the Madras Presidency (1855)

stem: With reference to the Madras Ryotwari reforms of 1864 and their agrarian consequences, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The reformed settlement guidelines of 1864 fixed the state's revenue demand ceiling at half of the net produce of the land for a duration of thirty years.

2. Even without the creation of a statutory class of Zamindars, the legal recognition of the Ryotwari patta as a transferable property right facilitated the growth of rent-receiving landlordism and unprotected tenancy.

3. Under the revenue regulations governing the Madras Presidency after 1864, a registered pattadar who sub-let his land to a sharecropper instead of cultivating it personally forfeited his occupancy title to the state.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Although the 1864 Madras Ryotwari reforms moderated theoretical state demand to 50% of net produce for 30 years, the free transferability of pattas and the complete legality of sub-letting enabled moneylenders and rich peasants to become rent-extracting landlords over unprotected sub-tenants.

exp.why: Following the 1855 survey and settlement proclamation, the Madras Presidency codified in 1864 that the state revenue assessment would be limited to 50% of the calculated 'net produce' (gross produce minus estimated cultivation costs) and fixed for 30-year intervals.

Because Ryotwari pattas could be mortgaged and sold for debt recovery, land increasingly passed into the hands of urban and rural moneylenders (Chettiars, Sahukars) and wealthy substantial peasants, who leased the land back to the original cultivators as tenants-at-will without the need for any formal Zamindari statute.

There was no legal requirement under Madras Ryotwari law that a registered pattadar must physically cultivate the soil himself. So long as the pattadar paid the stipulated state land revenue, he had the unrestricted right to sub-lease his land to sharecroppers or tenants-at-will at unregulated market rents, with zero forfeiture of title.

ref: Bipan Chandra, Rise and Growth of Economic Nationalism in India; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the introduction of the Mahalwari system in Northern India:
items: Statement-I: Regulation VII of 1822, which translated Holt Mackenzie's Minute of 1819 into law in the Ceded and Conquered Provinces, broke down administratively within a decade of its enactment.

Statement-II: The regulation dispensed with field-level surveys and records of custom, leaving the assessment of the state's revenue share to the unverified discretion of hereditary Taluqdars at a ceiling of one-third of the rental value.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Regulation VII of 1822 (based on Holt Mackenzie's 1819 Minute) failed not because it lacked surveys, but for the exact opposite reason: it mandated an impossibly complex field-by-field inquiry into agricultural yields, soils, and customary caste rights while fixing an oppressive state demand of 80% of the rental value.

exp.why: Holt Mackenzie's famous Minute of 1819 highlighted the existence of cohesive village communities in Northern India and led to Regulation VII of 1822. However, the administrative machinery proved completely unable to complete the settlements, and the system collapsed by the late 1820s.

Statement-II inverts the actual provisions of Regulation VII of 1822. Far from dispensing with surveys or relying on Taluqdars at a one-third rate, Regulation VII of 1822 required settlement officers to conduct an impossibly detailed, microscopic survey of every field's soil quality, gross yield, cultivation cost, and complex village tenurial customs, while pitching the state revenue demand at an exorbitant 80% (83% in some cases) of the rental value.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Imtiaz Husain, Land Revenue Policy in North India

stem: With reference to the overhaul of the Mahalwari system in the North-Western Provinces during the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The reduction of the state's revenue demand to 66% of the rental value and the standardisation of a 30-year settlement period were first introduced under Lord Cornwallis's Banaras Settlement Regulations of 1795.

2. Regulation IX of 1833, implemented under the supervision of Robert Merttins Bird, simplified the settlement process by estimating the aggregate rental value of an entire mahal rather than calculating the net produce of every individual cultivator's field.
3. James Thomason's administrative guidelines systematically curtailed the claims of superior Taluqdars in the North-Western Provinces in favour of direct settlements with village proprietary bodies.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under Governor-General William Bentinck's Regulation IX of 1833, Robert Merttins Bird (later aided by James Thomason) rescued the Mahalwari system by reducing the state demand from 80% to 66% of rental value for 30 years, assessing the aggregate rent of the mahal as a whole, and bypassing superior Taluqdars in favour of village coparcenary brotherhoods.

exp.why: Lord Cornwallis's Banaras Regulations of 1795 extended the Permanent Settlement (Zamindari) to Banaras, not the 30-year Mahalwari framework. It was Governor-General Lord William Bentinck's Regulation IX of 1833—executed by Robert Merttins Bird—that lowered the Mahalwari state demand from 80% to 66% of the rental value and fixed the settlement duration at 30 years (later reduced further to 50% under Lord Dalhousie's Saharanpur Rules of 1855).

Known as the 'Father of Land Settlements in Northern India', Robert Merttins Bird under Regulation IX of 1833 discarded the unworkable 1822 rule of calculating net produce for every field. Instead, soils were broadly classified, the total rental value of a fiscal estate (mahal) was estimated as an aggregate, and the village community apportioned the demand internally using a village map (shajra) and field register (khasra).

James Thomason (Lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces, 1843–53), who authored the famous Directions for Settlement Officers (1849), consistently sought to set aside parasitical Taluqdars (often compensating them only with a modest malikana allowance) and vest proprietary rights directly in village pattidari and bhaichara coparcenary communities.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Thomas R. Metcalf, The Aftermath of Revolt

stem: In the context of British land revenue administration in nineteenth-century northern India, the 'Saharanpur Rules of 1855' issued during the tenure of Lord Dalhousie were promulgated primarily to:

opts.A: reduce the State's Mahalwari revenue demand in the North-Western Provinces from 66 percent (two-thirds) to 50 percent (one-half) of the net rental assets.
opts.B: levy a compulsory differential water-cess on estates irrigated by the newly constructed Upper Ganga Canal while retaining the two-thirds revenue ceiling.
opts.C: pacify the rebellion-affected peasantry after the Revolt of 1857 by converting temporary Mahalwari assessments into permanent proprietary settlements.
opts.D: empower British revenue collectors to summarily auction the joint lands of Bhaichara village communities for arrears of local police cesses.

core: Recognizing that the 66 percent revenue demand under Regulation IX of 1833 remained destructively over-assessed, Lord Dalhousie issued the Saharanpur Rules of 1855, which reduced the state's Mahalwari demand to 50 percent (one-half) of the net rental value or net assets of the estate.

exp.why: Option A is correct: Under Merttins Bird and James Thomason's Regulation IX of 1833, the state's revenue demand in the Mahalwari areas of the North-Western Provinces had been lowered from 83 percent (under Regulation VII of 1822) to 66 percent (two-thirds) of the net rental value. However, even a two-thirds extraction caused widespread agrarian distress, forced sales, and revenue defaults. Consequently, during the resettlement of Saharanpur district in 1855 under Governor-General Lord Dalhousie, the 'Saharanpur Rules' were promulgated, further moderating the state's demand to 50 percent (one-half) of the presumptive net rental assets. Option B is incorrect because although the Upper Ganga Canal was inaugurated in 1854 under Dalhousie, the Saharanpur Rules of 1855 specifically reformed the core Mahalwari land revenue ceiling from 66 percent to 50 percent rather than retaining the two-thirds ceiling. Option C is incorrect due to chronological and policy misplacement: the Saharanpur Rules were issued in 1855 before the Revolt of 1857, and the Mahalwari system remained a temporary, periodically revised settlement rather than a permanent settlement. Option D is incorrect because the 1855 rules were designed to moderate excessive revenue assessments rather than expand summary auction powers for local police cesses.

ref: Shekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition Ch. 3; Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India

stem: With reference to the institutional structure of the Mahalwari system in northern and north-western India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under British revenue law, a 'Mahal' was strictly synonymous with a single geographical village and could not legally comprise a part of a village or a group of several villages.

2. In Bhaichara and Pattidari tenures, the co-sharing village community was held jointly and severally liable for the entire revenue assessed on the Mahal, requiring the brotherhood to make good the deficit if an individual co-sharer defaulted.

3. The Lambardar acted as the officially recognized representative headman of the Mahal who signed the revenue engagement with the colonial government and collected the assessed shares from the village proprietors.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: In the Mahalwari system, a 'Mahal' was a fiscal estate (which could be one village, part of a village, or several villages) whose proprietary body bore joint and several liability for the total revenue demand, represented before the colonial state by the Lambardar.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect: While the term 'Mahal' often coincided with a single village, in British revenue law a 'Mahal' was strictly defined as a fiscal unit or estate assessed under a single revenue engagement. Depending on local tenurial history, a Mahal could legally consist of a single village, a fraction or division (patti) of a large village, or even a cluster of several villages held by a single proprietary body or talukdar.

Statement 2 is correct: A foundational principle of the Mahalwari settlement in Bhaichara (customary brotherhood sharing according to actual possession) and Pattidari (ancestral fractional share) villages was joint and several responsibility. While internal apportionment among co-sharers followed village custom or ancestral shares, the entire proprietary body of the Mahal was collectively responsible to the state for the full lump-sum assessment, and the community had to cover the arrears of any defaulting member to prevent the attachment or sale of the estate.

Statement 3 is correct: To avoid negotiating with hundreds of individual co-sharers in a village brotherhood, the British revenue administration recognized the village headman—known as the Lambardar (from the English word 'Numberdar', denoting the holder of a registered number in the collector's roll)—who signed the revenue agreement (kabuliyat) on behalf of the Mahal, collected the apportioned revenue from co-sharers, and deposited it into the government treasury in return for a small percentage commission (pachotra).

ref: B.H. Baden-Powell, The Land-Systems of British India Vol. II; Spectrum Modern India Ch. 27

stem: Consider the following statements regarding British land revenue policy in Oudh (Awadh) during the mid-nineteenth century:
items: Statement-I: Following the suppression of the Revolt of 1857, Lord Canning reversed the pre-revolt agrarian policy in Oudh and granted the Talukdars permanent, hereditary, and transferable proprietary rights over their estates through royal Sanads.

Statement-II: Although the Summary Settlement of 1856 had bypassed the Talukdars as 'interlopers' and settled revenue directly with village proprietors, the peasantry unexpectedly joined hands with their traditional Talukdar overlords against the British during the uprising of 1857.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The failure of the 1856 Summary Settlement in Oudh to win peasant loyalty—demonstrated when village cultivators rallied behind their dispossessed Talukdars during the Revolt of 1857—convinced Lord Canning to execute a complete political reversal after 1858, restoring the Talukdars via Sanads as conservative bulwarks of British rule.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct: After the recapture of Lucknow in March 1858, Governor-General Lord Canning issued the famous Oudh Proclamation (initially confiscating proprietary rights in the soil of Oudh) and subsequently executed the 'Talukdari Settlement' of 1858-1859. Through formal imperial grants (Sanads), the British restored the Talukdars to their estates and conferred upon them full, permanent, hereditary, and transferable proprietary title over the villages, transforming them into a loyal landed aristocracy ('breakwaters in the storm').

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I: Immediately after annexing Oudh in February 1856, the British administration (influenced by James Thomason's North-Western Provinces school) conducted the Summary Settlement of 1856, which treated the Talukdars as parasitic usurpers with no genuine right in the soil and stripped them of nearly half their villages in favour of subordinate village proprietors and peasants. However, British over-assessment and harsh cash collection alienated the peasantry, who retained deep social, clan, and paternalistic ties to their old chieftains. When the Revolt of 1857 broke out, the peasants marched right behind the dispossessed Talukdars against the British. This shock convinced Canning that bypassing the traditional rural elite had been a fatal political blunder, directly prompting the post-1858 restoration of the Talukdars.

ref: Thomas R. Metcalf, The Aftermath of Revolt: India, 1857-1870; NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III (Rebels and the Raj)

stem: With reference to the 'Malguzari' land revenue settlement introduced by the British in the Central Provinces during the 1860s, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Unlike the Maratha administration which treated Malguzars as village proprietors, the British stripped them of proprietary status and settled revenue directly with individual cultivators on the Madras Ryotwari model.
2. Similar to the Bengal Permanent Settlement of 1793, the revenue demand payable by the Malguzars to the colonial state in the Central Provinces was fixed in perpetuity without periodic revision.

3. Following the policy of non-intervention in internal estate management, the Central Provinces settlement refrained from recording or protecting any subordinate occupancy tenants within Malguzari villages.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Malguzari settlement of the Central Provinces was a hybrid agrarian system in which the British artificially conferred Zamindari-like proprietary title (Milkiyat) upon former Maratha-era village revenue farmers (Malguzars), while combining it with Mahalwari-style periodic assessments (every 20-30 years) and statutory protection for graded classes of occupancy tenants.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it reverses the historical roles of the Maratha and British administrations: Under the Maratha rulers (the Bhonsles of Nagpur), the 'Malguzars' (or Patels) were merely village revenue farmers or tax collectors who held no proprietary right over the village soil. When the British organized the regular settlement of the Central Provinces in the 1860s, they conferred full proprietary status (Milkiyat or landlordship) upon these Malguzars over the villages they farmed, rather than adopting the Madras Ryotwari model for the primary Malguzari tracts.

Statement 2 is incorrect: Although the Malguzars were granted proprietary rights analogous to Zamindars, the state's revenue demand in the Central Provinces was never fixed in perpetuity. Instead, the assessment followed the Mahalwari framework of the North-Western Provinces, wherein the village (Mahal) was assessed as a unit and the revenue demand was fixed only temporarily for periodic terms ranging from 20 to 30 years.

Statement 3 is incorrect: Having learned from the unprotected plight of ryots under the 1793 Bengal Permanent Settlement, British settlement officers in the Central Provinces intervened extensively in landlord-tenant relations from the very inception of the 1860s settlements. They surveyed, recorded, and legally protected graded tiers of subordinate holders—including 'Malik-Maqbuza' (plot-proprietors who paid revenue through the Malguzar), 'Absolute Occupancy Tenants', and 'Occupancy Tenants'—whose rents were fixed by the Settlement Officer rather than left to the arbitrary discretion of the Malguzar.

ref: B.H. Baden-Powell, The Land-Systems of British India Vol. II (Central Provinces); Dharma Kumar (ed.), Cambridge Economic History of India Vol. 2

stem: With reference to the colonial agrarian economy of the Punjab and the Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In the Punjab, the British implemented a modified Mahalwari settlement anchored in self-cultivating village brotherhoods with relatively moderate assessments to secure the political loyalty of a key military recruiting province.
2. The Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900 imposed a complete prohibition on all permanent sales and mortgages of agricultural land between any inhabitants of the province.

3. By barring non-agriculturist urban moneylenders from acquiring land while permitting transfers within statutory 'agricultural tribes', the 1900 Act inadvertently fostered the rise of a powerful class of rich 'agriculturist moneylenders'.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: To prevent peasant uprisings in the vital military recruiting ground of Punjab, the British enacted the Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900, which prohibited permanent land transfers from statutory 'agricultural tribes' to urban 'non-agricultural' moneylenders, but permitted intra-tribal land transfers—thereby fueling the emergence of rich peasant-moneylenders.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct: After annexing the Punjab in 1849, the Lawrence brothers and the Punjab school of administrators bypassed the older Sikh-era jagirdars and settled revenue under a village-based Mahalwari system (predominantly Bhaichara and Pattidari communities of peasant proprietors). Because the Punjab served as a strategic frontier and later became the primary recruiting ground for the British Indian Army after 1857, assessments were kept comparatively moderate and massive canal colonies were developed to preserve peasant prosperity and loyalty.

Statement 2 is incorrect: The Punjab Land Alienation Act of 1900 did not impose a blanket prohibition on all land transfers across the province. Instead, it divided the population by caste and community into statutory 'agricultural tribes' and 'non-agricultural' classes. It restricted the permanent alienation (sale or foreclosure) of land from a member of an 'agricultural tribe' to a 'non-agriculturist' (such as urban Bania, Khatri, or Arora moneylenders) and limited temporary usufructuary mortgages by non-agriculturists to a maximum of 20 years, while leaving land transfers between members of designated agricultural tribes legally permissible.

Statement 3 is correct: Because the Act of 1900 shut out urban mercantile moneylenders from permanently acquiring peasant land on foreclosure while explicitly allowing members of statutory 'agricultural tribes' to buy and mortgage land from one another, wealthier landowners and affluent peasants stepped into the rural credit market. Over the early twentieth century, these 'agriculturist moneylenders' displaced urban Sahukars and accumulated substantial landholdings from indebted smallholders of their own or allied agricultural tribes.

ref: Mridula Mukherjee, Colonizing Agriculture: The Myth of Punjab Exceptionalism; Shekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition Ch. 3

stem: With reference to a comparative overview of the three major land revenue settlements in British India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In terms of the total cultivated area of British India, the Permanent Zamindari Settlement covered the largest proportion (approximately 51 percent), followed by the Ryotwari system (30 percent) and the Mahalwari system (19 percent).

2. Unlike the Permanent Settlement which rendered the state's land revenue demand inelastic in the face of rising agricultural prices, both the Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements preserved fiscal elasticity for the colonial state through periodic revisions.

3. Across all three settlements, the creation of alienable private property in land combined with rigid cash revenue demands tied to statutory deadlines accelerated the transfer of land into the hands of moneylenders and non-cultivating intermediaries.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Of the total cultivated area of British India, the Ryotwari system covered the largest share (about 51 percent), followed by the Mahalwari system (about 30 percent) and the Permanent Zamindari Settlement (about 19 percent); despite structural differences in assessment elasticity, all three systems commodified land and fueled rural indebtedness.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect because it inverts the territorial shares of the Permanent and Ryotwari settlements: Across British India, the Ryotwari system covered the largest proportion of the total cultivated area—approximately 51 percent (encompassing Madras, Bombay, Berar, East Bengal/Assam, and Coorg). The Mahalwari system covered the second largest area—approximately 30 percent (North-Western Provinces, Oudh, Punjab, and Central Provinces). The Permanent Zamindari Settlement covered the smallest share—approximately 19 percent (Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, Varanasi division, and northern districts of Madras).

Statement 2 is correct: Under the Permanent Settlement of 1793, the state's cash revenue demand was fixed in perpetuity, meaning the colonial government could not capture any share of the expanding agrarian surplus as cultivation extended and agricultural prices rose in the nineteenth century. Recognizing this fiscal loss, British administrators made both the Ryotwari and Mahalwari settlements temporary, revising revenue rates periodically (every 20 to 30 years) so the state could enhance its collections in step with rising prices and rental values.

Statement 3 is correct: Regardless of whether proprietary rights were vested in a Zamindar, an individual Ryot, or a village Mahal, British rule transformed land into a mortgageable, saleable commodity and enforced inflexible cash revenue collections scheduled before harvest peaks. To meet these rigid deadlines during poor monsoons or price slumps, landowners and peasants borrowed at usurious rates, enabling mercantile moneylenders and absentee landlords to acquire vast tracts of land through civil court decrees and distress sales across all three zones.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence & History of Modern India; NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part III

stem: With reference to the evolution of tenancy legislation in colonial Bengal during the second half of the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Bengal Rent Act (Act X) of 1859, a peasant acquired occupancy rights as a 'settled ryot' by cultivating any land within the same village for twelve continuous years, whereas the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 narrowed this criterion to require twelve years of continuous possession of the exact same plot of land.

2. The Bengal Rent Act of 1859 abolished the legal authority of Zamindars to compel the personal attendance of ryots at their estate courts (cutcherries), a coercive power previously conferred by Regulation VII of 1799.

3. While the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 strengthened the tenure security and rent-enhancement protections of middle-tier occupancy ryots, it left sharecroppers (bargadars or adhiyars) largely devoid of statutory occupancy rights.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Bengal Rent Act (Act X) of 1859 suffered from a fatal legal loophole because it tied the 12-year occupancy rule to the continuous cultivation of the exact same plot, allowing Zamindars to evade occupancy accrual by periodically shifting tenants across plots. Following the Pabna Agrarian Leagues (1873–76), the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 plugged this loophole by granting 'settled ryot' occupancy status to any peasant who cultivated any land within the same village for 12 continuous years.

exp.why: This statement reverses the statutory evolution between 1859 and 1885. Under Act X of 1859, a peasant could claim occupancy rights only if he proved continuous possession of the exact same plot of land for 12 years; Zamindars easily defeated this by forcing tenants to exchange plots before the 12th year expired. The Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 closed this loophole by stipulating that a peasant became a 'settled ryot' with occupancy rights if he held any land in the same village (not necessarily the same plot) continuously for 12 years.

Under the notorious Haftam (Regulation VII of 1799), Zamindars had been empowered to compel the personal attendance of ryots at their estate cutcherries for rent settlement without judicial oversight. Section 11 of the Bengal Rent Act (Act X) of 1859 explicitly withdrew and abolished this arbitrary power to compel attendance.

The primary beneficiaries of the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885 were substantial occupancy ryots and jotedars, who secured protection against arbitrary eviction and unbridled rent enhancement. However, actual tillers operating as under-ryots or sharecroppers (bargadars/adhiyars) who paid a share of the produce were generally treated as tenants-at-will or agricultural labourers without occupancy status.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 3 (Pabna Agrarian Leagues)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ecological and institutional consequences of British land revenue administration in South India:
items: Statement-I: During the nineteenth century, the traditional system of decentralized tank irrigation and customary community-led maintenance of water bodies (Kudimarammat) suffered widespread decay across the Madras Presidency.

Statement-II: The Ryotwari settlement individualized revenue liability onto specific surveyed plots and vested ownership of village waste and commons (poramboke) in the colonial state, eroding the collective village institutions that had historically financed and organized tank desilting.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
