After Britain abandoned the Gold Standard in September 1931 and the pound depreciated against gold, rupee gold prices rose, triggering an export of over £240 million worth of gold from India to London between 1931 and 1937. As John Maynard Keynes noted at the time, this massive influx of Indian 'distress gold' played a vital role in replenishing the Bank of England's reserves and stabilizing the pound sterling. Option A is incorrect because the RBI was not even operational until April 1935 and no mandatory confiscation occurred. Option B is incorrect because gold exports were driven by rural distress liquidations rather than capital goods bullion swaps. Option D is incorrect because the silver rupee remained legal tender throughout the period.

ref: Dietmar Rothermund, India in the Great Depression 1929–1939;NCERT Themes in Indian History Part III

stem: With reference to the structural causes and administrative context of the Great Bengal Famine of 1943, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The famine was triggered primarily by a widespread failure of the southwest monsoon across eastern India in 1942–43 that reduced the province's rice harvest to less than half of the preceding decade's average.

2. The colonial government's 'Denial Policy' in coastal Bengal—involving the confiscation of country boats and surplus rice stocks to deny supplies to a potential Japanese invasion—severely disrupted internal grain transport, fishing livelihoods, and local market integration.

3. The financing of Allied war expenditure in India through massive currency expansion against blocked 'Sterling Balances' in London generated acute wartime inflation that eroded the real purchasing power of rural agricultural labourers and artisans.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Great Bengal Famine of 1943 was an anthropogenically aggravated 'entitlement failure' rather than a simple monsoon-induced crop collapse: wartime money-printing against blocked Sterling Balances, the loss of Burma rice imports, military procurement, and the 'Boat and Rice Denial' policies caused rice prices to skyrocket beyond the reach of rural wage labourers, fishermen, and artisans.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. As documented by the Woodhead Famine Inquiry Commission (1944–45) and later analyzed in Amartya Sen's landmark study on 'exchange entitlements', there was no generalized failure of the southwest monsoon across eastern India in 1942–43. Although a localized cyclone and fungal brown-spot disease affected parts of coastal Midnapore in October 1942, total rice availability in Bengal in 1943 was only marginally (around 5%) below the preceding five-year average and was actually 11% higher than in 1941—a year in which no famine occurred. The famine was driven by price hyperinflation, speculative hoarding, war-time procurement, and administrative breakdowns rather than a 50% harvest collapse.

Statement 2 is correct. Following the Japanese occupation of Burma in early 1942, British military authorities implemented a scorched-earth 'Denial Policy' across coastal districts of southern and eastern Bengal (such as Midnapore, Bakarganj, Khulna, and Chittagong). Under the 'Rice Denial' scheme, agents compulsorily bought up alleged surplus rice stocks, triggering market panic; under the 'Boat Denial' scheme, over 46,000 country boats capable of carrying ten or more passengers were confiscated or destroyed, paralysing riverine rice transport and destroying the livelihoods of fishermen and boatmen—two occupational groups that suffered the highest famine mortality.

Statement 3 is correct. Under the wartime financial settlement between Britain and India, the Government of India paid in rupees for huge Allied military procurement, troop maintenance, and war supplies inside India, while Britain merely credited equivalent pounds into a blocked 'Sterling Balance' account at the Bank of England (which could not be spent until after the war). The Reserve Bank of India treated these blocked sterling credits as backing to print massive quantities of paper rupees, expanding India's money supply nearly fivefold. While urban war-industry workers received subsidized food rations, rural landless agricultural labourers, huskers, fishermen, and artisans saw foodgrain prices quadruple while their nominal money wages stagnated, causing a catastrophic collapse in their food entitlements.

ref: Amartya Sen, Poverty and Famines (1981); Woodhead Famine Inquiry Commission Report (1945); Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947

stem: With reference to the early institutional development of the Covenanted Civil Service under the East India Company, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Lord Cornwallis sought to professionalize the civil service by substantially raising official salaries, strictly forbidding private trade, and enforcing promotion on the basis of seniority.

2. The Court of Directors established Fort William College at Calcutta in 1800 to retain metropolitan control over the two-year foundational training of all European recruits, replacing Lord Wellesley's earlier college at Haileybury.

3. The Charter Act of 1793 legally codified the reservation of all principal civil offices under the Company carrying an annual salary above five hundred pounds exclusively for the Covenanted Civil Servants.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lord Cornwallis laid the structural foundation of an exclusive, high-salaried Covenanted Civil Service insulated from private trade and formalized by the Charter Act of 1793, while Lord Wellesley's autonomous initiative in founding Fort William College at Calcutta (1800) was curtailed by the Court of Directors in favour of the East India College at Haileybury (1806) in England.

exp.why: Lord Cornwallis (Governor-General, 1786–93) reorganized the Company's patronage-ridden bureaucracy by separating commercial and revenue administration, strictly prohibiting civil servants from engaging in private trade or accepting presents/bribes, substantially raising their salaries to remove the pretext for corruption, and laying down the rule of promotion strictly by seniority.

This statement swaps the origins and institutional roles of the two colleges. Fort William College at Calcutta was established in November 1800 by Governor-General Lord Wellesley—without prior sanction from the Court of Directors—to provide a three-year training in Oriental languages, law, and history to young recruits in India. Fearing the loss of metropolitan patronage and objecting to the expense, the Court of Directors disapproved of Wellesley's scheme, reduced Fort William College to a mere language school for Bengal civilians, and established their own East India College at Haileybury in England (starting at Hertford Castle in 1806) to impart two years of foundational training before recruits sailed to India.

The Charter Act of 1793 gave statutory force to Cornwallis's administrative policy of Europeanization by stipulating that all civil vacancies in Indian offices below the rank of Councillor must be filled from among the Company's Covenanted Servants of the Presidency, and that posts carrying emoluments above 500 pounds per annum were reserved exclusively for Covenanted Civil Servants according to seniority.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 6; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26 (Development of Civil Services)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the transition from the patronage system to open competition in the Company's civil service:
items: Statement-I: Under the provisions of the Charter Act of 1833, the patronage system of the Court of Directors was abolished and replaced by an open competitive examination in London shaped by Lord Macaulay's recommendations on a generalist liberal education.

Statement-II: Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 statutorily declared that no native of the British territories in India should be disabled from holding any place, office, or employment under the East India Company purely by reason of religion, place of birth, descent, or colour.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 made a landmark statutory pledge of non-discrimination in public employment, the Court of Directors successfully defeated the 1833 proposal for limited competition; genuine open competition began only after the Charter Act of 1853 stripped the Directors of their patronage and led to the Macaulay Committee Report of 1854.

exp.why: Although the original draft of the Charter Act of 1833 proposed a limited fourfold nomination-cum-competition system at Haileybury, the Court of Directors fiercely resisted losing their valuable patronage and got the competition machinery suspended in 1834–37. The patronage system of the Court of Directors was finally abolished only twenty years later under the Charter Act of 1853, following which the Committee on the Indian Civil Service chaired by Lord Macaulay (November 1854) designed the open competitive examination based on generalist university subjects, first held in London in 1855.

Section 87 of the Charter Act of 1833 formally enacted the theoretical principle of equality of eligibility, declaring that no native of the British territories in India, nor any natural-born subject of His Majesty resident therein, should by reason only of his religion, place of birth, descent, colour, or any of them be disabled from holding any place, office, or employment under the Company. Despite remaining unimplemented for Covenanted posts during Company rule, this clause later became a key constitutional argument cited in Queen Victoria's Proclamation of 1858 and by early Indian nationalists.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the Indian Civil Service in the second half of the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Indian Civil Service Act of 1861 reserved a specified schedule of principal executive and judicial offices in the Regulation Provinces exclusively for members of the Covenanted Civil Service.

2. The Statutory Civil Service introduced by Lord Lytton in 1878–79 provided for filling up to one-sixth of covenanted posts through an open competitive examination conducted annually in the Presidency towns for Indian university graduates.
3. During Lord Lytton's viceroyalty, the maximum permissible age for appearing in the Covenanted Civil Service examination in London was reduced from twenty-one to nineteen years.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Post-1858 colonial bureaucracy ring-fenced superior administrative posts through the Indian Civil Service Act of 1861 and curtailed educated middle-class Indian entry in the late 1870s by lowering the London exam age limit to 19 while channeling limited Indian appointments into Lytton's patronage-based Statutory Civil Service.

exp.why: The Indian Civil Service Act of 1861 regularized previous non-covenanted appointments while attaching a statutory Schedule that reserved all principal civil executive, revenue, and judicial posts in the Regulation Provinces exclusively for members of the Covenanted Civil Service recruited through the annual competitive examination held in England under the supervision of the Civil Service Commissioners.

Lord Lytton's Statutory Civil Service (instituted in 1878–79 under the statutory authority of the Government of India Act of 1870) explicitly avoided open competition and was designed to bypass Western-educated middle-class nationalists. It empowered Provincial Governments to nominate Indians of 'good family and high social standing' (aristocratic and landed elites) to up to one-sixth of the posts hitherto reserved for the Covenanted Civil Service, subject to the approval of the Governor-General in Council and the Secretary of State for India.

The maximum age limit for the London ICS examination—which had been 23 in 1853, lowered to 22 in 1860, and to 21 in 1866—was further reduced to 19 years under orders issued by Secretary of State Lord Salisbury in 1876 and implemented during Lord Lytton's viceroyalty in 1878. This drastic reduction made it virtually impossible for Indian students to complete university education and compete in London, triggering the historic all-India Civil Service agitation led by Surendranath Banerjea and the Indian Association.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the recommendations of the Aitchison Commission on Public Services (1886) appointed during the viceroyalty of Lord Dufferin, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It recommended the abolition of the Statutory Civil Service and the reorganization of the civil services into three distinct tiers: Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate Civil Services.
2. It accepted the demand of the Indian National Congress for holding simultaneous competitive examinations in England and India for recruitment to the Imperial Civil Service.
3. To restrict the entry of older Indian university graduates, it recommended lowering the maximum age limit for the London competitive examination from twenty-one to nineteen years.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Aitchison Commission (1886) replaced the archaic Covenanted/Uncovenanted dichotomy and failed Statutory Civil Service with the three-tier Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate structure and raised the London exam age limit to 23, while firmly rejecting the nationalist demand for simultaneous examinations in India.

exp.why: Appointed by Lord Dufferin in 1886 under Sir Charles Aitchison, the Public Service Commission recommended dropping the anomalous terms 'Covenanted' and 'Uncovenanted', abolishing Lord Lytton's unpopular Statutory Civil Service, and restructuring the bureaucracy into three clear tiers: the Imperial Indian Civil Service (recruited in England), the Provincial Civil Service (recruited in each province and absorbing a small number of transferred Imperial posts), and the Subordinate Civil Service.

The Aitchison Commission explicitly rejected the nationalist demand for holding simultaneous competitive examinations in India and England, arguing that the Imperial Civil Service must remain predominantly British in training and character and that holding open written examinations in India would produce unequal communal and regional representation.

Far from lowering the age limit from 21 to 19 (which had already been done in 1876–78 under Salisbury and Lytton), the Aitchison Commission recommended raising the minimum and maximum age limits for the London examination to 19 and 23 years respectively (implemented in 1892) to restore a fairer chance for Indian graduates travelling to England.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947, Ch. 2; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the question of Indianization and recruitment to the superior civil services between 1893 and 1917:
items: 1. Although the British House of Commons passed a resolution in 1893 supporting simultaneous Indian Civil Service examinations in England and India, the Government of India declined to implement it, and no examination was held in India prior to the First World War.

2. The Islington Commission (1912–15) recommended that 25 percent of the superior posts in the Indian Civil Service should be filled in India partly by direct recruitment and partly by promotion from the Provincial Service, while 75 percent should continue to be recruited in England.

3. The Islington Commission recommended abolishing the Secretary of State's control over the Imperial Services and transferring all recruitment powers to a statutory Public Service Commission located in Calcutta.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Despite the House of Commons passing Herbert Paul's non-binding resolution for simultaneous ICS exams in 1893, colonial executive resistance kept recruitment for the Imperial Civil Service confined to London before World War I, with the Islington Commission (1912–15) proposing only a cautious 75:25 split between English and Indian recruitment channels while retaining the Secretary of State's control.

exp.why: In June 1893, primarily through the efforts of Dadabhai Naoroji and British radical MPs led by Herbert Paul, the House of Commons unexpectedly passed a non-binding resolution in favour of holding simultaneous ICS examinations in England and India. However, when referred to the Government of India and Provincial Governments, the colonial bureaucracy unanimously opposed its execution on political and security grounds, rendering the 1893 resolution a dead letter; the first ICS examination in India was actually held only in 1922 at Allahabad.

The Royal Commission on the Public Services in India (Islington Commission, appointed in 1912 with members including G.K. Gokhale and Abdur Rahim; report signed in 1915 and published in 1917) rejected single-channel simultaneous exams on identical terms and instead proposed two separate avenues for the ICS: 75 percent of vacancies to be recruited in England through open competition, and 25 percent (including the listed posts already open to Indians) to be filled in India partly by promotion from the Provincial Civil Service and partly by direct recruitment in India.

The Islington Commission neither recommended abolishing the Secretary of State's control over the Imperial Services nor proposed transferring recruitment to a statutory Public Service Commission in Calcutta (moreover, the imperial capital had already shifted to Delhi in 1911–12). The statutory mandate for a Public Service Commission in India originated later under Section 96C of the Government of India Act, 1919, and was operationalized in October 1926 following the Lee Commission Report (1924).

ref: B.R. Tomlinson / Cambridge History of India; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the reforms in the superior civil services following the Government of India Act, 1919 and the Lee Commission Report (1924), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Lee Commission recommended that the Secretary of State for India should continue to recruit and control the All-India Services operating in the 'Transferred' provincial departments such as the Indian Educational Service and the Indian Agricultural Service, while transferring control of the Indian Civil Service and Indian Police to the Provincial Governments.
2. The first competitive examination in India for the Indian Civil Service was held at Allahabad in 1922 under the direct supervision of the newly constituted Federal Public Service Commission.

3. To preserve a permanent British majority in the higher bureaucracy, the Lee Commission rejected the concept of racial parity and fixed the maximum ceiling of Indian recruitment in the Indian Civil Service at one-third of the total cadre.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under the Dyarchy framework of 1919, the Lee Commission (1924) preserved the Secretary of State's control over security and revenue-critical All-India Services in the 'Reserved' sphere (ICS, IP, IMS, Irrigation Engineers) while provincializing services in the 'Transferred' departments, accelerating ICS Indianization to achieve 50:50 parity in 15 years, and catalysing the setup of the Central Public Service Commission in 1926.

exp.why: This statement inverts the Lee Commission's division between 'Reserved' and 'Transferred' spheres under Provincial Dyarchy. The Lee Commission (1924) recommended that the Secretary of State for India should continue to recruit and control the All-India Services operating in the 'Reserved' fields—namely the Indian Civil Service (ICS), the Indian Police (IP), the Indian Medical Service (IMS), and the Irrigation branch of the Indian Service of Engineers. Conversely, for the All-India Services operating in the 'Transferred' provincial departments (Indian Educational Service, Indian Agricultural Service, Indian Veterinary Service, and the Roads and Buildings branch of the Indian Service of Engineers), further recruitment by the Secretary of State was halted and recruitment and control were devolved to the Provincial Governments.

While the first competitive examination in India for the ICS was indeed held at Allahabad in February 1922 pursuant to the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, no Public Service Commission existed in India in 1922; the 1922 Allahabad examination was conducted under the supervision of the Civil Service Commissioners of London. The Central Public Service Commission (chaired by Sir Ross Barker) was established only on 1 October 1926 following the Lee Commission's recommendation, and it was redesignated as the Federal Public Service Commission only under the Government of India Act, 1935 (effective April 1937).

The one-third Indian recruitment formula (33 percent rising by 1.5 percent annually) belonged to the earlier Montagu-Chelmsford Report (1918). The Lee Commission (1924) superseded that slower pace and explicitly adopted a 40:40:20 recruitment ratio for the ICS (40 percent Europeans directly recruited, 40 percent Indians directly recruited, and 20 percent Indians promoted from the Provincial Civil Services) designed to achieve 50:50 racial parity between Europeans and Indians in the Indian Civil Service cadre within 15 years (by 1939).

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 6; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 26

stem: With reference to the provisions governing the Civil Services and Public Service Commissions under the Government of India Act, 1935, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Even after the introduction of Provincial Autonomy, the power to make fresh appointments to the Indian Civil Service (ICS), the Indian Police (IP), and the Indian Medical Service (Civil) continued to vest only in the Secretary of State for India.

2. While the members of a Provincial Public Service Commission were appointed by the Governor on the binding advice of the Provincial Council of Ministers, the members of a Joint Public Service Commission serving two or more provinces were appointed directly by the Secretary of State in Council.

3. The Act abolished the constitutional safeguards regarding tenure and non-votable salaries for All-India Service officers serving in the provinces, empowering the Provincial Premier to dismiss them.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Under the Government of India Act, 1935, the British Parliament insulated the key imperial steel-frame services (ICS, IP, and IMS Civil) from elected provincial ministries by retaining the Secretary of State's exclusive control over their recruitment and dismissal, while keeping Public Service Commission appointments within the discretionary domain of the Governor-General and Governors.

exp.why: Under Section 244 of the Government of India Act, 1935, while recruitment by the Secretary of State to several transferred technical services had ceased following the Lee Commission (1924), appointments to the three core imperial services—the Indian Civil Service (ICS), the Indian Police (IP), and the Indian Medical Service (Civil)—continued to be made exclusively ('only') by the Secretary of State for India.

Under Section 265(1) of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Chairman and members of a Provincial Public Service Commission were appointed by the Governor 'in his discretion' (not on the binding advice of the Council of Ministers), and those of the Federal Public Service Commission by the Governor-General 'in his discretion'. Where two or more provinces agreed under Section 264(2) to set up a Joint Public Service Commission, the agreement specified which Governor or Governors would exercise the power of appointment in their discretion, not the Secretary of State.

Far from abolishing constitutional safeguards, Sections 240, 247, and 52(1)(c) of the 1935 Act entrenched them: no member of a Secretary of State's service could be dismissed by any authority subordinate to the Secretary of State, their salaries and pensions were 'charged' (non-votable) expenditure on provincial/federal revenues, and the Governor was vested with a 'special responsibility' to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of civil servants.

ref: Government of India Act, 1935 (Sections 240, 244, 247, 264 & 265); B.L. Grover & Alka Mehta, Modern Indian History, Ch. on Constitutional Developments.

stem: Which one of the following accurately describes the structural reorganization of rural and district policing introduced by Lord Cornwallis through the Police Regulations of 1791 (subsequently codified in the Cornwallis Code of 1793)?

opts.A: Zamindars were relieved of their police duties, districts were divided into police circles (thanas) placed under salaried Indian officers (Darogas), and overall district police supervision was vested in the European District Judge-Magistrate rather than the Revenue Collector.
opts.B: The Revenue Collector was designated as the District Magistrate with direct command over both the rural Darogas and the Zamindari thanadars to ensure seamless coercion in land revenue realization.
opts.C: A separate provincial cadre of European Superintendents of Police was established in every district to command the village watchmen (chowkidars), completely stripping both the District Judge and the Collector of police powers.
opts.D: Policing authority in the interior was handed back to the hereditary Faujdars and Kotwals under the appellate supervision of the Nizamat Adalat at Murshidabad.

core: Lord Cornwallis's Police Regulations of 1791 dismantled the feudal Zamindari policing system and separated revenue collection from police and magisterial power by placing salaried Indian Darogas under the European District Judge-Magistrate.

exp.why: Option A is correct: Under the Police Regulations of December 1791 (incorporated into Regulation XXII of the Cornwallis Code, 1793), Cornwallis stripped the Zamindars of their traditional thanadari policing powers and disbanded their armed retainers. Each district was divided into compact police jurisdictions (thanas) of roughly 20 square miles (400 sq. miles area) under a government-paid Indian officer called a Daroga, assisted by barkandazes. In keeping with Cornwallis's Whiggish principle of separation of powers, the Revenue Collector was divested of magisterial and police authority, and the Darogas were placed directly under the supervision of the European District Judge-Magistrate (Zila Judge). Option B is incorrect because the Collector was made Collector-Magistrate in charge of district police only much later under William Bentinck's reforms (and after 1859/1861). Option C is incorrect because a separate district SP cadre across provinces emerged only under the Indian Police Act of 1861. Option D confuses Cornwallis's 1791 reforms with Warren Hastings' earlier and short-lived experiment (1774–1781) with native Faujdars.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; Spectrum's A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. on Constitutional, Administrative and Judicial Developments.

stem: With reference to the institutional evolution of the colonial police administration in India prior to the Indian Police Act of 1861, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In 1808, Lord Minto's administration created the office of Superintendent of Police (SP) for important divisions in the Bengal Presidency to coordinate anti-dacoity operations with the assistance of intelligence informers (goyendas).

2. Lord William Bentinck created a separate cadre of European District Superintendents of Police in every district in 1829 in order to make police administration completely independent of the Revenue Collector.

3. Following the annexation of Sindh in 1843, Sir Charles Napier organized a regular provincial police force modelled on the Royal Irish Constabulary under its own officers, distinct from both the military and the revenue establishment.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Before 1861, British policing swung between specialized anti-dacoity supervision (1808 SPs), Bentinck's 1829 fiscal retrenchment that abolished the SP and fused the Collector-Magistrate as district police head, and Napier's 1843 Sindh Constabulary model which later inspired the 1861 Police Act.

exp.why: By Regulation X of 1808 during Lord Minto's governor-generalship, the office of Superintendent of Police (SP) was created first for the divisions of Calcutta, Dacca, and Murshidabad (and extended in 1810 to Patna, Benares, and Bareilly) specifically to combat widespread dacoity through centralized coordination and the use of spies/informers (goyendas).

Statement 2 inverts William Bentinck's reform. In 1829, driven by financial austerity and complaints about the oppressive goyenda spy system, Bentinck abolished the office of the Superintendent of Police, transferred its supervisory duties to the newly created Divisional Commissioners of Revenue and Circuit, and merged the offices of Collector and Magistrate—making the Collector-Magistrate the direct head of the district police.

After annexing Sindh in 1843, Sir Charles Napier established a self-contained, semi-military provincial police organization modelled on the Royal Irish Constabulary. Commanded by its own Captain of Police at the provincial level and European lieutenants in the districts, the Sindh model became the prototype for reforms in Bombay (1853), Madras (1859), and ultimately the Police Commission of 1860.

ref: B.L. Grover & Alka Mehta, Modern Indian History; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the reorganization of the police system in British India after the Revolt of 1857:
items: Statement-I: Under the Indian Police Act of 1861, enacted on the recommendations of the Police Commission of 1860 (headed by M.H. Court), the civil police were organized strictly on a provincial basis under an Inspector-General of Police, while at the district level the Superintendent of Police was placed under the general criminal control and direction of the District Magistrate.

Statement-II: The Police Commission of 1860 sought to insulate law-and-order administration from the revenue bureaucracy by completely divesting the District Magistrate of executive supervision over the police and establishing a unified All-India Police Command at Calcutta.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Indian Police Act of 1861 institutionalized a provincial police hierarchy under an Inspector-General while intentionally preserving the supremacy of the District Magistrate (Collector) over the District Superintendent of Police in matters of law and order, avoiding any unified national police chief.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Appointed in August 1860 under the chairmanship of M.H. Court, the Police Commission laid the blueprint for the Indian Police Act (Act V of 1861). It established a civil constabulary organized separately within each province under an Inspector-General of Police (IGP). At the district level, it instituted a system of 'dual control': internal departmental discipline and operational command lay with the District Superintendent of Police (SP), but Section 4 of the Act placed the district police under the 'general control and direction' of the District Magistrate.

Statement-II is incorrect. Although the 1860 Commission abolished the old military police and relieved the District Magistrate of the internal disciplinary management of the police force, it explicitly refused to strip the District Magistrate of general executive control over criminal administration in the district, viewing the District Magistrate-Collector as the indispensable pivot of British imperial authority. Moreover, the 1861 Act did not create any centralized All-India Police Command at Calcutta; police remained strictly provincial.

ref: Indian Police Act, 1861 (Section 4); Spectrum's A Brief History of Modern India, Evolution of Civil Services and Police.

stem: With reference to the Indian Police Commission of 1902–03 (the Frazer Commission) appointed during the Viceroyalty of Lord Curzon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It threw open the senior Imperial Police cadre of District Superintendents of Police to direct recruitment of educated Indians through simultaneous competitive examinations held in London and Calcutta.

2. To prevent the politicization of ordinary policing, it recommended the immediate winding up of central intelligence agencies and opposed the creation of specialized Criminal Investigation Departments (CID) in the provinces.
3. It abolished the supervisory authority of the District Magistrate over the District Superintendent of Police and vested appellate magisterial powers in the Provincial Inspector-General of Police.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Andrew Frazer Police Commission (1902–03) reinforced the racial glass ceiling by restricting direct Indian entry to the newly created Provincial rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP), while building the modern colonial surveillance apparatus through Provincial CIDs and the Central Department of Criminal Intelligence (DCI).

exp.why: The Frazer Commission (1902–03) explicitly maintained the racial monopoly of Europeans over the senior officer ranks (Assistant and District Superintendents of Police), recruited via examination in England. For educated Indians, the Commission recommended creating a separate Provincial Police Service with the newly instituted rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (DySP) as the ceiling for direct Indian recruitment, allowing promotion of Indians to SP only in rare, exceptional cases.

Far from opposing specialized intelligence wings, the Frazer Commission was the architect of the modern colonial intelligence machinery. It recommended establishing a specialized Criminal Investigation Department (CID) under a Deputy Inspector-General (DIG) in every province to handle organized crime, railways, and political surveillance, alongside a Central Department of Criminal Intelligence (DCI) under the Government of India (replacing the old Thagi and Dakaiti Department).

While the Frazer Commission criticized excessive day-to-day meddling by some District Magistrates in internal police discipline and transfers, it upheld the core principle of the 1861 Act that the District Magistrate, as the head of the criminal administration of the district, must retain general supervisory control and direction over the District SP. It never vested judicial or magisterial powers in the Inspector-General.

ref: Report of the Indian Police Commission, 1902–03 (Sir Andrew Frazer); Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2.

stem: With reference to the reorganization of the British Indian Army after the Revolt of 1857 and the subsequent struggle for Indianization of its officer corps, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Acting on the recommendations of the Peel Commission (1859), the British reorganized Indian regiments on the principle of 'division and counterpoise' by mixing castes and communities to prevent unified solidarity, while excluding Indians from artillery units.

2. The Eden Commission (1879) strengthened the autonomy of the three separate Presidency Armies of Bengal, Madras, and Bombay and opened the King's Commission to Indian officers on an equal footing with British officers.

3. The Indian Sandhurst Committee (1925–26), chaired by Sir Andrew Skeen, criticized the segregationist 'Eight-Unit Scheme' and recommended the establishment of a military college in India to accelerate the Indianization of the commissioned officer corps.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Post-1857 colonial military policy rested on the Peel Commission's principle of 'counterpoise' (heterogeneous mixing of castes/regions, higher European-to-Indian ratios, and British monopoly over artillery) and strict racial exclusion of Indians from King's Commissions until post-WWI nationalist pressure led to the Skeen Committee (1925–26).

exp.why: Following the Peel Commission (1859), the ratio of Europeans to Indians was raised (roughly 1:2 in Bengal and 1:3 in Madras and Bombay), Indians were completely excluded from European artillery and arsenals (except a few mountain batteries later), and regiments were organized on the policy of 'division and counterpoise'—balancing different castes, regions, and religious communities ('martial races' vs. 'non-martial races') across companies and regiments so that no homogeneous pan-Indian solidarity could emerge.

Statement 2 is incorrect on both counts. First, the Ashley Eden Commission (1879) recommended abolishing the archaic system of three separate Presidency Armies (Bengal, Madras, and Bombay) and unifying the Indian Army under a single Commander-in-Chief divided into four territorial commands (formally implemented in 1895). Second, throughout the 19th century, Indians were strictly barred from receiving the King's/Queen's Commission and could rise no higher than the subordinate Viceroy's Commission (Subedar-Major/Risaldar-Major), ranking below the junior-most British subaltern; King's Commissions were opened to Indians only at the end of World War I (1918).

The Indian Sandhurst Committee (1925–26), chaired by Lt.-Gen. Sir Andrew Skeen (with Indian members including Motilal Nehru, M.A. Jinnah, and Tej Bahadur Sapru), recommended abandoning Lord Rawlinson's discriminatory 'Eight-Unit Scheme' (1923)—which segregated Indian King's Commissioned Officers into just eight designated units so that no British officer would ever have to serve under an Indian officer—and proposed establishing an Indian military academy modelled on Sandhurst by 1933 to achieve 50% Indianization of the officer cadre by 1952.

ref: Bipan Chandra et al., India's Struggle for Independence; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. on Colonial Army.

stem: With reference to the early judicial organization under the East India Company in Bengal during the tenure of Warren Hastings, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Mofussil Diwani Adalat (1772) : District civil court presided over by an Indian Daroga-i-Adalat under the appellate supervision of the District Collector
2. Sadar Nizamat Adalat (1772) : Apex criminal court presided over directly by the European District Collector to confirm capital sentences
3. Supreme Court at Fort William (1774) : Crown Court established under the Regulating Act of 1773 with jurisdiction over British subjects and Company servants in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa
4. Act of Settlement (1781) : Exempted the official actions of the Governor-General-in-Council and matters of revenue collection from the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Warren Hastings' Judicial Plan of 1772 vested civil jurisdiction (Mofussil Diwani Adalat) directly in the European Collector while leaving criminal justice (Faujdari/Nizamat Adalats) nominally under Nawab-appointed Muslim law officers supervised by the Company. Subsequent jurisdictional clashes between the Governor-General-in-Council and the Crown's Supreme Court (1774) were resolved in favour of the executive and revenue administration by the Act of Settlement of 1781.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Under Warren Hastings' Judicial Plan of 1772, the Mofussil Diwani Adalat (district civil court) was presided over directly by the European District Collector as the judge (assisted by native Qazis and Pandits for personal laws). Appeals from the Mofussil Diwani Adalat in suits exceeding Rs 500 lay to the Sadar Diwani Adalat at Calcutta, which was presided over by the Governor and members of his Council, not the Collector.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. Under the 1772 Plan, the Sadar Nizamat Adalat (apex criminal court) was presided over by an Indian judge styled the Daroga-i-Adalat (representing the Nawab/Nazim), assisted by the Chief Qazi, Chief Mufti, and three Maulvis, while the Governor-in-Council exercised general supervisory control over its proceedings. The District Collector only exercised general surveillance over the district-level Mofussil Faujdari Adalat.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Established in 1774 by a Royal Charter pursuant to the Regulating Act of 1773 (with Sir Elijah Impey as Chief Justice), the Supreme Court of Judicature at Fort William exercised civil, criminal, admiralty, and ecclesiastical jurisdiction over all British subjects in Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa, residents of Calcutta, and all persons employed directly or indirectly in the service of the Company.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Following bitter conflicts between the Supreme Court and the Supreme Council (exemplified by the Nandakumar, Patna, and Cossijurah cases), the British Parliament passed the Act of Settlement (Declaratory Act) of 1781. It exempted the Governor-General-in-Council for acts done in their official capacity, excluded revenue matters and zamindars/revenue farmers from the Supreme Court's jurisdiction, and recognized the appellate authority of the Company's Sadar Diwani Adalat.

ref: B.L. Grover, A New Look at Modern Indian History, Ch. on Warren Hastings; M.P. Jain, Outlines of Indian Legal and Constitutional History.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the judicial and administrative reforms under Lord Cornwallis:
items: Statement-I: Under the Cornwallis Code of 1793, the District Collector was divested of all judicial and magisterial powers, and the separate revenue courts (Mal Adalats) were abolished by transferring revenue suits to the regular District Diwani Adalats.

Statement-II: Lord Cornwallis operated on the Whig administrative principle that the security of private landed property under the Permanent Settlement required the revenue-collecting executive to be institutionally separated from the judiciary adjudicating revenue disputes and made amenable to civil courts for official excesses.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Cornwallis Code of 1793 institutionalized the separation of revenue administration from civil justice in Bengal. To guarantee the security of landed property envisaged by the Permanent Settlement, Cornwallis abolished the Collector-led Mal Adalats and subordinated executive revenue officials to the jurisdiction of independent District Diwani Adalats.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Reversing the 1787 arrangement that had combined revenue collection, civil justice, and magistracy in the hands of the District Collector, the Cornwallis Code (May 1793) stripped the Collector of all judicial and magisterial powers, leaving him solely as a revenue-collecting officer. The separate revenue courts (Mal Adalats) presided over by Collectors were abolished, and all revenue suits were transferred to the reconstituted District Diwani Adalats presided over by covenanted District Judges.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. Inspired by Whig notions of limited government and the protection of private property, Cornwallis reasoned that if the Collector who assessed and demanded revenue also sat as the judge in the Mal Adalat hearing complaints of wrongful exaction, zamindars and landholders could never enjoy true security of property under the Permanent Settlement. Consequently, he separated the executive from the judiciary and made Company Collectors and executive officers personally liable to be sued by Indian subjects in civil courts for official wrongs.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2; Spectrum's A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26.

stem: With reference to the judicial reforms introduced during the Governor-Generalship of Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835), consider the following statements:
items: 1. He abolished the four Provincial Courts of Appeal and Circuit established by Lord Cornwallis, transferring their criminal circuit functions initially to Commissioners of Revenue and Circuit and subsequently to District and Sessions Judges.

2. To alleviate the hardship of litigants in the Upper Provinces, he established a separate Sadar Diwani Adalat and a Sadar Nizamat Adalat at Allahabad, and created the higher judicial post of Principal Sadar Amin open to Indians.
3. He abolished the use of Persian and made English the compulsory language of judicial proceedings across all subordinate, district, and appellate courts in British India.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Bentinck dismantled Cornwallis's cumbersome and expensive judicial hierarchy by abolishing the Provincial Courts of Appeal and Circuit, decentralizing appellate justice through new Sadar Adalats at Allahabad, expanding Indian participation up to the rank of Principal Sadar Amin, and introducing vernacular languages in lower courts alongside English in higher courts.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Bentinck criticized Cornwallis's four Provincial Courts of Appeal and Circuit for causing massive judicial arrears and prolonged detention of undertrials. By Regulation I of 1829, he transferred their criminal circuit functions to Commissioners of Revenue and Circuit, and between 1831 and 1833 he abolished the Provincial Courts altogether, authorizing the transfer of sessions duties to District Judges (thereby creating the office of District and Sessions Judge).

Statement 2 is correct. Because litigants from the North-Western (Upper) Provinces had to travel tremendous distances to Calcutta for appeals, Bentinck set up a separate Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat at Allahabad (1831–1832). Driven by Utilitarian economy and the need to clear judicial backlogs, he also expanded the judicial agency of Indians in 1831 by creating the superior post of Principal Sadar Amin (above Munsiffs and Sadar Amins), empowered to try civil suits up to Rs 5,000.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Bentinck did not make English the compulsory language across all subordinate and district courts. Rather, he terminated the monopoly of Persian as the exclusive court language by allowing litigants the option to use Persian or local vernacular languages in lower and subordinate courts, while substituting English for Persian only in the Supreme Court and higher judicial proceedings.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India; Spectrum's A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26 (Development of Judiciary in British India).

stem: With reference to the codification of laws and institutional unification of the judiciary in nineteenth-century British India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The First Law Commission, appointed in 1834 under the chairmanship of Lord Macaulay pursuant to the Charter Act of 1833, prepared the draft of the Penal Code, though its formal statutory enactment took place only after the transfer of power to the British Crown in 1858.
2. The Charter Act of 1833 abolished the dual judicial system in the Presidency towns by merging the Crown's Supreme Courts with the Company's Sadar Adalats into unified High Courts.
3. The First Law Commission was constituted as a permanent statutory body in London under the Board of Control to review all regulations passed by the Presidency Governments.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: While the Charter Act of 1833 centralized legislative power and initiated legal codification through Macaulay's First Law Commission in 1834, the actual enactment of the great procedural and substantive codes (CPC 1859, IPC 1860, CrPC 1861) and the institutional fusion of Supreme and Sadar Courts under the Indian High Courts Act (1861) occurred only in the immediate aftermath of the Revolt of 1857.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 53 of the Charter Act of 1833, the First Law Commission was established in 1834 under Thomas Babington Macaulay. Although Macaulay submitted the draft Penal Code in 1837, prolonged official deliberations and the upheaval of 1857 delayed its enactment until after the Crown takeover—resulting in the passage of the Code of Civil Procedure (1859), the Indian Penal Code (1860), and the Code of Criminal Procedure (1861).

Statement 2 is incorrect. The dual judicial system in the Presidency towns—comprising the Crown's Supreme Courts and the Company's Sadar Diwani and Sadar Nizamat Adalats—continued long after 1833. Their amalgamation into unified High Courts at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras was brought about nearly three decades later under the Indian High Courts Act of 1861 (with the courts formally inaugurated in 1862 during the tenure of Lord Canning).

Statement 3 is incorrect. Under the Charter Act of 1833, the First Law Commission was appointed by the Governor-General-in-Council and functioned in India (at Calcutta), not as a permanent body in London under the Board of Control. Notice also that the Charter Act of 1833 had already deprived the Bombay and Madras Presidencies of their independent law-making powers.

ref: M.P. Jain, Outlines of Indian Legal and Constitutional History; Spectrum's A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26.

stem: With reference to the Ilbert Bill controversy (1883–1884) during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon, which one of the following statements accurately describes the statutory compromise enacted by the Imperial Legislative Council in January 1884?

opts.A: The Bill was completely withdrawn, leaving Indian Covenanted Civil Servants permanently barred from exercising any criminal jurisdiction over European British subjects in both the Presidency towns and the mofussil.
opts.B: Jurisdiction to try European British subjects in criminal cases was transferred exclusively to the Presidency High Courts, stripping both European and Indian District Magistrates in the mofussil of such powers.
opts.C: Indian District Magistrates and Sessions Judges were empowered to try European British subjects in the mofussil, provided that the European accused was granted the right to demand trial by a jury of which at least half the members were Europeans or Americans.
opts.D: Indian judges were permitted to try European British subjects in civil and revenue disputes in the mofussil, while criminal jurisdiction remained restricted exclusively to European Justices of the Peace.

core: The Ilbert Bill (1883) sought to abolish the racial anomaly under which Indian ICS officers rising to become District Magistrates or Sessions Judges in the mofussil could not try European British subjects in criminal cases. Fierce racial agitation by non-official Europeans forced Lord Ripon into the Concordat of 1884, which conferred nominal jurisdiction on Indian judges while allowing any European accused to demand a jury composed of at least 50% Europeans or Americans.

exp.why: Option (C) is correct. Under the Code of Criminal Procedure of 1872/1882, while Indian magistrates in Presidency towns could try Europeans, in the mofussil (countryside) only European British subjects could act as magistrates or sessions judges to try European offenders. When Indian Covenanted Civil Servants (such as Behari Lal Gupta and Surendranath Banerjea's contemporaries) reached the seniority of District Magistrates and Sessions Judges, Law Member Sir C.P. Ilbert introduced a Bill in 1883 to remove this racial disqualification. Following an organized 'White Mutiny' led by the European and Anglo-Indian Defence Association, the Government enacted a modified law in January 1884 (Act III of 1884): Indian District Magistrates and Sessions Judges were granted jurisdiction to try Europeans, but a European British subject brought before a District Magistrate or Sessions Judge (whether Indian or European) was given the statutory right to claim trial by a jury of which not less than half the members had to be Europeans or Americans, effectively hollowing out the principle of judicial equality. Option (A) is incorrect because the Bill was amended rather than completely withdrawn. Option (B) is incorrect because mofussil District Magistrates and Sessions Judges retained jurisdiction subject to the jury proviso. Option (D) is incorrect because Indian judges in the mofussil already exercised civil jurisdiction over Europeans since Macaulay's Black Act of 1836.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947, Ch. 2; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 4.

stem: With reference to the Federal Court of India established under the Government of India Act, 1935, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It possessed exclusive original jurisdiction in disputes between the Central Government and the Provinces involving the interpretation of the Government of India Act, 1935.
2. The Governor-General was empowered under the Act of 1935 to refer any question of law of public importance to the Federal Court for its advisory opinion.

3. Upon its inauguration in 1937, it replaced the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London as the final court of appeal for all constitutional, civil, and criminal disputes arising in British India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Inaugurated on 1 October 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935, the Federal Court of India exercised original federal, appellate constitutional, and advisory jurisdictions, serving as the institutional forerunner of the Supreme Court of India. However, throughout colonial rule, it remained subordinate to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London, which continued as the ultimate court of appeal until 1949.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Section 204 of the Government of India Act, 1935, the Federal Court (established in October 1937 with Sir Maurice Gwyer as the first Chief Justice) was vested with exclusive original jurisdiction in any dispute between the Federation (Centre) and any of the Provinces, or between Provinces inter se, if and insofar as the dispute involved any question of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depended, particularly the interpretation of the 1935 Act.

Statement 2 is correct. Section 213 of the Government of India Act, 1935 conferred advisory jurisdiction on the Federal Court, empowering the Governor-General, in his discretion, to refer to the Federal Court for consideration and report any question of law of such a nature and of such public importance that it was expedient to obtain the opinion of the Court upon it (the direct precursor to Article 143 of the Constitution of India).

Statement 3 is incorrect. The Federal Court was not the final court of appeal for British India upon its inauguration in 1937. Under Section 208 of the Government of India Act, 1935, appeals still lay from decisions of the Federal Court to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London (without leave in original constitutional cases, and with leave of the Federal Court or His Majesty in Council in other cases). Moreover, ordinary civil and criminal appeals from Provincial High Courts that did not involve a certified question of constitutional interpretation bypassed the Federal Court altogether and went directly to the Privy Council until the Federal Court (Enlargement of Jurisdiction) Act, 1947 and the Abolition of Privy Council Jurisdiction Act, 1949.

ref: D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 1; M.P. Jain, Outlines of Indian Legal and Constitutional History.

stem: With reference to the early institutional milestones of education in British India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Calcutta Madrasah (1781) : Established by Warren Hastings to train Muslim law officers to assist judges in the East India Company's courts
2. Sanskrit College, Banaras (1791) : Founded by Jonathan Duncan for the study of Hindu law and philosophy to provide qualified pandits for the judicial administration
3. Serampore College (1818) : Established officially by the East India Company under Lord Hastings to train Indian recruits for the uncovenanted civil services
4. General Committee of Public Instruction (1823) : Constituted to administer the annual state grant of one lakh rupees sanctioned under Section 43 of the Charter Act of 1813
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Early East India Company educational patronage (Calcutta Madrasah, 1781 and Banaras Sanskrit College, 1791) was driven by the pragmatic administrative necessity of training Indian legal assessors (qazis, muftis, and pandits) for the Adalat system, distinct from independent European missionary initiatives such as the Danish-chartered Serampore College (1818). The state's statutory financial commitment of one lakh rupees under the Charter Act of 1813 only became operational after the constitution of the General Committee of Public Instruction in 1823.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Warren Hastings established the Calcutta Madrasah in 1781 for the study of Muslim law and related subjects so as to maintain a regular supply of qualified Indian Muslim law officers (qazis and muftis) to assist European judges in the Company's Diwani and Nizamat Adalats.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Jonathan Duncan, the British Resident at Banaras, founded the Sanskrit College in 1791 for the preservation and cultivation of Hindu laws, literature, and philosophy, primarily to supply qualified Hindu pandits to assist European judges in interpreting Dharmashastra texts.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Serampore College (1818) was NOT an official East India Company institution established to train civil servants; it was founded by the Baptist Missionary trio—William Carey, Joshua Marshman, and William Ward—in the Danish settlement of Serampore (Frederiksnagore) to impart theological and liberal arts education. By contrast, Fort William College (1800) had been established by Lord Wellesley in Calcutta to train young European recruits of the Covenanted Civil Service.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Although Section 43 of the Charter Act of 1813 directed the East India Company to set apart not less than one lakh rupees annually for the revival of literature and the promotion of scientific knowledge among the inhabitants of British India, the grant remained largely unutilized until 1823, when the General Committee of Public Instruction was formally constituted in Calcutta to disburse the funds.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29 (Development of Education); Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India

stem: Consider the following statements regarding educational policies in British India during the first half of the nineteenth century:
items: Statement-I: Following Lord Macaulay's Minute and Lord William Bentinck's Resolution of March 1835, the Government decided to allocate its limited educational funds solely to impart knowledge of Western sciences and literature through the medium of English to a small class of elite Indians.

Statement-II: Between 1843 and 1853, James Thomason, as Lieutenant-Governor of the North-Western Provinces, developed a comprehensive scheme of vernacular village and tehsildari schools to train local revenue officials and familiarise cultivators with land records.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Macaulay's Minute (1835) and Bentinck's Resolution enshrined the 'Downward Filtration Theory' favouring English-medium higher education for the urban upper and middle classes, James Thomason's vernacular schooling scheme in the North-Western Provinces (1843–53) represented a contrasting utilitarian counter-model driven by the administrative exigencies of the Mahalwari land revenue settlement. Thomason's regional success later inspired Wood's Despatch of 1854 to abandon the Downward Filtration Theory in favour of vernacular mass schooling.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Settling the Orientalist-Anglicist controversy in favour of the Anglicists, Lord Macaulay's Minute (February 2, 1835) and Lord William Bentinck's Resolution (March 7, 1835) laid down that the scanty governmental funds earmarked for education would be spent exclusively on imparting Western sciences and literature through the English language. Under the 'Downward Filtration Theory', the government aimed to educate a small group of upper- and middle-class Indians who would act as interpreters between the British rulers and the masses.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. Between 1843 and 1853, Lieutenant-Governor James Thomason pioneered a comprehensive vernacular elementary education experiment (comprising halqabandi village schools and tehsildari schools) in the North-Western Provinces to teach reading, writing, arithmetic, agricultural accounts, and mensuration in the vernacular so that patwaris and peasant proprietors could understand Mahalwari revenue records. Rather than explaining the Anglicist Downward Filtration policy of Statement-I, Thomason's vernacular model was a pragmatic regional departure from it, demonstrating the viability of state-supported mass vernacular instruction that Wood's Despatch (1854) subsequently recommended for all of British India.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition

stem: With reference to Sir Charles Wood's Despatch of 1854, often described as the 'Magna Carta of English Education in India', consider the following statements:
items: 1. It formally repudiated the 'Downward Filtration Theory', urging the Government of India to assume responsibility for the education of the masses and introducing a system of grants-in-aid to encourage private educational enterprise.
2. To create administrative uniformity across the Presidencies, it recommended that English should serve as the sole medium of instruction at both the primary school and collegiate levels.

3. While recommending the establishment of Universities at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras on the model of the University of London, it mandated compulsory Christian scriptural instruction in all government-run schools and colleges.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Sir Charles Wood's Despatch (1854) created a comprehensive graded hierarchy of education from primary schools to universities, rejecting the Downward Filtration Theory and instituting grants-in-aid for private institutions. Crucially, it bifurcated the medium of instruction—mandating Indian vernaculars at the school level and English for higher collegiate studies—while strictly preserving secular instruction in government institutions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Wood's Despatch (1854) formally rejected the Downward Filtration Theory (at least on paper) by asking the Government of India to shoulder responsibility for the education of the general population. Recognizing that the state alone could not finance mass education, it introduced a structured system of grants-in-aid to stimulate and support privately managed schools and colleges.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Wood's Despatch did NOT recommend English as the sole medium of instruction at all levels. Instead, it prescribed a bifurcated approach: Indian vernacular languages were to be the medium of instruction for primary and school-level education of the masses, whereas English was to be the medium of instruction for higher (collegiate and university) studies.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Although Wood's Despatch recommended establishing affiliating and examining Universities at Calcutta, Bombay, and Madras on the institutional model of the University of London (which were subsequently established in 1857), it explicitly mandated that education imparted in government-run schools and colleges must be strictly secular, adhering to the policy of religious neutrality.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29 (Wood's Despatch, 1854)

stem: With reference to the recommendations and mandate of the Hunter Education Commission (1882–83) appointed during the Viceroyalty of Lord Ripon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It recommended that the control and management of primary education be transferred to the newly created District and Municipal Boards, with primary instruction imparted through the vernacular languages.
2. It proposed a sweeping restructuring of Indian Universities by reducing the size of University Senates and vesting the power of college affiliation directly in the Governor-General-in-Council.

3. To diversify secondary education, it recommended that high school curricula be bifurcated into two distinct streams—a literary stream leading to University entrance and a vocational-commercial stream for practical careers.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Appointed by Lord Ripon in 1882 to review the progress of education since Wood's Despatch of 1854, the Hunter Commission's terms of reference were strictly confined to primary and secondary education, excluding university administration. It linked primary schooling with Ripon's local self-government reforms by devolving management to District and Municipal Boards, and introduced a two-track literary and vocational bifurcation at the high school stage.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The Hunter Commission emphasized that the state's special care was required for the extension and improvement of primary education through the vernacular medium, and recommended transferring the control and management of primary schools to the newly established District and Municipal Boards created under Lord Ripon's local self-government resolution of 1882, with earmarked local funds.

Statement 2 is incorrect. The inquiry of the Hunter Education Commission (1882–83) was explicitly confined to primary and secondary education; university functions and governance were excluded from its purview. The reduction in the size of University Senates, the increase in nominated official Fellows, and the vesting of strict affiliation powers in the Government were recommendations of the Raleigh Commission (1902), enacted through Lord Curzon's Indian Universities Act of 1904.

Statement 3 is correct. Addressing the overly academic nature of secondary schools, the Hunter Commission recommended that secondary (high school) education be divided into two distinct divisions: one literary stream preparing students for the University Entrance (Matriculation) examination, and another practical stream of a commercial, vocational, and non-literary character preparing students for business and industrial pursuits.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29 (Hunter Education Commission, 1882–83)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Raleigh Commission (1902) and the Indian Universities Act of 1904 enacted during the Viceroyalty of Lord Curzon:
items: Statement-I: Indian nationalists led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale strongly opposed the Indian Universities Act of 1904 as a retrograde measure aimed at officializing university administration and restricting the growth of privately managed nationalist colleges.

Statement-II: Based on the recommendations of the Raleigh Commission, the Indian Universities Act of 1904 empowered universities to appoint their own professors and lecturers, equip laboratories, and provided for an annual government grant of five lakh rupees for five years to improve higher education.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Lord Curzon's Indian Universities Act of 1904 embodied a sharp colonial contradiction: pedagogically, it transformed Indian universities from mere examining bodies into teaching and research institutions supported by an annual grant of Rs 5 lakh; politically, however, it drastically reduced the size of University Senates, filled them with government-nominated Fellows, imposed stringent affiliation rules on private colleges, and vested veto power over Senate regulations in the Government.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Nationalists led by Gopal Krishna Gokhale condemned the Indian Universities Act of 1904 inside and outside the Imperial Legislative Council because it curtailed university autonomy to suppress burgeoning nationalist sentiment among educated youth. Specifically, the Act reduced the number of Fellows of a University (to between 50 and 100), ensured that the vast majority of Fellows were nominated by the Government rather than elected, made the conditions for affiliation of private colleges highly stringent (subject to periodic Senate inspection and ultimate government sanction), and empowered the Government to veto, amend, or frame University Senate regulations directly.

Statement-II is correct, but it does not explain Statement-I. Following the Raleigh Commission Report (1902), the 1904 Act did expand the academic scope of universities beyond conducting examinations—requiring them to make provision for the promotion of study and research, appoint university professors and lecturers, set up laboratories and museums, and sanctioning Rs 5 lakh per annum for five years toward improving higher education and universities. However, nationalists did not oppose the Act because of these academic improvements or financial grants; rather, they opposed it because of its authoritarian political provisions (nominated majorities in Senates, government veto power, and bureaucratic stranglehold over private Indian colleges).

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29 (Indian Universities Act, 1904); Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947

stem: With reference to the evolution of educational policy in British India during the early twentieth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In its Resolution on Education Policy of 1913, the Government of India refused to accept the principle of compulsory primary education, but urged provincial governments to assume the responsibility of providing free elementary education to the poorer and more backward sections of society.

2. The Sadler University Commission (1917–19), which included Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin Ahmad as Indian members, held that any qualitative improvement of university education required a prior structural reorganization of secondary education.

3. The Sadler Commission recommended a twelve-year school course up to the Intermediate stage, stipulating that students should enter three-year university degree courses only after passing the Intermediate examination rather than the Matriculation examination.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: After rejecting Gopal Krishna Gokhale's Elementary Education Bill (1911), the British Government issued the Resolution on Education Policy (1913), declining statutory compulsion while endorsing free elementary schooling for backward classes and a university in every province. Shortly thereafter, the Sadler Commission (1917–19) laid the structural blueprint of modern Indian schooling (the 10+2+3 pattern) by detaching the Intermediate stage from universities and placing it under separate Boards of Secondary and Intermediate Education.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Although the Maharaja of Baroda had introduced compulsory primary education in his princely state in 1906 and Gopal Krishna Gokhale had strongly advocated it in the Imperial Legislative Council (1911), the Government of India in its Resolution on Education Policy (February 1913) refused to take up the responsibility of compulsory primary education. Instead, it accepted the policy of removing illiteracy by urging provincial governments to provide free elementary education to the poorer and more backward sections, alongside encouraging private voluntary efforts.

Statement 2 is correct. Appointed in 1917 under the chairmanship of Dr. M.E. Sadler (Vice-Chancellor of Leeds University) to study and report on the problems of Calcutta University, the Commission included two distinguished Indian members—Sir Ashutosh Mukherjee and Dr. Ziauddin Ahmad. A central premise of the Sadler Report was that the improvement of secondary education was an essential precondition for the improvement of university education.

Statement 3 is correct. The Sadler Commission recommended that the school course should cover 12 years, and that the dividing line between university and secondary courses should be drawn at the Intermediate examination rather than the Matriculation examination. It proposed creating separate Boards of Secondary and Intermediate Education to administer high school and intermediate colleges, followed by a three-year degree course at the university stage—the direct precursor of India's modern 10+2+3 educational structure.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 29 (Government Resolution on Education Policy 1913 & Sadler University Commission 1917–19)

stem: With reference to late colonial blueprints on educational policy in British India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Hartog Committee (1929) : Recommended immediate nationwide compulsory primary education through the rapid multiplication of elementary schools

2. Wardha Scheme of Basic Education (1937) : Proposed seven years of free and compulsory education in the mother tongue centered around a productive manual craft, excluding English from the curriculum
3. Sergeant Plan of Education (1944) : Envisaged a phased forty-year reconstruction timeline for India to attain the standard of universal educational parity already prevailing in England
prompt: How many of the above pairs are correctly matched?
core: Late colonial educational policy oscillated between the Hartog Committee's bureaucratic call for 'consolidation over expansion' under Dyarchy, the Gandhian Wardha Scheme's self-supporting craft pedagogy in the mother tongue, and the post-war Sergeant Plan's state-led 40-year blueprint for universal literacy.

exp.why: Pair 1 is incorrectly matched. Appointed as an auxiliary committee of the Indian Statutory (Simon) Commission in 1929, the Philip Hartog Committee sharply criticized the rapid, unplanned quantitative expansion of primary schools carried out by Indian ministers under Provincial Dyarchy after 1919. Highlighting acute 'wastage' (premature withdrawal of pupils before achieving permanent literacy) and 'stagnation' (retention of a child in the same class for more than one academic year), the Hartog Committee explicitly opposed hasty compulsory education and recommended a policy of consolidation, qualitative improvement, and closing down inefficient single-teacher schools.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. Formulated by the Zakir Husain Committee following Mahatma Gandhi's articles in the Harijan and endorsed at the October 1937 All-India National Education Conference at Wardha, Nai Talim (Basic Education) envisaged free and compulsory education for seven years (ages 7 to 14) delivered exclusively in the mother tongue. Its pedagogy integrated intellectual learning around a basic productive manual craft (such as spinning and weaving) to bridge the manual-intellectual divide and excluded the teaching of English and sectarian religion at the basic stage.

Pair 3 is correctly matched. Prepared in 1944 by Sir John Sargent, Educational Adviser to the Government of India, on behalf of the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE), the Post-War Educational Development Plan recommended pre-primary nursery schooling (ages 3–6) and free, universal, compulsory basic education for children aged 6–14 (divided into Junior Basic and Senior Basic stages). Nationalist critics, however, objected to its defeatist timeline, as it projected that India would require 40 years to reach the educational level that Britain had already achieved by 1939.

ref: Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 30 (Development of Education); Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following regulatory measures introduced by the East India Company to govern the printing press in India:
items: 1. Enactment of Licensing Regulations making it a penal offence to start or use a press without a prior gubernatorial licence, forcing Raja Rammohan Roy to cease publication of Mirat-ul-Akbar.

2. Imposition of wartime pre-publication censorship requiring every newspaper to submit all proof sheets, including advertisements, for prior inspection by the Chief Secretary to the Government before printing.
3. Replacement of prior licensing stipulations with a statutory requirement merely to file a precise declaration of the premises of the printer and publisher.
4. Abolition of the office of the pre-publication Censor and its substitution with general editorial guidelines prohibiting animadversions on the Court of Directors.
prompt: Which one of the following represents the correct chronological sequence of the measures given above, from earliest to latest?
core: Company-era press regulation evolved from Wellesley's wartime pre-censorship (1799) to Hastings' administrative relaxation (1818), hardened into Adams' prior-licensing regime targeting Indian reformist journals (1823), and culminated in Metcalfe's liberal registration framework (1835).

exp.why: Chronological Position 3 (1823): Acting Governor-General John Adams promulgated the Licensing Regulations of 1823 after the deportation of James Silk Buckingham of the Calcutta Journal. The ordinance required every printer and publisher to obtain a prior license from the Governor-General-in-Council on pain of a Rs 400 fine or imprisonment, and gave the executive arbitrary power to revoke licenses. Directed primarily against Indian-language and reformist journals, it compelled Raja Rammohan Roy to shut down his Persian weekly, Mirat-ul-Akbar, in protest.
