Although Shiv Narayan Agnihotri was initially an active Brahmo Samaj preacher in Lahore, after breaking away to found the Dev Samaj in 1887, he progressively abandoned Brahmo monotheism in favour of an atheistic and naturalistic philosophy that placed supreme spiritual reverence on the human Guru—ultimately proclaiming himself as the 'Dev Bhagwan Atma' (the ideal Guru) essential for the eternity and liberation of the human soul. Its text, the Deva Shastra, emphasized the eternity of the soul, the supremacy of the Guru, and strict social ethics such as abstinence from bribery, gambling, intoxicants, and non-vegetarian food.

Statement 2 is correct. Tulsi Ram, an Agra banker revered by his followers as Shiv Dayal Saheb (or Swamiji Maharaj), founded the Radhaswami Movement in 1861. The sect believes in one Supreme Being, the absolute spiritual authority of the living Guru, the company of pious devotees (Satsang), and a simple social life. It rejected temple rituals and ascetic renunciation, asserting that secular householder duties are fully compatible with spiritual salvation.

Statement 3 is correct. Founded at Qadian in Gurdaspur district of Punjab in 1889 by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad, the Ahmadiyya Movement described itself as standing on the model of the Brahmo Samaj with respect to universal tolerance and human rights. While defending Islam against Christian missionaries and Arya Samaj polemics and adopting a messianic theology (wherein Mirza Ghulam Ahmad claimed to be the promised Messiah/Mahdi), the movement opposed violent jihad against non-Muslims, endorsed the separation of the mosque from the state, and promoted Western liberal education among Indian Muslims.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 9 (Socio-Religious Reform Movements: General Features and Survey)

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation) in the Madras Presidency:
items: Statement-I: The Justice Party contested the 1920 Madras Presidency Legislative Council elections held under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms, whereas the Indian National Congress boycotted them as part of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

Statement-II: While in office under the system of provincial Dyarchy (1920–1926), the Justice Party refrained from introducing statutory communal quotas in public employment or regulating Hindu temple endowments, viewing state intervention as a threat to traditional social autonomy.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Justice Party (founded in 1916 by T.M. Nair, P. Theagaraya Chetty, and C. Natesa Mudaliar) diverged from the Congress boycott of the 1920 elections because it viewed the colonial constitutional apparatus of Dyarchy as an indispensable lever to break the near-monopoly of Brahmins in the provincial bureaucracy. Once in office, the Justice Party actively used legislative and executive power to issue the historic Communal Government Orders (1921–1922) and enact the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act to bring temple administration under secular state oversight.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Following the Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms), elections to the reformed provincial Legislative Councils were held in November 1920. While the Indian National Congress boycotted the elections under Mahatma Gandhi's Non-Cooperation programme, the Justice Party (South Indian Liberal Federation) participated, won 63 out of 98 elected seats in the Madras Legislative Council, and formed the first ministry under A. Subbarayalu Reddiar and later the Raja of Panagal.

Statement-II is incorrect. Far from refraining from state intervention, the entire structural rationale for the Justice Party's entry into the Councils under Dyarchy was to use state power to dismantle caste monopoly in public administration and religious institutions. The Justice Party ministry issued the landmark First and Second Communal Government Orders (G.O. No. 613 of September 1921 and G.O. No. 658 of August 1922) mandating proportional representation for non-Brahmins, Backward Classes, Muslims, Christians, and Depressed Classes in government services, and enacted the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act (passed in 1925, enforced as Act II of 1927) to regulate vast temple endowments.

ref: Shekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 7; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence

stem: With reference to colonial legislative interventions in marriage and social customs in British India, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Native Marriage Act (Civil Marriage Act) of 1872 applied universally to all Hindu, Muslim, and Christian subjects across British India to legalize inter-caste marriages without requiring any declaration regarding religious belief.

2. The Age of Consent Act of 1891, championed by Parsi reformer Behramji Malabari, amended the penal law to raise the age of consent for sexual intercourse for all girls, married or unmarried, from ten to twelve years.

3. The Child Marriage Restraint Act of 1929 (Sarda Act) was the first pan-Indian social legislation to prescribe minimum marriageable ages for boys and girls across all religious communities in British India.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Colonial marriage legislation evolved from a narrow, disclaimer-bound civil marriage statute in 1872 (restricted practically to Brahmos due to orthodox opposition) to indirect penal regulation of consummation via the Age of Consent Act (1891), and finally to universal statutory minimum marriage ages across all communities under the Sarda Act (1929).

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. Although Keshab Chandra Sen campaigned for a progressive marriage law, stiff resistance from orthodox religious groups forced the colonial government to drastically narrow the scope of the Native Marriage Act (Act III of 1872). It applied ONLY to contracting parties who explicitly signed a formal declaration that they did not profess the Hindu, Muhammadan, Christian, Parsi, Buddhist, Sikh, or Jaina religion—making it effectively a Brahmo Marriage Act. Only through Hari Singh Gour's Special Marriage (Amendment) Act of 1923 were Hindus, Buddhists, Sikhs, and Jains permitted to marry under the Act without renouncing their faith.

Statement 2 is correct. Catalyzed by Behramji Malabari's 'Notes on Infant Marriage and Enforced Widowhood' (1884) and the tragic death of ten-year-old bride Phulmoni Dasi in 1889, the Age of Consent Act, 1891 (introduced by Sir Andrew Scoble) raised the age of consent for girls from 10 to 12 years, classifying sexual intercourse with a girl below 12 (even within marriage) as rape.

Statement 3 is correct. Sponsored by Rai Sahib Harbilas Sarda and enacted in 1929 (coming into force on April 1, 1930), the Child Marriage Restraint Act fixed the minimum marriageable age at 14 years for girls and 18 years for boys. Unlike the 1872 Act, it applied universally across all religious communities in British India without requiring any renunciation of personal faith.

ref: Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 9; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideological trajectory of 19th-century socio-religious reform movements in India:
items: Statement-I: Alongside fostering modern cultural awakening and nationalist self-confidence, several late 19th-century socio-religious reform movements inadvertently contributed to the growth of communal consciousness in colonial India.

Statement-II: In seeking indigenous legitimacy against colonial cultural hegemony, many reformers relied heavily on scriptural infallibility, idealized an ancient 'Golden Age' defined in exclusively religious terms, and treated the medieval period largely as an era of cultural decline.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While 19th-century reform movements attacked social evils and restored cultural self-respect, their reliance on religious scriptures, ancient revivalism, and competitive proselytization (such as Shuddhi and Tabligh/Tanzim) created compartmentalized historical memories that undermined composite secular identity.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Historiographical analysis shows that because the social base of 19th-century reform movements was primarily the educated urban middle class and their idiom was overwhelmingly religious, their compartmentalized appeals to distinct religious communities inadvertently laid cultural fault lines that aided communal polarization in the 20th century.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. By anchoring social reform in scriptural authority (such as the Vedas or early Islamic texts), glorifying an ancient Hindu 'Golden Age' while depicting the medieval Indo-Islamic period as one of decadence—or conversely looking solely to West Asian Islamic history for inspiration—and engaging in competitive conversion/reconversion drives like Shuddhi and Tabligh, revivalist streams alienated other religious communities and reinforced communal consciousness.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India, Ch. 9; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 8 (Limitations of Reform Movements)

stem: Consider the following pairs of 19th-century social reformers and the institutions or initiatives founded by them:
items: 1. Kandukuri Veeresalingam : Rajahmundry Social Reform Association
2. K. Sridharalu Naidu : Bombay Native General Library and the weekly Darpan
3. Balshastri Jambhekar : Reorganized the Veda Samaj into the Brahmo Samaj of Southern India
4. Behramji M. Malabari : Seva Sadan (1908)
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Regional socio-religious reform across the Madras and Bombay Presidencies was spearheaded by pioneers such as Kandukuri Veeresalingam in Andhra, K. Sridharalu Naidu in Madras, and Balshastri Jambhekar and Behramji Malabari in Western India.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Kandukuri Veeresalingam Pantulu (1848–1919), regarded as the father of the Telugu Renaissance, started the journal Vivekavardhini (1874), founded the Rajahmundry Social Reform Association (1878) to champion widow remarriage and girls' education, and later established the Hitakarini Samaj (1906).

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The Bombay Native General Library and the Anglo-Marathi weekly Darpan (1832) were founded by Balshastri Jambhekar (1812–1846), the pioneer of social reform through journalism in Bombay. K. Sridharalu Naidu was a reformer in the Madras Presidency.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The Veda Samaj (established in Madras in 1864 under the inspiration of Keshab Chandra Sen) was reorganized into the Brahmo Samaj of Southern India in 1871 by K. Sridharalu Naidu, who translated the books of the Brahmo Dharma into Tamil and Telugu.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Parsi social reformer Behramji M. Malabari, along with his friend Diwan Dayaram Gidumal, founded the Seva Sadan in Bombay in 1908 to care for destitute, exploited, and discarded women of all castes and provide them with education, medical, and welfare services.

ref: Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 9

stem: With reference to the literary works and periodicals associated with 19th-century socio-religious reform in India, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Tritiya Ratna (1855) : Jyotirao Phule
2. Shatapatre (published in Prabhakar) : Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar
3. Somaprakash : Gopal Hari Deshmukh
4. Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq : Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Vernacular plays, epistolary essays, and reformist periodicals served as the primary vehicles for 19th-century ideologues to critique priestly orthodoxy, caste oppression, and social stagnation across Maharashtra, Bengal, and North India.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Written by Jyotirao Phule in 1855, Tritiya Ratna ('The Third Eye') is considered the first modern social play in Marathi. It dramatizes how a Brahmin priest exploits an ignorant peasant couple through astrological rituals and how critical education—the 'third eye'—emancipates the Shudra-Atishudra peasantry from mental slavery.

Pair 2 is incorrectly matched. The famous series of social reform letters titled Shatapatre ('Hundred Letters') was penned between 1848 and 1850 in the Marathi weekly Prabhakar by Gopal Hari Deshmukh (1823–1892), who wrote under the pen name 'Lokahitawadi'.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. Somaprakash was a prestigious Bengali weekly newspaper launched in 1858 by Dwarkanath Vidyabhusan under the direct inspiration and editorial planning of Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar. It championed widow remarriage, criticized indigo planters, and was later targeted by Lord Lytton's Vernacular Press Act of 1878.

Pair 4 is correctly matched. Tahzib-ul-Akhlaq ('The Mohammedan Social Reformer') was an influential Urdu journal started by Sir Syed Ahmad Khan in December 1870 upon his return from England to combat religious orthodoxy and promote scientific rationalism and modern education among Indian Muslims.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 3; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 9

stem: Consider the establishment of the following socio-religious reform organizations in the 19th century:
items: 1. Prarthana Samaj in Bombay
2. Tattvabodhini Sabha in Calcutta
3. Satyashodhak Samaj in Pune
4. Paramahansa Mandali in Bombay
prompt: What is the correct chronological sequence of the establishment of the above organizations, from the earliest to the latest?
core: Tracking the institutional chronology of 19th-century reform reveals the transition from early rationalist-Upanishadic circles in Bengal (Tattvabodhini Sabha, 1839) and secret anti-caste societies in Bombay (Paramahansa Mandali, 1849) to open theistic reform (Prarthana Samaj, 1867) and radical non-Brahmin mobilization (Satyashodhak Samaj, 1873).

exp.why: Prarthana Samaj (Item 1) was founded in Bombay in 1867 by Dr. Atmaram Pandurang (with the inspiration of Keshab Chandra Sen) and gained immense momentum when M.G. Ranade and R.G. Bhandarkar joined it in 1870.

Tattvabodhini Sabha (Item 2) is the earliest among the four, founded on October 6, 1839, in Calcutta by Debendranath Tagore to propagate Rammohun Roy's rationalist-monotheistic ideas and conduct a systematic study of India's past before he revitalized the Brahmo Samaj in 1842.

Satyashodhak Samaj (Item 3) is the latest among the four, established on September 24, 1873, in Pune by Jyotirao Phule to liberate the Bahujan/Shudra-Atishudra masses from Brahmanical ritual and socio-economic exploitation (preceding Swami Dayananda Saraswati's Arya Samaj, which was founded in 1875).

Paramahansa Mandali (Item 4) was founded in 1849 in Bombay by Dadoba Pandurang, Mehtaji Durgaram, and others as a secret radical society whose members broke caste taboos by partaking of food cooked by lower-caste individuals. Thus, the exact chronological order is 2 (1839) -> 4 (1849) -> 1 (1867) -> 3 (1873).

ref: NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History / Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 9

stem: In October 1851, two existing political bodies in Calcutta—one primarily representing the class interests of the landed aristocracy and the other comprising English-educated intellectuals modeled on London's reformist societies—amalgamated to overcome their respective political limitations. Ahead of the renewal of the East India Company's Charter in 1853, this newly formed body sent a comprehensive petition to the British Parliament demanding the establishment of a separate legislature of a popular character, separation of executive from judicial functions, reduction in the salaries of higher officials, and the abolition of salt duty and abkari taxes. Which one of the following political organizations is described above?
core: The British Indian Association (1851) represented the institutional synthesis of early Bengal politics through the merger of the Landholders' Society (1838) and the Bengal British India Society (1843). Its 1852 Charter petition pioneered structured constitutional demands for a representative legislature and administrative Indianization, even while retaining an upper-class zamindari bias.

exp.why: Option (B) is correct. Neither the Landholders' Society (founded in 1838 to safeguard zamindari interests) nor the Bengal British India Society (founded in 1843 by George Thompson and Young Bengal intellectuals to collect information on the condition of the general public) achieved substantial political leverage independently. Consequently, in October 1851, the two bodies merged to form the British Indian Association in Calcutta, with Raja Radhakanta Deb as President and Debendranath Tagore as Secretary. Its 1852 petition to the British Parliament prior to the Charter Act of 1853 demanded a separate popular legislature, separation of executive and judicial functions, reduction of higher civil service salaries, and abolition of salt duty, abkari, and stamp duties; this partially influenced the Charter Act of 1853 to add six legislative members to the Governor-General's Council. Option (A) is incorrect because the Bengal British India Society (1843) was one of the two parent bodies that dissolved into the 1851 merger. Option (C) is incorrect because the Indian Association of Calcutta was founded much later in 1876 by Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose precisely because the British Indian Association had remained dominated by conservative landlords. Option (D) is incorrect because the Madras Native Association was established in 1852 by Gazulu Lakshminarasu Chetty in the Madras Presidency.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 10 (Beginning of Modern Nationalism in India)

stem: With reference to the political organizations established during the second half of the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The East India Association was organized by Dadabhai Naoroji in London to counter ethnocentric assertions of Asian inferiority and to acquaint British Parliamentarians with Indian administrative grievances.

2. To build political synergy between metropolitan agitators and Indian public opinion, the East India Association subsequently established branches in the presidency cities of Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.

3. The India League of 1875 was founded in London by Sisir Kumar Ghosh to lobby the Secretary of State for India directly, whereas the London Indian Society was started in Calcutta to promote vernacular political journalism.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Early Indian nationalism operated on a dual geographic front: metropolitan advocacy in London led by Dadabhai Naoroji's East India Association (1866) to influence the British electorate and Parliament, and vernacular middle-class mobilization in Bengal led by Sisir Kumar Ghosh's India League (1875).

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Dadabhai Naoroji organized the East India Association in London in December 1866 (superseding the London Indian Society of 1865). An immediate catalyst was the need to refute racist papers read before the London Ethnological Society (such as those by John Crawfurd) asserting the intellectual and moral inferiority of Asians, while systematically educating British MPs and the public on the economic drain and administrative grievances in India.

Statement 2 is correct. Unlike earlier short-lived committees in England, the East India Association actively sought financial and moral backing from India; in 1869, Dadabhai Naoroji visited India and established branches of the Association in Bombay, Calcutta, and Madras.

Statement 3 is incorrect because it swaps the locations and objectives of the two organizations. The India League was founded in Calcutta (not London) in September 1875 by Sisir Kumar Ghosh and his associates associated with the Amrita Bazar Patrika to stimulate a sense of nationalism among the people and encourage political education among the Indian middle class. Conversely, the London Indian Society was established in London in 1865 by Indian students and leaders including Dadabhai Naoroji, W.C. Bonnerjee, Pherozeshah Mehta, and Badruddin Tyabji.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 4; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the Indian Association of Calcutta (1876), founded by Surendranath Banerjea and Ananda Mohan Bose, consider the following statements:
items: 1. To break the monopoly of the landed aristocracy over Bengal politics and broaden its social base, the Association lowered its annual membership subscription for peasants and artisans to only one rupee.

2. It launched the all-India Civil Services agitation of 1877 in protest against Lord Lytton's decision to abolish competitive examinations in London and replace them wholly with nomination by princely states.
3. Prior to the founding of the Indian National Congress, it convened an All-India National Conference in Calcutta in 1883 to unite regional political leaders on a common constitutional platform.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Association of Calcutta (1876) marked a decisive shift from zamindari politics to mass-oriented middle-class nationalism by lowering subscription barriers, organizing ryot unions during the Bengal Tenancy Bill debates, spearheading the 1877 ICS age-reduction protest across India, and convening the 1883 and 1885 National Conferences.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Whereas the conservative British Indian Association charged an exorbitant annual subscription of Rs 50—effectively restricting membership to wealthy zamindars—the Indian Association fixed its regular annual fee at Rs 5 and reduced it to only Re 1 for peasants and working-class members. It also established branches in mofussil towns and organized massive ryot meetings demanding occupancy rights ahead of the Bengal Tenancy Act of 1885.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Lord Lytton never abolished the competitive examination in London. The all-India Civil Services agitation of 1877—during which Surendranath Banerjea undertook a historic tour of northern, western, and southern India—was triggered by the Secretary of State Salisbury and Viceroy Lytton's 1876 decision to reduce the maximum age limit for appearing in the Open Competitive Examination for the Indian Civil Service from 21 to 19 years, which severely disadvantaged Indian candidates. The Association demanded raising the age limit and holding simultaneous ICS examinations in England and India.

Statement 3 is correct. In December 1883, prompted by the Ilbert Bill controversy and the conviction of Surendranath Banerjea in a contempt of court case, the Indian Association sponsored the first All-India National Conference at Albert Hall in Calcutta, attended by over a hundred delegates from across India, followed by a second session in December 1885.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947, Ch. 2

stem: Consider the following pairs of pre-Congress regional political organizations in Western and Southern India and their founders and distinct initiatives:
items: 1. Poona Sarvajanik Sabha : Founded by Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi and M.G. Ranade; established indigenous arbitration courts (Nyaya Sabhas) and conducted agrarian famine inquiries in the Deccan
2. Bombay Association (1852) : Founded by Jagannath Shankarsheth and Dadabhai Naoroji; petitioned the British Parliament against the exclusionary and expensive character of Company administration
3. Madras Mahajan Sabha : Founded by Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, and Badruddin Tyabji; mobilized public opinion against Lord Lytton's reactionary policies and the Ilbert Bill controversy
4. Bombay Presidency Association : Founded by M. Viraraghavachari, G. Subramania Iyer, and P. Anandacharlu; coordinated the political activities of local mofussil associations at annual conferences
prompt: Which of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: Regional political associations in the Bombay and Madras Presidencies evolved in two waves: the 1852 Charter-era associations led by mercantile-intellectual coalitions, and the more assertive 1870–1885 middle-class bodies led by professional lawyers and journalists that directly laid the organizational groundwork for the Indian National Congress.

exp.why: Pair 1 is correctly matched. Established in April 1870 by Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi ('Sarvajanik Kaka'), S.H. Chiplunkar, and Mahadev Govind Ranade, the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha required every member to hold a mukhtyarnama (power of attorney) signed by at least 50 citizens. It pioneered swadeshi arbitration courts (Nyaya Sabhas) to settle civil disputes outside costly colonial courts and published rigorous statistical reports on peasant indebtedness during the Deccan famine and agrarian riots of the 1870s.

Pair 2 is correctly matched. The Bombay Association, founded in August 1852 on the model of the British Indian Association of Calcutta by Jagannath Shankarsheth (Nana Shankarsheth), Dadabhai Naoroji, Naoroji Furdunji, and Bhau Daji Lad, was the first political association in the Bombay Presidency and submitted memorials to the British Parliament ahead of the 1853 Charter renewal.

Pair 3 is incorrectly matched. The Madras Mahajan Sabha was founded in May 1884 by M. Viraraghavachari, G. Subramania Iyer (B. Subramaniya Aiyer), and P. Anandacharlu in Madras to coordinate the activities of local mofussil associations at annual conferences, not by the Bombay 'Trimurti' of Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, and Badruddin Tyabji.

Pair 4 is incorrectly matched. The Bombay Presidency Association was established in January 1885 by Pherozeshah Mehta, K.T. Telang, and Badruddin Tyabji in response to the reactionary policies of Lord Lytton and the Anglo-Indian agitation against the Ilbert Bill.

ref: Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 10; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 4

stem: Consider the following pre-Congress political organizations established during the nineteenth century:
items: 1. Poona Sarvajanik Sabha
2. British Indian Association
3. Madras Mahajan Sabha
4. East India Association
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of their establishment, from the earliest to the latest?
core: Tracing the chronological trajectory of pre-1885 political associations reveals the steady institutional maturation of Indian nationalism: from the 1851–52 Charter-era landed and mercantile petitions, through the 1866 metropolitan advocacy in London and 1870 Deccan civic representation, to the 1884–85 Presidency-wide federations immediately preceding the Congress.

exp.why: The Poona Sarvajanik Sabha (1) was founded in April 1870 by Ganesh Vasudeo Joshi, S.H. Chiplunkar, and M.G. Ranade in Maharashtra, placing it third in the chronological sequence.

The British Indian Association (2) was established in October 1851 in Calcutta through the amalgamation of the Landholders' Society (1838) and the Bengal British India Society (1843), making it the earliest among the four organizations.

The Madras Mahajan Sabha (3) was founded in May 1884 by M. Viraraghavachari, G. Subramania Iyer, and P. Anandacharlu (distinct from the earlier Madras Native Association of 1852), making it the latest among the four organizations.

The East India Association (4) was organized by Dadabhai Naoroji in London in December 1866, placing it second in the sequence. Thus, the exact chronological order is 2 (1851) -> 4 (1866) -> 1 (1870) -> 3 (1884), corresponding to Option (A).

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 10

stem: With reference to the inaugural session of the Indian National Congress held in December 1885, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Originally scheduled to be hosted in Poona with the active cooperation of the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha, the venue had to be shifted to Bombay due to an outbreak of cholera in Poona.
2. Surendranath Banerjea abstained from attending the inaugural Bombay session due to sharp ideological disagreements with the Moderate method of constitutional petitioning.
3. While Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee presided over the first session attended by 72 delegates, Allan Octavian Hume assumed the office of General Secretary of the Congress.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The birth of the Indian National Congress in December 1885 was the culmination of parallel all-India organizational efforts; Surendranath Banerjea's absence at the inaugural Bombay session was purely a scheduling coincidence with the Second National Conference in Calcutta, not an ideological rift.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. The March 1885 circular issued by A.O. Hume and other leaders originally decided to convene the 'Indian National Union' conference at Poona in December 1885, with the Poona Sarvajanik Sabha serving as the host reception committee. However, an outbreak of cholera in Poona on the eve of the conference necessitated an urgent shift of venue to Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College in Bombay.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Surendranath Banerjea was himself a leading architect of Moderate constitutional nationalism and shared identical political methods and objectives with the founders of the INC. He could not attend the inaugural Bombay session in December 1885 only because the Indian Association of Calcutta had already scheduled and convened the Second All-India National Conference in Calcutta during the exact same days (25–27 December 1885). Recognizing that two parallel all-India bodies were redundant, Banerjea and the National Conference merged completely with the Indian National Congress at its second session in Calcutta in December 1886.

Statement 3 is correct. The first session of the Indian National Congress at Bombay (28–30 December 1885) was attended by 72 non-official Indian delegates (predominantly lawyers, journalists, and educators) and presided over by Womesh Chandra Bonnerjee, while A.O. Hume served as the first General Secretary.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 11 (Indian National Congress: Foundation and the Moderate Phase)

stem: With reference to the historiographical debate surrounding the foundation of the Indian National Congress (INC) in 1885, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Early Indian nationalists willingly collaborated with retired British civil servant A.O. Hume in founding the Indian National Congress, utilizing his presence as a 'lightning conductor' to shield the nascent all-India political body from immediate official suppression.

Statement-II: As recorded by Gopal Krishna Gokhale in William Wedderburn's 1913 biography of A.O. Hume—a work later cited by Lala Lajpat Rai to advance the 'Safety Valve' critique—colonial authorities in the 1880s harboured such acute suspicion of political agitation that any purely Indian-led all-India organization would have been suppressed at birth.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Extremist leader Lala Lajpat Rai (1916) used William Wedderburn's 1913 biography of A.O. Hume to argue that the INC was conceived by Lord Dufferin and Hume as a 'safety valve' to defuse popular discontent, liberal nationalists and modern historians point to Gopal Krishna Gokhale's observation in the same biography that Indian leaders consciously used Hume as a 'lightning conductor' to prevent the colonial bureaucracy from strangling the nascent all-India movement at birth.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Early Indian leaders were politically conscious patriots who recognized the utility of having a retired British ICS officer like A.O. Hume at the forefront of organizing the INC in 1885. In modern historiography (such as Bipan Chandra's analysis drawing on Gokhale), Hume functioned as a 'lightning conductor'—absorbing official hostility so that an all-India nationalist organization could take root safely.

Statement-II is correct and directly explains Statement-I. In William Wedderburn's biography of A.O. Hume (1913)—which Lala Lajpat Rai later invoked in 'Young India' (1916) to propound the 'Safety Valve' theory—Gopal Krishna Gokhale explicitly stated that in 1885, 'no Indian could have started the Indian National Congress' because the official distrust of political agitation was so intense that the colonial authorities would have immediately found a way to suppress the movement had an Indian stepped forward to lead it. This explains why Indian nationalists associated with Hume.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Beginning of Modern Nationalism in India

stem: With reference to the institutional conventions and early annual sessions of the Indian National Congress during the Moderate phase (1885–1905), consider the following statements:
items: 1. At the 1888 Allahabad session, the Congress adopted a formal rule that no resolution would be passed on any subject if an overwhelming majority of either the Hindu or the Muslim delegates objected to it, alongside observing the convention that the President must belong to a province other than the one hosting the session.
2. Kadambini Ganguly, one of the first women graduates in the British Empire, became the first woman to preside over an annual session of the Indian National Congress at Calcutta in 1890.
3. Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the annual session of the Indian National Congress only once during the Moderate phase (1885–1905).
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: To forge a secular all-India national identity and allay minority apprehensions, the early Congress instituted structural safeguards such as the 1888 Allahabad communal consensus rule and the inter-provincial presidency convention. It also symbolically included educated women like Kadambini Ganguly (who addressed the 1890 session), though no woman presided over the Congress until Annie Besant in 1917.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. To reassure religious minorities (particularly in the wake of Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's opposition), the Congress at its 4th session in Allahabad (1888, presided over by George Yule) passed a formal rule that no resolution would be adopted if an overwhelming majority of Hindu or Muslim delegates objected to it. Furthermore, to promote pan-Indian integration, an unwritten convention was strictly followed that the President of a session had to belong to a region other than where the session was being held.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Kadambini Ganguly, the first woman graduate of Calcutta University, addressed the 1890 Calcutta session of the INC (proposing the vote of thanks to President Pherozeshah Mehta), symbolizing the commitment of the national movement to women's upliftment. However, she did not preside over the session. Annie Besant (Calcutta, 1917) was the first woman President of the INC, and Sarojini Naidu (Kanpur, 1925) was the first Indian woman President.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Dadabhai Naoroji presided over the INC twice during the Moderate phase (1885–1905): first at the 2nd session in Calcutta (1886) and second at the 9th session in Lahore (1893). He presided a third time at the historic Calcutta session in 1906.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 6; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the evolution of British official policy toward the Indian National Congress during the late nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: Statement-I: Within five years of the inception of the Indian National Congress, the attitude of the colonial state shifted from Lord Dufferin's initial gesture of hosting a garden party for delegates at the 1886 Calcutta session to issuing an official circular in 1890 prohibiting government employees from attending Congress meetings.

Statement-II: Following the 1887 Madras session, the Moderate leadership formally discarded constitutional petitions and published vernacular pamphlets such as the Tamil 'Congress Catechism' to organize a peasant no-revenue campaign across the Presidencies.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: British official neutrality toward the INC evaporated rapidly between 1887 and 1890 not because the Moderates abandoned constitutional methods, but because nationalists began translating their economic and administrative critique into vernacular pamphlets—such as Viraraghavachari's Tamil 'Congress Catechism'—threatening to awaken mass political consciousness against colonial rule.

exp.why: Statement-I is correct. Initially, Viceroy Lord Dufferin maintained a posture of polite neutrality and even invited the delegates of the 1886 Calcutta session (as 'distinguished visitors') to a garden party. However, by 1888, in his St. Andrew's Day dinner speech, Dufferin publicly derided the Congress as representing only a 'microscopic minority'. In 1890, the colonial government institutionalized this hostility by barring government servants from attending Congress sessions even as observers.

Statement-II is incorrect. Around the 1887 Madras session, nationalists did publish and distribute vernacular pamphlets—most notably the Tamil 'Congress Catechism' written by M. Viraraghavachari and Bengali nationalist songs/dramas—to explain the drain of wealth and the need for representative councils to the common people, which alarmed Lord Dufferin. However, the Moderates never discarded constitutional petitions or called for a peasant no-revenue campaign; their goal was lawful political education rather than direct mass defiance.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5 & 6; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947

stem: During the Moderate phase (1885–1905), the Indian National Congress devoted substantial financial and organizational energy to establishing the British Committee of the Indian National Congress in London (1889) and publishing its weekly journal, 'India'. Which one of the following best explains the underlying strategic premise behind this overseas campaign?

opts.A: They believed that the British Crown had constitutionally delegated complete fiscal autonomy to the Viceroy's Executive Council, which could only be overruled by a judicial decree of the Privy Council in London.
opts.B: They held that the British public and Parliament were fundamentally just and fair-minded, and remained unaware of how the colonial bureaucracy in India was subverting British liberal principles through 'un-British' rule.
opts.C: They sought to forge a formal electoral alliance with the nascent British Labour Party to replace the office of the Secretary of State for India with a directly elected Imperial Federation.
opts.D: They concluded that constitutional agitation within India was legally prohibited under the Indian Councils Act of 1861, leaving parliamentary lobbying in London as the sole lawful avenue for reform.

core: Moderate political methodology rested on the distinction between enlightened British democratic ideals at home and the autocratic colonial bureaucracy ('Anglo-Indian bureaucracy') operating in India. By educating British voters and Members of Parliament through the British Committee in London (1889) and the journal 'India', they hoped to compel Westminster to reform the 'un-British' administration in India.

exp.why: Option B is correct. The Moderates (such as Dadabhai Naoroji, W.C. Bonnerjee, and Gopal Krishna Gokhale) operated on the strategic premise that the British people and Parliament were inherently lovers of liberty and justice, and that India's grievances stemmed from the reactionary and autocratic colonial bureaucracy ('un-British rule') in India hiding the true state of Indian affairs from the British public. Consequently, in 1889, the British Committee of the INC was founded in London (chaired by William Wedderburn, with William Digby as secretary) and the journal 'India' was launched in 1890 to directly inform British public opinion and Parliament. Option A is incorrect because fiscal control rested with the Secretary of State for India-in-Council accountable to Parliament, not the Privy Council. Option C is incorrect because the Moderates primarily allied with sympathetic Radical Liberals (like Charles Bradlaugh and Henry Cotton) long before the British Labour Party became a major force. Option D is incorrect because constitutional agitation in India was never prohibited under the 1861 Act.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 6; Dadabhai Naoroji, Poverty and Un-British Rule in India

stem: With reference to the economic critique of colonialism developed by the early nationalists during the late nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Early nationalist economists argued that the large-scale inflow of British foreign capital into Indian railways, mines, and plantations did not catalyse indigenous industrialization, but instead deepened the economic drain and political subjugation of India.

2. To protect traditional artisans from deindustrialization, Moderate economists like M.G. Ranade and R.C. Dutt opposed modern machine-based factory production and advocated a return to self-sufficient village handicraft economies.

3. The 'Home Charges', identified by Dadabhai Naoroji as a primary channel of the drain of wealth, included the administrative expenses of the India Office in London, pensions of British officials, and interest on the Indian public debt raised in Britain.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Moderate economic critique (led by Dadabhai Naoroji, M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, and R.C. Dutt) dismantled the colonial myth of benevolent modernization by demonstrating how 'Home Charges' and guaranteed returns on British railway capital drained India's investible surplus. Crucially, the Moderates were modernizers who championed state-supported, tariff-protected large-scale factory industrialization rather than village handicraft autarky.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Early nationalists like Dadabhai Naoroji, G.V. Joshi, M.G. Ranade, and G. Subramania Iyer pierced through the colonial claim that British capital investment in railways and plantations was modernizing India. They pointed out that unlike in independent nations where foreign capital was borrowed and managed by domestic enterprise, foreign capital in India suppressed indigenous entrepreneurs, repatriated all profits and guaranteed 5% railway interest abroad, and created vested British financial interests that opposed Indian self-government.

Statement 2 is incorrect. While the Moderates lamented the destruction of traditional Indian handicrafts without any corresponding growth of modern industry (resulting in progressive ruralization), economists like M.G. Ranade, G.V. Joshi, and R.C. Dutt were ardent proponents of modern, machine-based large-scale factory industrialization. They demanded tariff protection for infant Indian industries, state-sponsored technical education, and indigenous banking—not a return to pre-modern village handicraft self-sufficiency (which emerged later under Gandhian economic thought).

Statement 3 is correct. 'Home Charges' constituted the official component of the economic drain remitted annually by the Government of India to the Secretary of State in London. It comprised civil and military pensions payable to retired British officers, the administrative upkeep of the India Office in London, purchase of military stores in Britain, and interest on the Indian public debt and guaranteed railway capital raised in London.

ref: Bipan Chandra, The Rise and Growth of Economic Nationalism in India; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 7

stem: With reference to the fiscal, tariff, and agrarian demands articulated by the Moderates in the Indian National Congress (1885–1905), consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Moderates supported the imposition of the countervailing cotton excise duties of 1894 and 1896 by the colonial government as a necessary progressive tax on wealthy Indian mill-owners to finance famine relief.

2. While demanding the abolition of the salt tax, the Moderates endorsed charging the military expenditure of British expeditions in Burma and Afghanistan to the Indian treasury on the ground that it modernized the Indian Army.

3. To protect peasant cultivators from rent extraction, the Moderates demanded the immediate abolition of the Permanent Settlement in Bengal and opposed the permanent fixation of state land revenue demand in Ryotwari areas.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Moderate fiscal nationalism systematically exposed how colonial taxation, tariff, and expenditure policies served British imperial and metropolitan interests at India's expense. They vehemently opposed the 1894/1896 countervailing cotton excise duties, condemned charging imperial frontier wars to the Indian taxpayer, and demanded the permanent fixation and reduction of the state's land revenue demand.

exp.why: Statement 1 is incorrect. When the colonial government imposed a 5% import duty on cotton goods in 1894 due to a fiscal deficit, pressure from Lancashire textile manufacturers forced the government to impose a 'countervailing excise duty' (1894 and 1896) on cotton fabrics manufactured in Indian mills. The Moderates unanimously condemned this countervailing excise duty as a blatant, partisan betrayal of nascent Indian industry to preserve Lancashire's competitive advantage.

Statement 2 is incorrect. Alongside campaigning against the regressive salt tax that hurt the poorest Indians, the Moderates fiercely criticized the colonial policy of using the Indian Army for British imperial expansion in Burma, Afghanistan, Tibet, and East Africa while charging the massive military expenditure of these trans-frontier wars to the impoverished Indian treasury instead of the British Exchequer.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Far from demanding the abolition of the Permanent Settlement, Moderate economists (most notably R.C. Dutt and G.V. Joshi) argued that the high and periodically revised land revenue assessments in Ryotwari and Mahalwari regions impoverished the peasantry and caused recurring famines. They therefore demanded a substantial reduction in land revenue and the extension of a Permanent Settlement—meaning a permanent fixation of the state's maximum land revenue demand—to Ryotwari and Mahalwari areas to shield cultivators from arbitrary periodic enhancements.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 7; R.C. Dutt, The Economic History of India in the Victorian Age

stem: With reference to the Indian Councils Act of 1892 and the constitutional agitation of the early nationalists, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Act maintained an official majority in the Imperial Legislative Council while conceding a non-official majority in the Provincial Legislative Councils.

2. It empowered members of the Legislative Councils to discuss the annual financial statement and address questions to the Executive on matters of public interest only after giving six days' prior notice, without any right to vote on the budget or ask supplementary questions.

3. It introduced the principle of indirect representation by authorizing local bodies such as universities, district boards, municipalities, and chambers of commerce to recommend non-official members to the Councils, without explicitly using the term 'election' in the statute.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 cautiously expanded legislative councils and introduced indirect nomination ('recommendation') and limited financial discussion, but retained an official majority in both Central and Provincial legislatures and withheld the right to vote on the budget or ask supplementary questions.

exp.why: The Indian Councils Act of 1892 retained an official majority in both the Imperial Legislative Council and the Provincial Legislative Councils. A non-official majority in the Provincial Legislative Councils was conceded for the first time only under the Indian Councils Act of 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms).

Under the 1892 Act, members were granted the right to discuss the annual financial statement (budget) and ask questions on matters of public interest subject to a mandatory six days' prior notice, but they could neither vote on the budget item-by-item nor ask supplementary questions—a limitation that led Moderates to intensify their slogan of 'No taxation without representation'.

Under the 'Kimberley Clause' (Section 1(4) of the 1892 Act), the Governor-General and provincial Governors were empowered to make rules under which bodies like municipalities, district boards, universities, and chambers of commerce could 'recommend' non-official members for nomination, introducing indirect election in practice while avoiding the word 'election' in the text of the Act.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 6; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 11

stem: With reference to the administrative and civil liberties agitation carried out during the Moderate phase (1885–1905) of the Indian National Congress, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In 1893, owing to the campaign of the Indian Parliamentary Committee in Britain, the House of Commons passed a resolution supporting simultaneous civil service examinations in England and India, though the Government of India declined to implement it.

2. The Aitchison Commission on Public Services (1886) accepted the Congress demand for simultaneous examinations in India and England and recommended a 50:50 parity between Europeans and Indians in the Imperial Civil Service within fifteen years.

3. Alongside demanding the separation of the judiciary from the executive and the extension of trial by jury, the Moderate leadership unanimously protested against the arrest of Bal Gangadhar Tilak and the deportation of the Natu brothers without trial in 1897.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Early Moderate nationalists fought tenaciously for the Indianisation of civil services and civil liberties, securing a non-binding House of Commons resolution on simultaneous ICS exams in 1893 and defending Tilak and the Natu brothers in 1897, even as the Aitchison Commission (1886) rejected simultaneous exams.

exp.why: In June 1893, Herbert Paul moved a resolution in the British House of Commons—backed by Dadabhai Naoroji, William Wedderburn, and the Indian Parliamentary Committee—in favour of holding simultaneous ICS examinations in England and India. Although the resolution passed by a narrow majority, Secretary of State Lord Kimberley and the Government of India refused to implement it.

The Aitchison Commission (1886), appointed by Lord Dufferin, explicitly rejected the Congress demand for holding simultaneous ICS examinations in India and England. Instead, it abolished the Statutory Civil Service, replaced the terms 'covenanted' and 'uncovenanted' with Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate Civil Services, and raised the maximum age limit to 23. The 50:50 parity between Europeans and Indians over 15 years was recommended much later by the Lee Commission (1924).

The Moderates consistently campaigned for the separation of executive and judicial functions, repeal of the Arms Act (1878), and protection of trial by jury. When the colonial state arrested B.G. Tilak for sedition and deported the Natu brothers of Poona without trial under Regulation XXV of 1827 in 1897, Moderate leaders (including Surendranath Banerjea, W.C. Bonnerjee, and G.K. Gokhale) and the 1897 Amravati Congress session unanimously condemned the repression as an assault on civil liberties and press freedom.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 8; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 4

stem: With reference to the Royal Commission on the Administration of the Expenditure of India (popularly known as the Welby Commission, 1895), consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was appointed by the British Government to inquire into the administration of military and civil expenditure in India and the apportionment of charges between the United Kingdom and India.
2. Dadabhai Naoroji served as the only Indian member on this Royal Commission, while Gopal Krishna Gokhale appeared before it in London as a witness to depose on Indian financial grievances.

3. Because the official Majority Report of the Commission did not endorse the nationalist critique of the Economic Drain and Home Charges, Dadabhai Naoroji, William Wedderburn, and W.S. Caine submitted a separate Minority Report.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Welby Commission (1895–1900) became a major institutional arena where Dadabhai Naoroji (as the first Indian member on a Royal Commission) and G.K. Gokhale (as chief nationalist witness) systematically exposed the unfair burden of Home Charges and military expenditure imposed on Indian revenues.

exp.why: Constituted in May 1895 under the chairmanship of Lord Welby, the Royal Commission was mandated to inquire into the administration and management of the military and civil expenditure of India and the equitable apportionment of those charges between the Governments of the United Kingdom and India.

Dadabhai Naoroji (then a Liberal MP in the House of Commons) was appointed to the Welby Commission, becoming the first and only Indian member on the body. In 1897, Gopal Krishna Gokhale (alongside Dinshaw Wacha, Surendranath Banerjea, and G. Subramania Iyer) travelled to London and gave celebrated oral and written testimony before the Commission.

When the Commission submitted its final report in 1900, the official Majority Report offered only minor accounting reliefs and refused to accept the nationalist Drain of Wealth critique. Consequently, the three pro-India members on the Commission—Dadabhai Naoroji, Sir William Wedderburn, and W.S. Caine—authored a famous dissenting Minority Report documenting the unjust financial burden placed on India.

ref: Bipan Chandra, The Rise and Growth of Economic Nationalism in India; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 11

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the attitude of the early nationalists towards labour legislation in late nineteenth-century India:
items: Statement-I: The early Moderate nationalists generally opposed the regulatory provisions of the Indian Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891, while simultaneously campaigning for legislative intervention to protect the indentured labourers working in the Assam tea plantations.
Statement-II: The Indian Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891 applied exclusively to European-owned plantation estates and exempted Indian-owned cotton textile mills from working-hour regulations.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Early Indian nationalists viewed the Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891 as Lancashire-driven measures designed to handicap infant Indian-owned textile mills, whereas they actively championed protective legislation for Assam tea plantation workers who were exploited by British planters under penal contract laws.

exp.why: Early Moderate nationalists and newspapers (such as the Amrita Bazar Patrika and Mahratta) opposed the Indian Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891 because they prioritized the survival of infant Indian-owned textile industries against British competition. Conversely, led by reformers like Dwarkanath Ganguli and Surendranath Banerjea, they launched vigorous campaigns and passed Congress resolutions (e.g., 1896 Calcutta session) demanding the abolition of penal contracts and protection for indentured coolies in Assam tea gardens.

Statement-II reverses the actual statutory scope of the Acts. The Indian Factories Acts of 1881 and 1891 were enacted under pressure from the Manchester/Lancashire textile lobby to regulate manufacturing factories—which were predominantly Indian-owned cotton textile mills in Bombay and Ahmedabad—while explicitly exempting British-owned tea and coffee plantations. In those plantations, European planters instead relied on the Inland Emigration Acts (such as the Act of 1882) to enforce penal indentured contracts against Indian workers.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 6 & 7; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947

stem: With reference to the United Indian Patriotic Association formed in the late nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It was founded in 1888 by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Badruddin Tyabji as an exclusively Muslim political organization to counter the platform of the Indian National Congress.

2. While opposing the Congress demand for elected Legislative Councils, the Association supported the Congress demand for holding simultaneous competitive examinations for the Indian Civil Service in India and England.
3. Following the enactment of the Indian Councils Act of 1892, the Association merged directly into the All-India Muslim League under the presidency of Aga Khan.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The United Indian Patriotic Association (1888), founded by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Raja Shiv Prasad Singh of Benaras, was a multi-community loyalist coalition of Hindu and Muslim aristocrats that opposed both representative councils and competitive ICS exams out of fear that open competition would displace traditional landed elites.

exp.why: The United Indian Patriotic Association was founded in August 1888 by Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Raja Shiv Prasad Singh of Benaras (not Badruddin Tyabji, who had presided over the 1887 Madras Congress session and defended the Congress against Sir Syed's criticisms). Furthermore, it was not an exclusively Muslim body; it included both Hindu and Muslim taluqdars, zamindars, and aristocrats of North India.

Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and the United Indian Patriotic Association strongly opposed both major political demands of the early Congress: representative legislative councils and simultaneous competitive ICS examinations in India. In his famous Lucknow (1887) and Meerut (1888) speeches, Sir Syed argued that in a society marked by uneven educational progress and social hierarchy, universal open competitive exams in India would marginalize the traditional landed aristocracy and Muslims in favour of educationally advanced groups such as the Bengali bhadralok.

After the passage of the Indian Councils Act of 1892, Sir Syed Ahmed Khan and Theodore Beck superseded the multi-religious Patriotic Association by founding the Mohammedan Anglo-Oriental (MAO) Defence Association of Upper India in December 1893, which restricted membership to Muslims and Englishmen. The All-India Muslim League was founded much later in December 1906 at Dhaka, eight years after Sir Syed's death in 1898.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 4 & 5; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the relationship between the early Indian National Congress and socio-religious reform:
items: Statement-I: At its second annual session in Calcutta (1886) presided over by Dadabhai Naoroji, the Indian National Congress resolved to confine its official deliberations to political and economic questions in which the entire nation had a common stake, leaving social reforms to separate platforms.

Statement-II: In protest against this exclusion of social reform from the Congress agenda, Mahadev Govind Ranade and Raghunath Rao resigned from the Indian National Congress in 1887 to establish the rival Indian National Social Conference.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: To prevent sectarian and caste divisions from fracturing an infant all-India political movement, Dadabhai Naoroji ruled in 1886 that the Congress must restrict itself to national political-economic issues, leading M.G. Ranade and Raghunath Rao to establish the Indian National Social Conference (1887) as a complementary sister body meeting in the same pandal.

exp.why: In his Presidential Address at the second Congress session in Calcutta (1886), Dadabhai Naoroji laid down the principle that 'a National Congress must confine itself to questions in which the entire nation has a direct participation, and it must leave the adjustment of social reforms and other class questions to class Congresses,' thereby keeping divisive socio-religious debates off the official political platform.

M.G. Ranade and Raghunath Rao did not resign from the Indian National Congress, nor was the Indian National Social Conference (founded at Madras in December 1887) a rival body. On the contrary, Ranade remained a pillar of the Moderate Congress, and the Social Conference functioned harmoniously as the virtual 'social reform cell' of the Congress, holding its annual sessions at the very same venue (pandal) immediately after the Congress session concluded—a practice that continued until 1895 in Poona, when B.G. Tilak's orthodox faction objected to sharing the Congress pandal.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 5; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 9 & 11

stem: With reference to the Partition of Bengal (1905) and the demographic restructuring of the Bengal Presidency, consider the following statements:
items: 1. While officially justified on grounds of administrative convenience due to the unwieldy population of the Bengal Presidency, the partition strategically sought to weaken Calcutta-centric nationalist politics.
2. Under the partition scheme of 1905, Bengali-speaking people were reduced to a linguistic minority in the newly created province of Eastern Bengal and Assam.

3. Home Secretary H.H. Risley explicitly articulated the political rationale of the colonial government by observing that a united Bengal was a formidable power, whereas a divided Bengal would pull in different directions.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The 1905 Partition of Bengal employed a dual demographic strategy to curb Indian nationalism: creating a Muslim-majority province in Eastern Bengal and Assam while simultaneously reducing Bengali speakers to a linguistic minority in 'Bengal proper' by retaining Hindi-speaking Bihar and Odia-speaking Orissa.

exp.why: Although the colonial government cited administrative inefficiency in governing a sprawling province of nearly 78 million people as the official reason, Lord Curzon's overarching political objective was to dethrone Calcutta as the nerve centre of Indian nationalism and divide the politically conscious Bengali intelligentsia.

This statement reverses the demographic geometry of the two provinces. In the newly carved province of Eastern Bengal and Assam (with Dacca as its capital), Bengali speakers remained an overwhelming linguistic majority alongside Assamese speakers, while Muslims formed a religious majority (roughly 18 million Muslims to 12 million Hindus). Conversely, it was in 'Bengal proper' (Western Bengal retained with Bihar and Orissa) that Bengali speakers were reduced to a linguistic minority of 17 million against 37 million Hindi and Odia speakers.

In December 1904, Home Secretary H.H. Risley candidly wrote in an official note: 'Bengal united is a power; Bengal divided will pull in several different ways. That is perfectly true and is one of the merits of the scheme.' This confirmed that curbing the nationalist challenge was the core imperative behind the partition.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 10; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 12

stem: With reference to the Indian freedom struggle, what was the primary historical significance of the massive public meeting held at the Calcutta Town Hall on August 7, 1905?

opts.A: It adopted Dadabhai Naoroji's historic four-point resolution declaring 'Swaraj' or self-government as the explicit political goal of the Indian National Congress.
opts.B: It marked the formal proclamation of the Swadeshi Movement through the passage of the famous Boycott Resolution targeting British goods such as Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt.
opts.C: It constituted the National Council of Education to establish an autonomous network of indigenous colleges in defiance of the Carlyle Circular.
opts.D: It launched an all-India passive resistance campaign calling for the immediate resignation of Indian members from Legislative Councils and the non-payment of land revenue.

core: Following the official announcement of the Partition of Bengal in July 1905, the Anti-Partition agitation transitioned into the formal Swadeshi and Boycott Movement on August 7, 1905, when the Boycott Resolution was passed at the historic Calcutta Town Hall meeting.

exp.why: Option B is correct because after the colonial government announced the partition decision in July 1905 (which later took formal effect on October 16, 1905), nationalist leaders convened a massive protest meeting at the Calcutta Town Hall on August 7, 1905. At this meeting, the formal Boycott Resolution was passed, calling upon Indians to abstain from purchasing British manufactures—especially Manchester cloth and Liverpool salt—until the partition order was withdrawn. Option A is incorrect because the 'Swaraj' resolution along with resolutions on Swadeshi, Boycott, and National Education was passed at the Calcutta Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1906 under Dadabhai Naoroji. Option C is incorrect because the National Council of Education was set up later in August 1906. Option D is incorrect because the August 7, 1905 resolution was initiated under Moderate leadership as a targeted economic pressure tactic rather than an all-India council boycott or non-payment of revenue campaign.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 12

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the ideological divergence within the Indian National Congress during the Swadeshi Movement (1905–1907):
items: Statement-I: At the Benares Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1905, the Moderate leadership endorsed the Swadeshi and Boycott movement within Bengal as a legitimate protest against the partition of the province.

Statement-II: The Moderates viewed the economic boycott of foreign goods as a precursor to an all-India passive resistance campaign involving the comprehensive boycott of government schools, law courts, and executive administration across all British Indian presidencies.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The fundamental tactical rift between the Moderates and Extremists between 1905 and 1907 centred on both the territorial reach and institutional depth of the Boycott programme: Moderates sought to restrict boycott strictly to foreign goods within Bengal, whereas Extremists sought to expand it nationwide into a full-fledged passive resistance movement boycotting colonial institutions.

exp.why: Presided over by Gopal Krishna Gokhale, the December 1905 Benares Session of the Indian National Congress condemned the Partition of Bengal and the reactionary regime of Lord Curzon, formally expressing support for the anti-partition and Swadeshi-Boycott agitation inside Bengal.

This statement describes the ideological stance of the Extremists (led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Lala Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Aurobindo Ghosh), not the Moderates. The Moderates firmly opposed extending the boycott beyond foreign goods to government schools, courts, municipalities, and legislative councils, and they equally resisted carrying the boycott agitation outside Bengal to the rest of India, hoping that the newly elected Liberal government in Britain (with John Morley as Secretary of State) would annul the partition through constitutional persuasion.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 10 & 11; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 12

stem: With reference to the regional spread and grassroots mobilization during the Swadeshi Era, consider the following pairs:
items: 1. Swadesh Bandhab Samiti (Barisal) : Ashwini Kumar Dutta
2. Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company (Tuticorin) : V.O. Chidambaram Pillai
3. Dacca Anushilan Samiti (East Bengal) : Pulin Behari Das
4. Bharat Mata Association (Madras Presidency) : Lala Harkishan Lal
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: During the Swadeshi Movement, mass mobilization operated through volunteer samitis, indigenous industrial ventures, and nascent revolutionary groups spanning Bengal, Madras, Maharashtra, and Punjab.

exp.why: The Swadesh Bandhab Samiti, founded by schoolteacher and nationalist leader Ashwini Kumar Dutta in Barisal (Eastern Bengal), emerged as the most influential volunteer organization of the Swadeshi Movement. Through its 159 branches, magic lantern lectures, patriot songs, arbitration committees, and social reform work, it successfully mobilized the largely Muslim peasantry of Barisal.

In the Madras Presidency, V.O. Chidambaram Pillai spearheaded the economic challenge to the British mercantile monopoly by establishing the Swadeshi Steam Navigation Company at Tuticorin in October 1906, operating two steamships ('S.S. Gallia' and 'S.S. Lavo') between Tuticorin and Colombo.

While Promotha Mitter, Jatindranath Bannerjee, and Barindra Kumar Ghosh were associated with the Calcutta Anushilan Samiti (1902), the Dacca Anushilan Samiti was organized in 1905–1906 under the leadership of Pulin Behari Das, swiftly growing into a tightly knit network of over 500 revolutionary branches across East Bengal.

The secret revolutionary Bharat Mata Association in the Madras Presidency was founded by Nilakanta Brahmachari and Vanchi Iyer (who later assassinated Robert Ashe, the Collector of Tirunelveli, in 1911). Lala Harkishan Lal, by contrast, was a prominent leader in Punjab who promoted the Swadeshi Movement through indigenous banking, insurance, and industrial entrepreneurship alongside Lala Lajpat Rai (while Ajit Singh founded the Anjuman-i-Mohisban-i-Watan, also known as the Bharat Mata Society, in Lahore).

ref: Sumit Sarkar, The Swadeshi Movement in Bengal; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 12 & 13

stem: With reference to the National Education Movement during the Swadeshi upsurge in Bengal, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The Anti-Circular Society, with Sachindranath Prasad Bose as its secretary, was formed to defy colonial administrative directives—such as the Carlyle Circular—that penalized educational institutions whose students participated in nationalist politics.

2. Following the establishment of the National Council of Education in August 1906, Taraknath Palit was appointed as the first Principal of the Bengal National College, whereas Aurobindo Ghosh separately founded the Bengal Technical Institute.

3. To enable Indian graduates to compete directly with Calcutta University degree-holders for civil service appointments, the National Council of Education mandated that all instruction under its aegis be imparted exclusively in the English medium.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Triggered by repressive colonial measures like the Carlyle Circular (October 1905), the Swadeshi National Education Movement birthed the National Council of Education (August 1906) to impart literary, scientific, and technical education through the vernacular medium under national control.

exp.why: In October 1905, R.W. Carlyle, the Chief Secretary of the Government of Bengal, issued a circular instructing district magistrates and collectors to withdraw grants, scholarships, and university affiliation from schools and colleges that failed to prevent their students from participating in Swadeshi demonstrations or picketing. In response, students led by Sachindranath Prasad Bose formed the Anti-Circular Society in November 1905 to organize alternative education for expelled students and sustain the boycott.

This statement swaps the historical roles of Aurobindo Ghosh and Taraknath Palit. When the National Council of Education (NCE) was formally constituted on August 15, 1906 (with Rashbehari Ghosh as its President), it established the Bengal National College and School with Aurobindo Ghosh resigning his post in Baroda to serve as its first Principal. Conversely, Taraknath Palit (who favoured purely technical instruction over radical nationalist politics) founded the Society for the Promotion of Technical Education, which established the Bengal Technical Institute on July 25, 1906.

Far from mandating English as the exclusive medium of instruction to seek government service, the defining pedagogical principle of the National Council of Education (inspired by Rabindranath Tagore's Shantiniketan and Satishchandra Mukherjee's Dawn Society) was to provide literary, scientific, and technical education 'on national lines and exclusively under national control' using the vernacular (Bengali) as the primary medium of instruction, with English retained only as a second language.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 10; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India

stem: With reference to the cultural, artistic, and indigenous scientific resurgence associated with the Swadeshi Movement, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Breaking away from the naturalist oil-painting conventions of Victorian academic art, Abanindranath Tagore drew inspiration from Mughal, Rajput, and Ajanta painting traditions to pioneer the Bengal School of Art.
2. Prafulla Chandra Ray established the Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works to promote indigenous scientific self-reliance and manufacturing.

3. While the Indian Society of Oriental Art was founded in 1907 during the Swadeshi upsurge with Nandalal Bose becoming the first recipient of its scholarship, Rabindranath Tagore's Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan was formally inaugurated as an autonomous university later during the Non-Cooperation era in 1921.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Swadeshi Movement catalysed an enduring cultural and scientific renaissance in Bengal, exemplified by Abanindranath Tagore's Bengal School of Art, the Indian Society of Oriental Art (1907), and Prafulla Chandra Ray's indigenous chemical enterprises.

exp.why: In the cultural sphere, Abanindranath Tagore rejected the colonial hegemony of Victorian naturalist academic art (popularized by British art schools and Raja Ravi Varma's oleographs) and looked inward to indigenous Ajanta frescoes, Mughal miniatures, and Rajput traditions, painting his iconic 'Bharat Mata' in 1905.

Chemist Acharya Prafulla Chandra Ray championed scientific Swadeshi by founding the Bengal Chemical and Pharmaceutical Works (originally begun as a small initiative in the 1890s and incorporated as a limited company in 1901, becoming a flagship model of Swadeshi enterprise during 1905–1908) alongside Jagadish Chandra Bose's pioneering physiological and physics research.

The Indian Society of Oriental Art was established in 1907 by Abanindranath and Gaganendranath Tagore (with support from European orientalists like E.B. Havell and Sister Nivedita), and Nandalal Bose became the first recipient of its prestigious scholarship in 1907. In contrast, although Rabindranath Tagore had started his Brahmacharya Ashrama school at Santiniketan in 1901, Visva-Bharati was formally founded and inaugurated as a centre for higher learning/autonomous university only in December 1921 during the Non-Cooperation phase.

ref: NCERT Class XII Themes in Indian History Part III; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 12

stem: With reference to the social base and mass mobilization during the Swadeshi and Boycott Movement (1905–1908), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Urban middle-class women stepped out of the domestic sphere in large numbers to participate in picketing shops selling foreign cloth and in protest processions.
2. The nationalist leadership organized province-wide no-rent and anti-zamindari agrarian campaigns across Eastern Bengal to mobilize the peasantry against colonial revenue policies.
3. Swadeshi activists intervened in labour grievances in foreign-owned enterprises, helping organize strikes among workers of the East Indian Railway and jute mills in Bengal.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While the Swadeshi Movement pioneered the participation of urban middle-class women, students, and sections of the industrial working class in nationalist politics, it failed to mobilize the wider peasantry (except in pockets like Barisal) because the bhadralok leadership had strong ties to intermediate landholding tenures and avoided anti-zamindari or no-rent agrarian programmes.

exp.why: The Swadeshi Movement marked a historic watershed in women's participation in the Indian national movement. Urban middle-class women, hitherto confined to the domestic sphere, joined processions, picketed shops selling foreign cloth and liquor, and observed Arandhan (non-cooking) on the day of Partition.
