prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: Jawaharlal Nehru rejected Mountbatten's 'Plan Balkan' (Dickie Bird Plan) in May 1947 because it proposed transferring sovereignty directly to individual provinces and sub-provinces, threatening the Balkanization of India. Conversely, the Congress accepted V.P. Menon's alternative plan of early transfer of power via Dominion Status precisely to prevent fragmentation and retain a strong Central Government.

exp.why: Nehru did not reject 'Plan Balkan' at Simla in May 1947 because of Dominion Status. Rather, he rejected it because the plan (prepared by Hastings Ismay and George Abell) proposed transferring power to individual provinces—and to partitioned sub-provinces of Bengal and Punjab—giving each the option to join the existing Constituent Assembly, form a new one, or stand out independently, which combined with the lapse of Paramountcy over Princely States would have fragmented India into numerous autonomous units.

Following Nehru's rejection of 'Plan Balkan', Reforms Commissioner V.P. Menon revived the formula he had earlier discussed with Vallabhbhai Patel: transferring power to two central governments (India and Pakistan) on the basis of Dominion Status well before June 1948. Congress leaders accepted Dominion Status because it guaranteed an early, peaceful transfer of central state machinery, continuity of the bureaucracy and armed forces, and a strong Centre capable of integrating the Princely States.

ref: V.P. Menon, The Transfer of Power in India, Ch. 14–15; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 37

stem: With reference to the Mountbatten Plan of June 3, 1947, consider the following pairs matching the provinces/regions with the specific constitutional mechanism adopted to ascertain their partition or accession:
items: 1. Bengal and Punjab : Provincial Legislative Assemblies met in two separate sections representing Muslim-majority and non-Muslim-majority districts, where a simple majority vote in either section decided in favour of partition
2. North-West Frontier Province : Direct vote by the existing Provincial Legislative Assembly at a special sitting without holding a plebiscite
3. Sindh : Referendum of the registered electorate of the province conducted under the supervision of the Governor-General
4. Sylhet district of Assam : Referendum of eligible voters in the district held after the Bengal Legislative Assembly voted for the partition of Bengal
prompt: How many of the pairs given above are correctly matched?
core: The Mountbatten Plan (June 3, 1947) employed differentiated mechanisms across regions: dual-section Legislative Assembly votes in Bengal and Punjab, a direct Legislative Assembly vote in Sindh, and popular referendums of eligible voters in the North-West Frontier Province and Sylhet district of Assam.

exp.why: Under the June 3 Plan, the Provincial Legislative Assemblies of Bengal and Punjab were required to meet in two parts: one representing the Muslim-majority districts and the other representing the rest of the province (based on the 1941 Census). If a simple majority of either part voted in favour of partition, division would take place and a Boundary Commission would demarcate the exact frontier.

In the North-West Frontier Province (NWFP), although a Congress ministry led by Dr. Khan Sahib commanded a majority in the Legislative Assembly, the June 3 Plan mandated a referendum of the eligible voters of the Provincial Legislative Assembly electorate (rather than an Assembly vote) to decide which Constituent Assembly the province would join. Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars boycotted the referendum because the option of an independent 'Pathanistan' was excluded.

No popular referendum was held in Sindh. Instead, the existing Sindh Provincial Legislative Assembly directly took the decision by voting as a whole at a special sitting on whether to join the existing Indian Constituent Assembly or a new Constituent Assembly for Pakistan.

Since Assam was overwhelmingly non-Muslim except for the contiguous Muslim-majority district of Sylhet, the June 3 Plan stipulated that if the Bengal Legislative Assembly voted in favour of partitioning Bengal, a referendum of the eligible voters of Sylhet district would be held to decide whether it should remain in Assam or be amalgamated with the new province of East Bengal.

ref: V.P. Menon, The Transfer of Power in India, Ch. 15; Spectrum Modern India, Ch. 24

stem: With reference to a structural comparison of the Cripps Mission (1942), the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), and the Mountbatten Plan (1947), consider the following statements:
items: 1. While the Cripps Proposal (1942) permitted any British Indian province unwilling to accept the new constitution to opt out of the Indian Union and attain separate Dominion status, the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946) denied individual provinces the right to secede from the Union and only allowed a province to opt out of its assigned Group after the first general elections under the new constitution.

2. Under both the Cripps Proposal (1942) and the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), the representatives of the British Indian provinces in the constitution-making body were to be elected indirectly by the members of the Provincial Legislative Assemblies rather than through direct universal adult suffrage.

3. Unlike the Cripps Proposal (1942) and the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), the Mountbatten Plan of June 3, 1947 abolished the legal right of Princely States to remain outside both Dominions by mandating their statutory accession to either India or Pakistan before August 15, 1947.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: A critical constitutional evolution between 1942 and 1947 lay in how provincial non-accession was treated: Cripps (1942) permitted provincial secession into separate Dominions, whereas the Cabinet Mission (1946) replaced sovereignty-secession with compulsory three-tier grouping and post-constitution group opt-outs. Under all three plans, legal paramountcy over Princely States was set to lapse rather than transfer statutorily.

exp.why: Under the 1942 Cripps Draft Declaration, any British Indian province not prepared to accept the new constitution had the right to retain its present constitutional position and subsequently form a separate Dominion. By contrast, the 1946 Cabinet Mission explicitly rejected a sovereign Pakistan and denied provinces the right to secede from the Union of India; a province could only choose, by a vote of its legislature after the first general election under the new constitution, to come out of the Group (Section A, B, or C) in which it had been placed.

Both the 1942 Cripps Proposal (which envisaged an electoral college of the entire membership of the lower houses of the Provincial Legislatures electing the constitution-making body by proportional representation) and the 1946 Cabinet Mission Plan (where provincial assemblies elected representatives divided into General, Muslim, and Sikh communities via proportional representation) rejected immediate direct election by universal adult suffrage on grounds of procedural delay.

The Mountbatten Plan of June 3, 1947 explicitly stated that His Majesty's Government's policy toward the Indian Princely States remained unchanged from the Cabinet Mission Memorandum of May 12, 1946. Legally, British Paramountcy lapsed on August 15, 1947 under Section 7 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 without any statutory mandate forcing accession, although Lord Mountbatten and Sardar Patel used diplomatic persuasion and geographical contiguity to secure their Instruments of Accession.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India, Ch. 8; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 35 & 37

stem: With reference to the legal and constitutional provisions of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, consider the following statements:
items: 1. From the appointed day of August 15, 1947, the Governor-General and the Provincial Governors were divested of all powers to act in their discretion or individual judgment and could exercise their constitutional functions only on the advice of their respective Council of Ministers.
2. The Act repealed the Government of India Act, 1935 in its entirety, vesting interim executive and administrative governance strictly in ordinances promulgated by the Constituent Assembly.

3. It empowered the Constituent Assembly of each Dominion to function simultaneously as the central legislature and granted it plenary authority to repeal or amend any Act of the British Parliament extending to the Dominion, including the Indian Independence Act itself.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Under Sections 6 and 8 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the Governor-General and Governors were transformed into purely nominal constitutional heads acting only on ministerial advice, the Constituent Assembly acquired sovereign plenary power to repeal any British statute, and the Government of India Act, 1935 (duly adapted) was retained as the provisional constitution.

exp.why: Under Section 8(2)(c) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, all provisions of the Government of India Act, 1935 requiring the Governor-General or any Provincial Governor to act in his discretion or exercise his individual judgment ceased to have effect from August 15, 1947. Consequently, they became strictly constitutional heads who could act only on the aid and advice of their respective Council of Ministers.

The Indian Independence Act, 1947 did not repeal the Government of India Act, 1935. On the contrary, Section 8(2) explicitly laid down that each of the new Dominions and all Provinces would continue to be governed as nearly as may be in accordance with the Government of India Act, 1935 (as adapted and modified by orders of the Governor-General under Section 9) until the Constituent Assembly framed a new Constitution.

Sections 6 and 8 of the Act vested full legislative sovereignty in the Constituent Assembly of each Dominion, enabling it to function in a dual capacity (as a constitution-making body and as the Dominion Legislature). Section 6(2) and 6(4) specifically empowered the Legislature of each Dominion to repeal or amend any existing or future Act of the UK Parliament extending to the Dominion, including the Indian Independence Act, 1947 itself.

ref: D.D. Basu, Introduction to the Constitution of India, Ch. 1; M. Laxmikanth, Indian Polity, Ch. 1

stem: With reference to the Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions (1947) appointed under the chairmanship of Sir Cyril Radcliffe, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Each Boundary Commission comprised the Chairman alongside voting members nominated by the Indian National Congress, the Muslim League, the Sikh Panthic Party, and the Chamber of Princes.

2. The Commissions were mandated to demarcate the boundaries of the two parts of Punjab and Bengal on the basis of ascertaining the contiguous majority areas of Muslims and non-Muslims, while also taking 'other factors' into account.
3. Although the boundary awards were finalized shortly before the transfer of power, Lord Mountbatten deferred their formal publication until August 17, 1947.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: The Punjab and Bengal Boundary Commissions (1947) were constituted strictly with a neutral Chairman (Sir Cyril Radcliffe) and four High Court Judges each (two nominated by the Congress and two by the Muslim League), without voting representation for the Sikh Panthic Party or Princely States. Their terms of reference combined religious demography ('contiguous majority areas') with 'other factors' (such as canal systems, communications, and economic viability), and the resulting Award was deliberately held back by Mountbatten until August 17, 1947 to insulate the British government from immediate administrative blame during the independence ceremonies.

exp.why: Each of the two Boundary Commissions (one for Punjab and one for Bengal) consisted solely of the Chairman, Sir Cyril Radcliffe, and four High Court Judges—two nominated by the Indian National Congress and two nominated by the All-India Muslim League. Neither the Sikh Panthic Party nor the Chamber of Princes had voting members on the Commissions, although Sikh and other representatives were permitted to present legal arguments and memoranda before the Punjab Commission.

Under the official terms of reference announced following the June 3 Plan, the Boundary Commissions were instructed to demarcate the boundaries of the two parts of Punjab and Bengal on the basis of ascertaining the contiguous majority areas of Muslims and non-Muslims, and in doing so, also to take into account 'other factors' (such as natural boundaries, communications, watercourses, and irrigation systems).

Sir Cyril Radcliffe completed and submitted the boundary awards to Viceroy Lord Mountbatten by August 12–13, 1947. However, Mountbatten deliberately withheld the formal publication of the Radcliffe Award until August 17, 1947—two days after the transfer of power—so that the departing British administration would not have to bear direct responsibility for containing the immediate communal backlash during the independence ceremonies in Karachi and New Delhi.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 38; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 8.3

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the Indian National Congress's acceptance of the Mountbatten Plan (June 3 Plan) in 1947:
items: Statement-I: In June 1947, the All India Congress Committee (AICC) accepted the territorial partition of India under the Mountbatten Plan—while explicitly rejecting the ideological 'Two-Nation Theory'—as an unavoidable necessity to secure an immediate transfer of power to a strong central authority.

Statement-II: The administrative paralysis experienced during the Interim Government (1946–47) and the looming threat of Balkanization by Princely States convinced the Congress leadership that a loose three-tier federal structure on the lines of the Cabinet Mission Plan was unworkable.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: The Congress leadership accepted the territorial partition of India under the June 3 Plan not out of ideological agreement with Jinnah's 'Two-Nation Theory', which the June 1947 AICC resolution explicitly repudiated, but as a pragmatic compromise to secure an immediate transfer of power to a strong, unified Indian state. The bitter experience of administrative deadlock inside the Interim Government after October 1946 and the danger of Princely States declaring independence convinced Patel and Nehru that a weak three-tier federal Centre under the Cabinet Mission Plan would lead to civil war and Balkanization.

exp.why: When the All India Congress Committee (AICC) met on June 14–15, 1947 to ratify the June 3 Plan (in a resolution moved by Govind Ballabh Pant and supported by Sardar Patel, Jawaharlal Nehru, and Mahatma Gandhi), it accepted the territorial division of Punjab and Bengal as a painful political necessity to arrest communal civil war and secure an immediate transfer of power over the rest of India to a strong central government, while explicitly rejecting the Muslim League's ideological 'Two-Nation Theory'.

Statement-II is historically accurate and directly explains Statement-I: the functioning of the Interim Government after the Muslim League's entry in October 1946 (where Finance Minister Liaquat Ali Khan obstructed proposals of Congress-led ministries) demonstrated that a weak three-tier federal Centre under the Cabinet Mission Plan would paralyze governance. Furthermore, Patel and Nehru realized that without an immediate transfer of power to a strong Dominion Centre, recalcitrant Princely States would exploit the lapse of paramountcy to Balkanize India. Thus, Statement-II directly explains why the Congress accepted Partition under the Mountbatten Plan in Statement-I.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 38; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India, Ch. 8

stem: With reference to the legal instruments formulated by the States Department in July–August 1947 to address the lapse of British Paramountcy, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Instrument of Accession signed by the Princely States prior to August 15, 1947, the rulers acceded to the Dominion of India only over three subjects—Defence, External Affairs, and Communications—without incurring any financial obligation or surrendering their internal autonomy.

2. The Standstill Agreement was a transitional legal covenant whereby an acceding ruler agreed to suspend monarchical governance and transfer interim district administration to the States Department until a popular legislature could be convened.
prompt: Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
core: Following the creation of the States Department in July 1947 under Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon, two distinct legal instruments were deployed to prevent juridical fragmentation upon the lapse of Paramountcy. The Instrument of Accession secured the constitutional union of Princely States with India strictly over three subjects (Defence, External Affairs, and Communications), while the Standstill Agreement ensured the uninterrupted continuation of pre-existing administrative arrangements (such as customs, railways, posts, and currency) between the states and the new Dominion.

exp.why: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel and V.P. Menon persuaded the rulers of the Princely States that the Instrument of Accession drafted prior to August 15, 1947 required them to surrender sovereignty to the Dominion of India only over three subjects—Defence, External Affairs, and Communications—spheres in which the states had never exercised autonomous authority even under British Paramountcy. Clauses 7 and 8 of the Instrument explicitly protected the internal sovereignty of the rulers and imposed no financial liability on the states.

The Standstill Agreement did not suspend monarchical rule or transfer internal district administration to the States Department. Rather, it was an administrative agreement executed alongside the Instrument of Accession providing that all existing agreements and administrative arrangements on matters of common concern (such as railways, posts and telegraphs, customs, excise, and currency) that had existed between the British Crown and the Princely State would continue unaltered between the Dominion of India and the State until new arrangements were made.

ref: V.P. Menon, The Story of the Integration of the Indian States, Ch. 5; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the political and diplomatic challenges in the integration of Princely States during 1947–48, consider the following statements:
items: 1. In Travancore, Dewan Sir C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar initially declared the state's intention to become an independent sovereign state upon the lapse of paramountcy, citing its maritime trade and strategic monazite reserves, before the Maharaja acceded to India in July 1947.

2. While the Nawab of Bhopal sought to organize a 'Third Force' of Princely States to resist joining the Constituent Assembly, the young Maharaja of Jodhpur briefly negotiated terms with Muhammad Ali Jinnah for access to the Karachi port before both signed the Instrument of Accession prior to August 15, 1947.

3. After the Nawab of Junagadh announced accession to Pakistan despite an overwhelming non-Muslim population and lack of geographical contiguity, nationalist leaders established a provisional government (Arzi Hukumat) under Samaldas Gandhi, and the state was integrated into India following a plebiscite in February 1948.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Before August 15, 1947, diplomatic skill backed by popular pressure overcame resistance from rulers and Dewans in Travancore, Bhopal, and Jodhpur, leaving only Junagadh, Jammu & Kashmir, and Hyderabad outside the Union at independence. In Junagadh, the Nawab's untenable accession to Pakistan triggered a popular uprising led by the Arzi Hukumat, the flight of the Nawab to Karachi, an invitation by Dewan Shah Nawaz Bhutto to the Government of India to intervene, and a February 1948 plebiscite in which over 99% of voters favored joining India.

exp.why: In June 1947, Sir C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar, the Dewan of Travancore, announced that Travancore would set itself up as an independent sovereign state after the lapse of British Paramountcy, leveraging its coastline and rich monazite sands (containing thorium). However, following a mass agitation launched by the Travancore State Congress and an assassination attempt on the Dewan in late July 1947, the Maharaja of Travancore telegraphed his acceptance of the Instrument of Accession to India.

Nawab Hamidullah Khan of Bhopal (then Chancellor of the Chamber of Princes) actively lobbied to create a 'Third Force' of autonomous Princely States and resisted joining the Constituent Assembly. Simultaneously, Maharaja Hanwant Singh of Jodhpur—a Hindu-majority border state—was enticed by Jinnah with a blank sheet of paper offering free use of the Karachi port and arms import privileges. Intervention by Sardar Patel, V.P. Menon, and Lord Mountbatten convinced both Jodhpur and Bhopal to sign the Instrument of Accession before August 15, 1947.

Although Junagadh in Kathiawar was surrounded by Indian territory and had a population that was over 80% non-Muslim, Nawab Mahabat Khanji announced accession to Pakistan on August 15, 1947. Its tributary states of Mangrol and Babariawad asserted their independence and acceded to India, while nationalists in Bombay and Kathiawar formed a provisional government (Arzi Hukumat) led by Samaldas Gandhi. Facing economic collapse and popular revolt, the Nawab fled to Pakistan, his Dewan (Shah Nawaz Bhutto) handed over administration to India in November 1947, and a popular plebiscite in February 1948 overwhelmingly ratified Junagadh's merger with India.

ref: V.P. Menon, The Story of the Integration of the Indian States, Ch. 6–8; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence, Ch. 6

stem: Consider the following events during the phase of Transfer of Power and Integration of States (1946–1948):
items: 1. Prime Minister Clement Attlee's Statement in the House of Commons fixing June 1948 as the deadline for the British withdrawal from India
2. Signing of the one-year Standstill Agreement between the Nizam of Hyderabad and the Dominion of India
3. Entry of the All-India Muslim League nominees into the Interim Government headed by Jawaharlal Nehru
4. Conduct of the popular plebiscite in the Princely State of Junagadh
prompt: Which one of the following is the correct chronological order of the above events, starting from the earliest?
core: A precise chronological grasp of the transition from 1946 to 1948 is essential to understand how constitutional negotiations overlapped with the integration of Princely States. The Muslim League joined the Interim Government in October 1946 (without joining the Constituent Assembly), prompting Attlee's February 1947 deadline statement; after Independence, Hyderabad signed a one-year Standstill Agreement with India in November 1947, prior to the February 1948 Junagadh plebiscite and the September 1948 Operation Polo.

exp.why: Prime Minister Clement Attlee made his historic statement in the British House of Commons on February 20, 1947, declaring the British intention to leave India by June 30, 1948 and announcing the replacement of Lord Wavell by Lord Mountbatten as Viceroy (second in sequence).

Seeking time to build up his military and diplomatic position after August 15, 1947, the Nizam of Hyderabad (Osman Ali Khan) signed a one-year Standstill Agreement with the Dominion of India on November 29, 1947 (third in sequence).

Following the formation of the Interim Government by Jawaharlal Nehru on September 2, 1946, Lord Wavell brought five nominees of the All-India Muslim League (led by Liaquat Ali Khan) into the Interim Government on October 26, 1946 (earliest in sequence).

After the Dewan of Junagadh invited the Government of India to restore order in November 1947, a popular plebiscite was conducted in Junagadh on February 20, 1948, where over 99% of the votes were cast in favor of accession to India (fourth in sequence, later followed by Operation Polo in Hyderabad in September 1948). Thus, the correct chronological order is 3-1-2-4.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India, Ch. 8; V.P. Menon, The Story of the Integration of the Indian States, Ch. 8 & 17

stem: With reference to the post-accession administrative consolidation and democratization of Princely States between December 1947 and January 1950, consider the following statements:
items: 1. The signing of the initial Instrument of Accession by the Princely States in August 1947 automatically extinguished the internal administrative autonomy of their rulers and legally merged their territories into adjacent provinces.

2. Smaller princely states lacking the financial and administrative viability to function as modern democratic units—beginning with the Orissa and Chhattisgarh states in December 1947—were integrated through Merger Agreements into contiguous provinces.

3. While contiguous clusters of states such as Saurashtra, Matsya, and PEPSU were amalgamated into 'States Unions' headed by a Rajpramukh, strategically sensitive or frontier states such as Himachal Pradesh, Kutch, Manipur, and Tripura were consolidated as Centrally Administered Areas.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: The integration of the Princely States occurred in two distinct legal phases: first, external accession on three subjects (Defence, External Affairs, Communications) in August 1947 via the Instrument of Accession; and second, internal territorial and administrative consolidation between December 1947 and 1950 via Merger Agreements and Covenants. This second phase transformed over 550 princely jurisdictions into integral constitutional units through a three-fold mechanism: merger into adjacent provinces (Part A), amalgamation into Rajpramukh-led States Unions (Part B), and conversion into Centrally Administered Chief Commissioner's Provinces (Part C).

exp.why: Signing the initial Instrument of Accession in August 1947 ceded authority to the Dominion of India only over Defence, External Affairs, and Communications, while explicitly preserving the rulers' internal sovereignty and administrative autonomy. To abolish internal princely autocracies and consolidate their territories, Sardar Patel and V.P. Menon had to negotiate a separate, second wave of Merger Agreements and Covenants of Amalgamation between December 1947 and 1949, in which rulers surrendered full internal jurisdiction in exchange for constitutional Privy Purses.

Beginning with the Eastern States Agency (Orissa and Chhattisgarh states) in December 1947, followed by the Deccan and Gujarat states, over 216 smaller princely states that lacked the revenue and administrative capacity to survive as standalone modern units signed Merger Agreements integrating them into contiguous British Indian provinces (which became Part A States under the 1950 Constitution).

Under the second and third mechanisms of Patel and Menon's consolidation policy, contiguous groups of states were united into viable 'States Unions' headed by a ruler designated as Rajpramukh (such as Saurashtra/Kathiawar, Matsya, Vindhya Pradesh, Madhya Bharat, PEPSU, Rajasthan, and Travancore-Cochin, which became Part B States), while states situated along international borders or requiring direct central oversight (such as Himachal Pradesh, Kutch, Bilaspur, Bhopal, Tripura, and Manipur) were taken over as Centrally Administered Areas (later Part C States).

ref: V.P. Menon, The Story of the Integration of the Indian States, Ch. 9–15; Bipan Chandra, India Since Independence, Ch. 6

stem: With reference to the evolution of judicial and revenue administration under Warren Hastings and Lord Cornwallis, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Judicial Plan of 1772, Warren Hastings established a District Diwani Adalat for civil disputes and a District Faujdari Adalat for criminal trials in each district, subject to appellate Sadar Adalats at Calcutta.

2. Guided by the principle of separation of powers, Warren Hastings completely divested the District Collector of all judicial and magisterial functions, whereas the Cornwallis Code of 1793 merged revenue collection and civil justice into the office of the Collector.

3. Under the Cornwallis Code of 1793, European British subjects in the districts were brought under the civil jurisdiction of local courts for claims involving native Indian subjects, and government officials were made answerable to civil courts for acts done in their official capacity.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: While Warren Hastings initially combined revenue collection and civil judicial powers in the District Collector (1772 and again in 1787), Lord Cornwallis enforced the Whiggish principle of separation of powers under the Cornwallis Code of 1793 by stripping the Collector of all judicial and magisterial powers and establishing the sovereignty of law over official actions.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Under Warren Hastings' Judicial Plan of 1772, each district was provided with a Mofussil Diwani Adalat (presided over by the Collector assisted by native law officers—Kazi and Pandit) for civil cases, and a Mofussil Faujdari Adalat (under Indian judicial officers supervised by the Collector) for criminal trials, with appeals lying to the Sadar Diwani Adalat and Sadar Nizamat Adalat at Calcutta.

Statement 2 is incorrect because it swaps the institutional architectures of Warren Hastings and Lord Cornwallis. Under Hastings (1772) and the subsequent reorganization of 1787, revenue collection, civil justice, and magisterial functions were concentrated in the hands of the District Collector. Conversely, Lord Cornwallis (via the Cornwallis Code of 1793) enforced strict separation of revenue and judicial administration, divesting the Collector of all judicial and magisterial powers and transferring them to a newly empowered District Judge.

Statement 3 is correct. The Cornwallis Code of 1793 established the principle of the rule of law in British India: European subjects residing in the interior (mofussil) were placed under the civil jurisdiction of local District Diwani Adalats for disputes with Indian subjects, and collectors and other executive officers were made amenable to the civil courts for official acts violating property or personal rights.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26 (Constitutional, Administrative and Judicial Developments); B.L. Grover, Evolution of Judicial System.

stem: In the context of British imperial expansion in India, consider a mechanism of hegemony wherein an Indian ruler was compelled to disband his native armed forces, accept the permanent stationing of a British military contingent within his territory funded either through an annual cash subsidy or the outright cession of territory, and surrender the right to conduct diplomatic negotiations or employ non-British Europeans without the prior consent of the East India Company. Which of the following policies and its chief architect does this mechanism best describe?

opts.A: The Policy of Ring-Fence systematized by Warren Hastings to create autonomous buffer zones
opts.B: The Policy of Subordinate Isolation initiated by Lord Hastings to assert the Doctrine of Paramountcy
opts.C: The Policy of Annexation under the pretext of maladministration formulated by Lord Dalhousie
opts.D: The Subsidiary Alliance System perfected by Lord Wellesley to establish British military supremacy

core: Lord Wellesley (1798–1805) transformed the earlier Anglo-French practice of hiring out troops into the comprehensive Subsidiary Alliance System, which structurally disarmed Indian princely states, insulated them from French diplomatic influence, and shifted the financial burden of the Company's standing army onto native treasuries and ceded territories.

exp.why: Option D is correct. Under Lord Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance System (1798–1805), an allied Indian ruler had to (1) accept the permanent stationing of a British military force within his territory and pay a subsidy for its maintenance (or cede territory in default/lieu of cash payment, as in the four stages of the system), (2) disband his own independent armed forces, (3) accept a British Resident at his court, and (4) refrain from employing any European other than the British or negotiating with any other Indian ruler without the Governor-General's consent. Option A is incorrect because Warren Hastings' Policy of Ring-Fence aimed at defending a neighbour's frontiers (such as Awadh) as a buffer zone to safeguard Company territories without systematically disarming the state or taking over its complete external diplomacy. Option B refers to the post-1813 phase under Lord Hastings, and Option C refers to Lord Dalhousie's annexationist measures (1848–1856).

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 5 (Expansion and Consolidation of British Power in India).

stem: With reference to the administrative, judicial, and public works reforms undertaken during the tenures of Lord William Bentinck and Lord Dalhousie, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Lord William Bentinck abolished the Provincial Courts of Appeal and Circuit established by Lord Cornwallis, and replaced Persian with vernacular languages in lower courts and English in the Supreme Court.
2. Lord Dalhousie divested the Military Board of its construction responsibilities and established a separate Public Works Department in each presidency with dedicated engineering cadres.

3. Open competitive examinations in London for recruitment to the Covenanted Civil Services were successfully operationalized during the tenure of Lord William Bentinck under the provisions of the Charter Act of 1833.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lord William Bentinck rationalized Cornwallis's expensive judicial hierarchy and modernized court languages, while Lord Dalhousie created the modern Public Works Department and witnessed the actual introduction of open competitive examinations for the Covenanted Civil Service under the Charter Act of 1853.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Because the four Provincial Courts of Appeal and Circuit set up by Lord Cornwallis had become notorious for arrears and delay, Lord William Bentinck (1828–1835) abolished them, transferring their functions to Commissioners of Revenue and Circuit and to District Judges. He also gave suitors the option to use vernacular languages in lower courts and replaced Persian with English in the Supreme Court.

Statement 2 is correct. Prior to Lord Dalhousie (1848–1856), public works construction was neglected under a Military Board. Dalhousie divested the Military Board of this duty, organized a separate Public Works Department (PWD) in every presidency, founded the Thomason College of Civil Engineering at Roorkee (1847/1854 expansion), and allocated substantial funds for the Ganges Canal and Grand Trunk Road.

Statement 3 is incorrect. Although the Charter Act of 1833 (during Bentinck's tenure) proposed a limited competition among candidates nominated by the Court of Directors and declared in Section 87 that no Indian should be barred from office by reason of religion or birth, the Court of Directors fiercely opposed the competition clause and it remained a dead letter. Open competitive examinations in London were actually introduced under the Charter Act of 1853 (followed by the Macaulay Committee Report of 1854) during the tenure of Lord Dalhousie.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26 & Appendices on Governor-Generals; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition.

stem: With reference to the administrative and political developments during the tenure of Lord Canning as the last Governor-General of the East India Company and the first Viceroy under the Crown, consider the following statements:
items: 1. Under the Indian Councils Act of 1861, the 'Portfolio System' introduced by Lord Canning received statutory recognition, empowering individual members of the Executive Council to take charge of specific departments.

2. The 'White Mutiny' that erupted during Lord Canning's tenure was an organized agitation by European planters and merchants protesting against the grant of criminal jurisdiction over European British subjects to Indian magistrates.
3. Following the Queen's Proclamation of 1858, Lord Canning formally renounced the Doctrine of Lapse and issued 'Sanads of Adoption' recognizing the right of loyal Indian princes to adopt heirs.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lord Canning presided over the institutional transition from Company rule to Crown rule (1856–1862), introducing the Portfolio System (1859/1861), pacifying princely states through Adoption Sanads, and resolving the 1859 'White Mutiny' of the Company's European troops who resisted automatic transfer to the Queen's Army without a bounty.

exp.why: Statement 1 is correct. Lord Canning introduced the Portfolio System in 1859, which was given statutory recognition by Section 8 of the Indian Councils Act, 1861. It replaced collective deliberation on every minor paper with departmental responsibility, laying the foundation of cabinet government in India.

Statement 2 is incorrect. It conflates the 'White Mutiny' of 1859–1860 under Lord Canning with the Ilbert Bill agitation of 1883 under Lord Ripon (and earlier Black Acts protests under Dalhousie/Canning). The historical 'White Mutiny' during Canning's viceroyalty (1859) was an armed protest and insubordination by the East India Company's European troops, who resented being mechanically transferred to the service of the British Crown under the Government of India Act, 1858 without their consent or a fresh re-enlistment bounty.

Statement 3 is correct. To turn Indian princely states into 'breakwaters in the storm', the Queen's Proclamation of 1858 renounced further territorial annexations, and Lord Canning issued formal 'Sanads of Adoption' to Hindu and Muslim rulers assuring them that the Crown recognized their right to adopt successors in accordance with their religious laws and customs.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 7 (The Revolt of 1857 - Aftermath) & Ch. 26.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding the administrative and legislative measures enacted during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon:
items: Statement-I: The First Factory Act of 1881, enacted during the tenure of Lord Ripon, comprehensively regulated the working hours and weekly holidays of all adult male and female textile workers across both British India and the Princely States.

Statement-II: Reversing the authoritarian centralism of Lord Lytton, Lord Ripon's Resolution of 1882 laid the foundation of fiscal and administrative decentralization by mandating rural and urban local boards with a majority of non-official members and non-official chairpersons wherever practicable.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: While Lord Ripon (1880–1884) championed liberal decentralization through the landmark Local Self-Government Resolution of 1882, the First Factory Act of 1881 was highly limited in scope—applying only to child labour in British Indian factories using mechanical power and employing at least 100 workers, while excluding adult workers, tea/coffee plantations, and Princely States.

exp.why: Statement-I is incorrect. The First Factory Act of 1881 had a very narrow scope: it dealt primarily with the problem of child labour (prohibiting employment of children under 7 years and limiting hours to 9 hours a day for children aged 7 to 12) in factories employing 100 or more workers and using mechanical power. It did not regulate working hours for adult male or female workers (women's hours were first regulated in the Second Factory Act of 1891 under Lord Lansdowne, and adult males in 1911), nor did it extend to Princely States or British-owned tea and coffee plantations.

Statement-II is correct. Unlike Lord Lytton's reactionary measures (such as the Vernacular Press Act of 1878 and the Arms Act of 1878), Lord Ripon pursued liberal reforms. His Resolution of May 18, 1882 on Local Self-Government envisaged local boards not merely as instruments of administrative efficiency, but as an instrument of 'political and popular education', stipulating that non-officials must form a majority on these bodies and be elected wherever feasible, with non-official chairpersons.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26 & Appendices; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence.

stem: Consider the following table regarding the Famine Commissions appointed by the British Government in India:
items: 1. Campbell Commission (1866) : Sir John Lawrence : Held that famine relief was a state responsibility rather than a matter to be left solely to voluntary charity, following administrative failure in the Orissa famine.

2. Strachey Commission (1880) : Lord Lytton : Advocated a shift to a 'moral strategy' emphasizing the early distribution of advances for seed and cattle and the appointment of a Famine Commissioner in affected provinces.

3. Lyall Commission (1897) : Lord Elgin II : Endorsed the foundational principles of the 1880 Commission while recommending greater flexibility in relief wages and freer grant of gratuitous relief during seasonal scarcities.

4. MacDonnell Commission (1900) : Lord Curzon : Formulated the first provisional Famine Code and recommended the creation of a dedicated annual Famine Insurance Grant (Famine Fund) in the central budget.
prompt: In how many of the above rows is the given information correctly matched?
core: British famine policy evolved through four major commissions: Campbell (1866, under John Lawrence), Strachey (1880, under Lytton, which birthed the provisional Famine Code and the Famine Insurance Grant), Lyall (1897, under Elgin II), and MacDonnell (1900, under Curzon, which emphasized 'moral strategy', agricultural banks, and a Famine Commissioner).

exp.why: Row 1 is correctly matched. Following the catastrophic Orissa famine of 1865–1866 during the viceroyalty of Sir John Lawrence, the George Campbell Commission (1866) criticized the government's rigid adherence to laissez-faire grain non-intervention and recommended that the state must actively organize famine relief and import food grains where necessary.

Row 2 is incorrectly matched because it swaps the recommendations of the Strachey Commission (1880) with those of the MacDonnell Commission (1900). Appointed by Lord Lytton under Sir Richard Strachey, the 1880 Commission laid down that it is the duty of the State to offer relief to the needy through employment for the able-bodied and gratuitous relief for the impotent poor, led to the formulation of the Provisional Famine Code (1883), and recommended the setting up of an annual Famine Insurance Grant (Famine Fund).

Row 3 is correctly matched. Following the widespread famine of 1896–1897 during the tenure of Lord Elgin II, a commission chaired by Sir James Lyall (former Lt.-Governor of Punjab) was appointed. It broadly upheld the principles laid down by the Strachey Commission of 1880 while suggesting operational modifications for greater flexibility in test works and gratuitous relief.

Row 4 is incorrectly matched because it attributes the Strachey Commission's recommendations to the MacDonnell Commission. Appointed by Lord Curzon in 1900 under Sir Anthony MacDonnell, the Commission emphasized a 'moral strategy' ('putting heart into the people') by providing prompt suspension/remission of land revenue, early distribution of taccavi advances for purchasing seed and cattle, promoting co-operative credit societies, and appointing a Famine Commissioner in a province where relief operations were expected to be extensive.

ref: Spectrum: A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. 26 (Development of Famine Policy); B.L. Grover, Modern Indian History.

stem: With reference to the recommendations of the Police Commission (1902–1903) appointed under the chairmanship of Sir Andrew Fraser during the Viceroyalty of Lord Curzon, consider the following statements:
items: 1. It recommended the abolition of the European officer cadre in the Imperial Police in favour of placing district police administration under the supervision of elected municipal boards.

2. It proposed dismantling the central intelligence machinery and decentralizing all political intelligence operations exclusively to District Magistrates without creating provincial Criminal Investigation Departments (CIDs).
3. It barred the direct recruitment of educated Indians to the rank of Sub-Inspector, mandating that all Sub-Inspectors be appointed solely through promotion from the rank of Head Constable.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: Lord Curzon appointed the Andrew Fraser Police Commission (1902–03) to modernize colonial policing and political surveillance. The Commission established Provincial CIDs and a Central Department of Criminal Intelligence, opened direct recruitment of educated Indians at the Sub-Inspector level and created the provincial rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police for Indians, while preserving European monopoly at the senior Superintendent level.

exp.why: The Fraser Commission did not abolish the European officer cadre or transfer police control to municipal boards. Instead, it retained the Imperial Police (Superintendents of Police recruited exclusively in England) at the apex of district administration, while creating a new Provincial Police Service rank of Deputy Superintendent of Police (DSP) for Indians.

The Commission recommended the exact opposite: it called for the creation of a specialized Criminal Investigation Department (CID) in every province under a Deputy Inspector-General (DIG) and the establishment of a Central Department of Criminal Intelligence (which evolved into the Intelligence Bureau) at the all-India level to monitor political activities and inter-provincial crime.

Far from barring direct recruitment of educated Indians as Sub-Inspectors, the Fraser Commission criticized the inefficiency of promoting semi-literate Head Constables and explicitly recommended that Sub-Inspectors be recruited directly from the educated Indian classes, while limiting the promotion of constables strictly to the rank of Head Constable.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 2 & 5; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence; Spectrum Modern India, Survey of Viceroys (Lord Curzon).

stem: With reference to the British Indian frontier policies towards Afghanistan in the second half of the nineteenth century, consider the following statements:
items: 1. John Lawrence's policy of 'Masterly Inactivity' was predicated on strict non-interference in internal Afghan succession struggles as long as frontier peace remained undisturbed and no foreign power intervened.
2. It was during the Viceroyalty of John Lawrence that the Second Anglo-Afghan War broke out, culminating in the signing of the Treaty of Gandamak.
3. Lord Lytton's policy of 'Proud Reserve' sought to replace ambiguous frontier relations with fixed scientific frontiers and spheres of British control over Afghan external relations.
prompt: Which of the statements given above are correct?
core: British policy towards Afghanistan oscillated between John Lawrence's cautious 'Masterly Inactivity' (1864–1869) and Lord Lytton's aggressive forward policy of 'Proud Reserve' (1876–1880). Lytton's insistence on stationing a permanent British Resident in Kabul provoked the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–1880) and the Treaty of Gandamak (1879).

exp.why: John Lawrence (Viceroy, 1864–1869) pursued the policy of 'Masterly Inactivity' as a pragmatic reaction to the disasters of the First Anglo-Afghan War. He recognized de facto rulers of Afghanistan without intervening in their civil wars, provided they maintained peace on the British frontier and did not seek military assistance from Russia or Persia.

The Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–1880) broke out during the Viceroyalty of Lord Lytton (1876–1880), not John Lawrence. After Amir Sher Ali fled and died, his son Yakub Khan signed the Treaty of Gandamak in May 1879 under Lord Lytton, ceding control of Afghan foreign policy to the British and accepting a permanent British Resident at Kabul.

Lord Lytton arrived in India with instructions from Benjamin Disraeli's Conservative ministry to abandon 'Masterly Inactivity' in favour of 'Proud Reserve', aiming to secure 'scientific frontiers' (controlling key mountain passes) and subordinate Afghanistan's foreign relations to British imperial security.

ref: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India; Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India, Ch. on Expansion and Consolidation of British Power & Viceroys.

stem: Which of the following administrative and legislative developments took place during the Viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921)?
items: 1. Appointment of the Saddler Commission to inquire into the problems and prospects of Calcutta University.
2. Appointment of Lord S.P. Sinha as the Governor of Bihar and Orissa, making him the first Indian to hold a provincial governorship under British rule.
3. Repeal of the Indian Press Act of 1910 and the Rowlatt Act of 1919.
4. Separation of the Railway Budget from the General Budget on the recommendations of the Acworth Committee.
prompt: Select the correct answer using the code given below:
core: Distinguishing the immediate post-First World War Viceroyalties of Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921) and Lord Reading (1921–1926) requires tracking when wartime repressive laws were enacted versus repealed. While the Rowlatt Act (1919), Saddler Commission (1917), and S.P. Sinha's governorship (1920) belong to Chelmsford's tenure, the repeal of the Rowlatt and Press Acts (1922) and the separation of the Railway Budget (1924) occurred under Lord Reading.

exp.why: The Calcutta University Commission, chaired by Dr. Michael Sadler, was appointed in 1917 and submitted its report in 1919 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Chelmsford (1916–1921), recommending the 12-year school plus 3-year degree structure and the creation of Boards of Secondary and Intermediate Education.

Satyendra Prasanna Sinha (Lord Sinha of Raipur), who had earlier been the first Indian member of the Viceroy's Executive Council (1909), was appointed Governor of Bihar and Orissa in December 1920 during the tenure of Lord Chelmsford.

While the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act (Rowlatt Act) was enacted in March 1919 under Lord Chelmsford, the repeal of both the Indian Press Act of 1910 and the Rowlatt Act of 1919 took place in 1922 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Reading (1921–1926), based on the recommendations of the Tej Bahadur Sapru Committee.

The Acworth Committee on Railways reported in 1921, and the actual separation of the Railway Budget from the General Budget was approved and implemented in 1924 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Reading (1921–1926), not Lord Chelmsford.

ref: Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947; Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India, Appendices on Governor-Generals and Viceroys.

stem: Consider the following statements regarding constitutional developments during the Viceroyalty of Lord Irwin (1926–1931):
items: Statement-I: The Harcourt Butler Committee (1927) recommended that the relationship of Paramountcy between the British Crown and the Indian Princely States should not be transferred without the Princes' consent to an Indian government in British India responsible to an Indian legislature.

Statement-II: Lord Irwin's Deepavali Declaration of October 1929 stated that the natural issue of India's constitutional progress was the attainment of Dominion Status, without fixing any statutory deadline or immediate timeline for its realization after the proposed Round Table Conference.
prompt: Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?

opts.A: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct and Statement-II explains Statement-I
opts.B: Both Statement-I and Statement-II are correct, but Statement-II does not explain Statement-I
opts.C: Statement-I is correct, but Statement-II is incorrect
opts.D: Statement-I is incorrect, but Statement-II is correct

core: During Lord Irwin's tenure, the Harcourt Butler Committee (1927–29) insulated the Princely States from a future responsible legislature in British India by asserting that Paramountcy rested directly with the British Crown. Separately, Irwin's Deepavali Declaration (October 31, 1929) sought to pacify nationalist agitation against the Simon Commission by affirming Dominion Status as an eventual goal without committing to any timeframe.

exp.why: The Indian States Committee (chaired by Sir Harcourt Butler, appointed in December 1927) examined the relationship between the Paramount Power and the Princely States. It declared that 'Paramountcy must remain paramount' and explicitly recommended that the Princes should not be handed over without their prior agreement to a new government in British India responsible to an Indian legislature.

Lord Irwin's Declaration of October 31, 1929 (Deepavali Declaration), made after consultation with Ramsay MacDonald's Labour government, clarified that implicit in the 1917 Montagu Declaration was that the natural issue of India's constitutional progress was the attainment of Dominion Status, and proposed a Round Table Conference after the publication of the Simon Commission Report. However, it deliberately avoided setting any statutory deadline for granting Dominion Status, nor does this declaration explain the Butler Committee's doctrine on Princely Paramountcy.

ref: Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition, Ch. 6 & 8; Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 21.

stem: With reference to the political and constitutional developments across the Viceroyalties of Lord Linlithgow (1936–1943) and Lord Wavell (1943–1947), consider the following statements:
items: 1. Both the first provincial general elections under the Government of India Act, 1935 and the resignation of the Congress Provincial Ministries in 1939 occurred during the Viceroyalty of Lord Linlithgow.
2. Both the publication of the C. Rajagopalachari Formula and the ensuing Gandhi-Jinnah talks of 1944 took place during the Viceroyalty of Lord Wavell.

3. Both the Royal Indian Navy (RIN) Mutiny and the arrival of the three-member British Cabinet Mission in 1946 occurred during the tenure of Lord Wavell prior to Lord Mountbatten's assumption of office.
prompt: How many of the statements given above are correct?
core: October 1943 marks the chronological boundary between the Viceroyalties of Lord Linlithgow (April 1936 – October 1943) and Field Marshal Lord Wavell (October 1943 – March 1947). Linlithgow presided over the 1937 elections, the 1939 Congress ministry resignations, the August Offer, the Cripps Mission, and the Quit India Movement, whereas Wavell presided over the 1944 C.R. Formula, the 1945 Simla Conference, the 1946 RIN Mutiny, and the 1946 Cabinet Mission.

exp.why: Lord Linlithgow assumed office in April 1936 and served until October 1943 (the longest-serving Viceroy of India). Both the provincial assembly elections held in the winter of 1936–37 under the Government of India Act, 1935 and the resignation of the Congress ministries in October–November 1939 (in protest against Linlithgow's unilateral declaration of India as a belligerent in World War II) occurred during his tenure.

Lord Wavell succeeded Lord Linlithgow in October 1943. In 1944, after Wavell authorized Mahatma Gandhi's release from detention on medical grounds, C. Rajagopalachari published his pamphlet 'The Way Out' (the C.R. Formula) in March–April 1944, leading to the Gandhi-Jinnah talks in Bombay in September 1944—all during Wavell's Viceroyalty.

The Royal Indian Navy (RIN) ratings' revolt broke out in February 1946 and the Cabinet Mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps, and A.V. Alexander) arrived in India in March 1946. Both occurred during Lord Wavell's tenure, a full year before Lord Mountbatten replaced him in March 1947.

ref: Bipan Chandra, India's Struggle for Independence, Ch. 26, 34, 36 & 37; Sumit Sarkar, Modern India 1885–1947.

stem: Consider the following specialized colonial commissions and committees appointed during British rule in India:
items: 1. Herschell Committee on Indian Currency
2. Aitchison Commission on Public Services
3. Whitley Royal Commission on Labour
4. Lee Commission on the Superior Civil Services in India
prompt: What is the correct chronological order of the appointment of the above commissions/committees, starting from the earliest to the latest?
core: Tracking specialized colonial commissions across domains—civil services, currency, and labour—illuminates the administrative evolution of the Raj across successive Viceroyalties: Aitchison Commission (Dufferin, 1886), Herschell Committee (Lansdowne, 1893), Lee Commission (Reading, 1923), and Whitley Commission (Irwin, 1929).

exp.why: The Herschell Committee on Indian Currency was appointed in 1892–1893 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Lansdowne (1888–1894) to examine the fall in the gold value of the silver rupee; following its report in 1893, Indian mints were closed to the unrestricted coinage of silver.

The Aitchison Commission on Public Services (chaired by Sir Charles Umpherston Aitchison) was appointed in 1886 during the Viceroyalty of Lord Dufferin (1884–1888). It recommended abolishing the Statutory Civil Service, reorganizing services into Imperial, Provincial, and Subordinate cadres, and raising the maximum age for ICS entry to 23.

The Royal Commission on Labour in India, chaired by John Henry Whitley (Whitley Commission), was appointed in 1929 (and reported in 1931) during the Viceroyalty of Lord Irwin (1926–1931) to inquire into existing conditions of industrial and plantation labour in India.

The Royal Commission on the Superior Civil Services in India, chaired by Lord Lee of Fareham (Lee Commission), was appointed in 1923 (and submitted its report in 1924) during the Viceroyalty of Lord Reading (1921–1926), recommending the immediate establishment of the Public Service Commission as envisaged in the Government of India Act, 1919 and a 50:50 European-Indian parity in the ICS within 15 years. Thus, the correct chronological sequence is 2 (1886) -> 1 (1893) -> 4 (1923) -> 3 (1929).

ref: Spectrum A Brief History of Modern India, Appendices on Commissions and Committees; Sekhar Bandyopadhyay, From Plassey to Partition.
